Hence, 1→γS→ℰ⁡(γS)1\to\gamma_{S}\to\mathcal{E}(\gamma_{S}), implying ℰ⁡(γS)∈𝒮~S′\mathcal{E}(\gamma_{S})\in\tilde{\mathcal{S}}_{S^{\prime}} for any ℰ∈𝒪S→S′\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime}}. Suppose that S=S′​RS=S^{\prime}R and S′S^{\prime} represents an inaccessible system, meaning its only free operation is the identity (𝒪S′→S′={idS′}\mathcal{O}_{S^{\prime}\to S^{\prime}}=\{\id_{S^{\prime}}\}), and there are no free operations from S′S^{\prime} to any other non-trivial system XX (i.e., 𝒪S′→X=∅\mathcal{O}_{S^{\prime}\to X}=\emptyset for X≠1,S′X\neq 1,S^{\prime}). In this case, the set of free states for S′S^{\prime} is empty because no state ρS′\rho_{S^{\prime}} can be transformed into a different state ρS′′\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}} via a free operation. Now, suppose there somehow exists a free state γS′​R∈𝒮S′​R\gamma_{S^{\prime}R}\in\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}R}. Since the partial trace operation is free, if we take ℰ=TrR\mathcal{E}=\Tr_{R} in Eq. (2), we would obtain TrR⁡[γS′​R]\Tr_{R}[\gamma_{S^{\prime}R}], which cannot be free as 𝒮S′\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}} is empty. Although such a theory is mathematically consistent with the initial three properties of free operations, the existence of a free state γS′​R∈𝒮S′​R\gamma_{S^{\prime}R}\in\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}R} when S′S^{\prime} is inaccessible appears unnatural. Therefore, we will only consider resource theories that adhere to the golden rule as defined in Definition 1.3.

In addition to Definitions 1.1 and 1.3, we consider several properties of the resource theory that facilitate the mathematical treatment.

Definition 1.4 (tensor product structure).

A resource theory has a tensor product structure if

  1. 4.

    relabelling of systems is free

  2. 5.

    if an operation is free, it is completely free: ℰ⊗idR∈𝒪S​R→S′​R\mathcal{E}\otimes\id_{R}\in\mathcal{O}_{SR\to S^{\prime}R} for all ℰ∈𝒪S→S′\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime}} and for all systems RR.

This definition matches that of Ref. [18]. Note that properties 4 and 5 concern composite systems. In particular, property 5, when combined with property 2 in Definition 1.1 indicates that the independent application of free operations in each subsystem is free: ℰ⊗ℱ∈𝒪S1​S2→S1′​S2′\mathcal{E}\otimes\mathcal{F}\in\mathcal{O}_{S_{1}S_{2}\to S_{1}^{\prime}S_{2}^{\prime}} when ℰ∈𝒪S1→S1′\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{S_{1}\to S_{1}^{\prime}} and ℱ∈𝒪S2→S2′\mathcal{F}\in\mathcal{O}_{S_{2}\to S_{2}^{\prime}}. This composition rule for free operations is the most natural condition to demand for composite systems, as it does not necessitate any interaction between the two systems.

However, the tensor product structure is not universally present in resource theories studied in the literature. To see this, let us consider constructions that begin with free states rather than free operations.

Definition 1.5 (resource non-generating (RNG) operations).

Suppose that the set of free states 𝒮S\mathcal{S}_{S} is given for each system SS. An RNG operation is defined as

𝒪S→S′RNG\coloneq{ℰ∈CPTPS→S′|ℰ(γS)∈𝒮S′,∀γS∈𝒮S}.\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime}}^{\mathrm{RNG}}\coloneq\{\mathcal{E}\in\mathrm{CPTP}_{S\to S^{\prime}}\,|\,\mathcal{E}(\gamma_{S})\in\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}},\ \forall\gamma_{S}\in\mathcal{S}_{S}\}. (3)

In other words, 𝒪S→S′RNG\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime}}^{\mathrm{RNG}} encompasses all channels that satisfy the golden rule. The other defining properties of free operations can be verified for RNG operations. Property 1, idS∈𝒪S→SRNG\id_{S}\in\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{RNG}}, holds because idS⁡(γS)∈𝒮S\id_{S}(\gamma_{S})\in\mathcal{S}_{S} for any γS∈𝒮S\gamma_{S}\in\mathcal{S}_{S}. Property 2 is also satisfied: if ℱ∈𝒪S→S′′\mathcal{F}\in\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime\prime}} and ℰ∈𝒪S′′→S′\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{S^{\prime\prime}\to S^{\prime}}, then for any γS∈𝒮S\gamma_{S}\in\mathcal{S}_{S}, ℱ⁡(γS)∈𝒮S′′\mathcal{F}(\gamma_{S})\in\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime\prime}} and thus ℰ⁡(ℱ⁡(γS))∈𝒮S′\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{F}(\gamma_{S}))\in\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}}, by the golden rule. Finally, Property 3 can be made compatible by requiring that the set of free states is such that TrR⁡[γS​R]∈𝒮S\Tr_{R}[\gamma_{SR}]\in\mathcal{S}_{S} for all γS​R∈𝒮S​R\gamma_{SR}\in\mathcal{S}_{SR}.

An instructive example can be found in the resource theory of entanglement.

Example 1.1 (non-entangling operations).

Suppose that each system is defined as a bi-partite composite system, Si=Ai​BiS_{i}=A_{i}B_{i}, where either AiA_{i} or BiB_{i} can be trivial. Define the set of free states 𝒮A|B\mathcal{S}_{A|B} as the set of all separable states SEPA​B\SEP_{AB}, as defined in Definition 1.1. Then, the set of RNG operations 𝒪S→S′RNG\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime}}^{\mathrm{RNG}} is referred to as non-entangling operations.

This definition yields a valid resource theory, studied in works such as Refs. [106, 107]. However, the non-entangling resource theory lacks the tensor product structure because the swap operation is considered free. For any separable state γS=∑ipi​ρA(i)⊗σB(i)\gamma_{S}=\sum_{i}p_{i}\rho^{(i)}_{A}\otimes\sigma^{(i)}_{B}, applying the swap operation results in γS′′=∑ipi​ρB(i)⊗σA(i)\gamma^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}=\sum_{i}p_{i}\rho^{(i)}_{B}\otimes\sigma^{(i)}_{A}, which remains separable. Now, consider the system S1​S2=A1​A2|B1​B2S_{1}S_{2}=A_{1}A_{2}|B_{1}B_{2}. For any (potentially entangled) state ρA1​A2\rho_{A_{1}A_{2}} and σB1​B2\sigma_{B_{1}B_{2}}, the product state ρA1​A2⊗σB1​B2\rho_{A_{1}A_{2}}\otimes\sigma_{B_{1}B_{2}} is separable, with respect to the A1​A2|B1​B2A_{1}A_{2}|B_{1}B_{2} partition. However, the swap operation acting between subsystems A1A_{1} and B1B_{1} yields the output state ρB1​A2⊗σA1​B2\rho_{B_{1}A_{2}}\otimes\sigma_{A_{1}B_{2}}, which is an entangled state for A1​A2|B1​B2A_{1}A_{2}|B_{1}B_{2} partition when either ρ\rho or σ\sigma is entangled itself.

Imposing the tensor product structure therefore excludes certain RNG resource theories like Example 1.1. However, this exclusion does not posit a significant conceptual problem. RNG theories are primarily considered because they represent the most relaxed definition of free operations, which is valuable for proving the impossibility of certain processes across all more restrictive resource theories [107]. Consequently, further constraining the theory by requiring a tensor product structure does not alter the conclusions of such fundamental no-go results.

The maximally relaxed operations consistent with the tensor product structure (Definition 1.4) can also be defined.

Definition 1.6 (completely resource non-generating (CRNG) operations).

Suppose that the set of free states 𝒮S\mathcal{S}_{S} is given for each system SS. CRNG operation is defined as

𝒪S→S′CRNG\coloneq{ℰ∈CPTPS→S′|(ℰ⊗idR)(γS​R)∈𝒮S′​R,∀γS​R∈𝒮S​R,∀R}.\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime}}^{\mathrm{CRNG}}\coloneq\{\mathcal{E}\in\mathrm{CPTP}_{S\to S^{\prime}}\,|\,(\mathcal{E}\otimes\id_{R})(\gamma_{SR})\in\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}R},\ \forall\gamma_{SR}\in\mathcal{S}_{SR},\ \forall R\}. (4)

CRNG for entanglement theory, analogous to Example 1.1, is termed separable operations [108, 109]. Other examples of CRNG operations include Gibbs-preserving operations [110], which correspond to scenarios where the set of free states contains only a single Gibbs state at a fixed temperature. Covariant operations [111, 112] are another example, where the free states are those that remain invariant under operations obeying a particular symmetry. Finally, maximally incoherent operations [113] arise when the free states are density matrices that are diagonal in a fixed basis. In these latter three cases, CRNG operations are also RNG operations.

We now consider a geometric property of the set of free operations

Definition 1.7 (convex resource theories).

A resource theory is convex if the set 𝒪S→S′\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime}} is convex.

Note that if 𝒪S→S′\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime}} is convex, then the set of free states 𝒮S′\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}} is also convex, but the converse is not true. Furthermore, the convexity enables the derivation of universal results that hold for general resource theories [114, 115].22 2 More recently, similar results have also been established for non-convex theories [116].

The majority of resource theories studied are convex. This is partly because the set of free operations can be made convex by allowing the use of classical randomness, i.e. choosing which operation to apply by rolling a die and forgetting about the result. Yet, there are notable counterexamples, such as the theories of non-Gaussianity [117] and randomness [118]. In Chapters 3 and 4, we will always assume the convexity of the theories under consideration.

Subsection 1 Resource monotones

As the name suggests, resource theories are concerned with the quantification and manipulation of resources. However, the axioms presented in Definition 1.1 do not explicitly define what constitutes a resource. Nevertheless, in most resource theories of interest, the definition of free operations is motivated by a specific resource. Broadly speaking, an operation is considered free if its implementation does not require the resource in question. Conversely, the notion of a resource can be inferred from the set of free operations. Specifically, a resource can be understood as a property of a quantum state that cannot be increased by any free operation.

Resource monotones provide a formal framework for this concept.

Definition 1.8 (resource monotones).

A function ℙ:⋃X𝒟X→ℝ\mathbb{P}:\bigcup_{X}\mathcal{D}_{X}\to\mathbb{R} is a resource monotone if

  1. 1.

    ℙ⁡(ρS)≥ℙ⁡(ρS′′)\mathbb{P}(\rho_{S})\geq\mathbb{P}(\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}), whenever ρS→ρS′′\rho_{S}\to\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}} and

  2. 2.

    ℙ⁡(γS)=0\mathbb{P}(\gamma_{S})=0, whenever γS∈𝒮S\gamma_{S}\in\mathcal{S}_{S}

The first condition implies that a resource monotone is non-increasing under free operations, thus respecting the preorder defined by →\to. The second condition is a normalisation, stipulating that free states, which should intuitively possess zero resource, are assigned a value of zero by the monotone. It is important to note that while ℙ⁡(ρS)≥ℙ⁡(ρS′′)\mathbb{P}(\rho_{S})\geq\mathbb{P}(\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}) is a necessary condition for the transformation ρS→ρS′′\rho_{S}\to\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}} to be possible, it is generally not a sufficient condition on its own. Therefore, resource monotones quantify the amount of resource in a state, although this quantification is often incomplete.

For any given resource theory, there can exist multiple resource monotones. If a family of monotones ℛ\mathcal{R} completely characterises the preorder, i.e.

ρ→ρ′⇔ℙ(ρ)≥ℙ(ρ′),∀ℙ∈ℛ,\displaystyle\rho\to\rho^{\prime}\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\mathbb{P}(\rho)\geq\mathbb{P}(\rho^{\prime}),\ \forall\mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{R}, (5)

then ℛ\mathcal{R} is termed a complete set of monotones. Such a family can be constructed in principle [104, 115], although it is hard to actually calculate them, in general. Interestingly, if a single monotone completely characterises all possible state transformations within a resource theory, then the preorder relation →\to defines a total order. This means that for any pair of states (ρ,ρ′)(\rho,\rho^{\prime}), either ρ→ρ′\rho\to\rho^{\prime} or ρ′→ρ\rho^{\prime}\to\rho (or both), and the converse is also true [119].

We now define some properties that can be useful. The first property we consider is the converse of the second condition in Definition 1.8.

Definition 1.9 (faithfulness).

A monotone ℙ\mathbb{P} is faithful if

ℙ(γS)=0⇔γS∈𝒮S.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\gamma_{S})=0\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\gamma_{S}\in\mathcal{S}_{S}. (6)

Thus, the existence of a faithful monotone provides a direct and convenient method to determine whether a given quantum state is a free state or not.

A useful feature of resource monotones is that they provide a means to compare the resource content of states belonging to different systems. We now introduce properties that relate the resourcefulness of composite systems to that of their constituent subsystems. First, observe that for any bipartite state ϱX​Y∈𝒟X​Y\varrho_{XY}\in\mathcal{D}_{XY}, the following inequalities hold:

ℙ⁡(ϱX​Y)≥max⁡{ℙ⁡(TrY​[ϱX​Y]),ℙ⁡(TrX​[ϱX​Y])},\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\varrho_{XY})\geq\max\left\{\mathbb{P}(\Tr_{Y}[\varrho_{XY}]),\mathbb{P}(\Tr_{X}[\varrho_{XY}])\right\}, (7)

This is because the partial trace operation is always considered free. In other words the resource content of a composite system, as quantified by any resource monotone, is always greater than or equal to the resource content of either of its marginal systems. However, the relationship between the resource of the composite system and the sum of the resources of its marginals is not fixed and depends on the specific monotone.

Definition 1.10 (additivity of resource monotones).

A resource monotone ℙ\mathbb{P} is

  • •

    strongly additive if ℙ⁡(ϱX​Y)=ℙ⁡(TrY​[ϱX​Y])+ℙ⁡(TrX​[ϱX​Y])\mathbb{P}(\varrho_{XY})=\mathbb{P}(\Tr_{Y}[\varrho_{XY}])+\mathbb{P}(\Tr_{X}[\varrho_{XY}]), ∀ϱX​Y∈𝒟X​Y\forall\varrho_{XY}\in\mathcal{D}_{XY},

  • •

    strongly super-additive if ℙ⁡(ϱX​Y)≥ℙ⁡(TrY​[ϱX​Y])+ℙ⁡(TrX​[ϱX​Y])\mathbb{P}(\varrho_{XY})\geq\mathbb{P}(\Tr_{Y}[\varrho_{XY}])+\mathbb{P}(\Tr_{X}[\varrho_{XY}]), ∀ϱX​Y∈𝒟X​Y\forall\varrho_{XY}\in\mathcal{D}_{XY},

  • •

    strongly sub-additive, if ℙ⁡(ϱX​Y)≤ℙ⁡(TrY​[ϱX​Y])+ℙ⁡(TrX​[ϱX​Y])\mathbb{P}(\varrho_{XY})\leq\mathbb{P}(\Tr_{Y}[\varrho_{XY}])+\mathbb{P}(\Tr_{X}[\varrho_{XY}]), ∀ϱX​Y∈𝒟X​Y\forall\varrho_{XY}\in\mathcal{D}_{XY}.

More relaxed versions of these conditions can be defined for product states. A resource monotone ℙ\mathbb{P} is

  • •

    additive if ℙ⁡(ρX⊗σY)=ℙ⁡(ρX)+ℙ⁡(σY)\mathbb{P}(\rho_{X}\otimes\sigma_{Y})=\mathbb{P}(\rho_{X})+\mathbb{P}(\sigma_{Y}), ∀ρX∈𝒟X\forall\rho_{X}\in\mathcal{D}_{X}, ∀σY∈𝒟Y\forall\sigma_{Y}\in\mathcal{D}_{Y}.

  • •

    super-additive if ℙ⁡(ρX⊗σY)≥ℙ⁡(ρX)+ℙ⁡(σY)\mathbb{P}(\rho_{X}\otimes\sigma_{Y})\geq\mathbb{P}(\rho_{X})+\mathbb{P}(\sigma_{Y}), ∀ρX∈𝒟X\forall\rho_{X}\in\mathcal{D}_{X}, ∀σY∈𝒟Y\forall\sigma_{Y}\in\mathcal{D}_{Y}.

  • •

    sub-additive, if ℙ⁡(ρX⊗σY)≤ℙ⁡(ρX)+ℙ⁡(σY)\mathbb{P}(\rho_{X}\otimes\sigma_{Y})\leq\mathbb{P}(\rho_{X})+\mathbb{P}(\sigma_{Y}), ∀ρX∈𝒟X\forall\rho_{X}\in\mathcal{D}_{X}, ∀σY∈𝒟Y\forall\sigma_{Y}\in\mathcal{D}_{Y}.

Strong (super-/sub-) additivity always implies (super-/sub-) additivity. In addition, if a monotone is (strongly) additive, it is also (strongly) super-additive and (strongly) sub-additive. A monotone may be neither (strongly) super-additive nor (strongly) sub-additive. For example, a monotone might satisfy ℙ⁡(ρX⊗σY)≥ℙ⁡(ρX)+ℙ⁡(σY)\mathbb{P}(\rho_{X}\otimes\sigma_{Y})\geq\mathbb{P}(\rho_{X})+\mathbb{P}(\sigma_{Y}) for some states ρX,σY\rho_{X},\sigma_{Y}, but for other states ρX′,σY′\rho^{\prime}_{X},\sigma^{\prime}_{Y}, it might satisfy ℙ⁡(ρX′⊗σY′)≤ℙ⁡(ρX′)+ℙ⁡(σY′)\mathbb{P}(\rho^{\prime}_{X}\otimes\sigma^{\prime}_{Y})\leq\mathbb{P}(\rho^{\prime}_{X})+\mathbb{P}(\sigma^{\prime}_{Y}).

These additivity properties place constraints on how resources behave under the composition of physical systems. For instance, the existence of a strongly super-additive monotone is a crucial ingredient in proving the no-go theorem presented in Chapter 4. Nevertheless, the absence of a particular type of additivity property does not directly imply any result, as monotones provide necessary but not sufficient conditions for state transformations to be feasible.

A convenient way to construct resource monotones is by using divergences between quantum states that satisfy the data-processing inequality, as exemplified by Proposition 3.1 and Definition 3.7.

Proposition 1.2 (monotones from data-processing inequality).

Suppose that 𝔻\mathbb{D} is a divergence between quantum states that follows the data-processing inequality and faithfulness. Then

ℙ⁡(ρS)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\rho_{S}) \coloneqinfγS∈𝒮S𝔻(ρS∥γS),\displaystyle\coloneq\inf_{\gamma_{S}\in\mathcal{S}_{S}}\mathbb{D}(\rho_{S}\|\gamma_{S}), (8)
ℙ⁡(ρS)\displaystyle\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\mathbb{P}$}(\rho_{S}) \coloneqinfγS∈𝒮S𝔻(γS∥ρS),\displaystyle\coloneq\inf_{\gamma_{S}\in\mathcal{S}_{S}}\mathbb{D}(\gamma_{S}\|\rho_{S}), (9)

are faithful resource monotones.

Proof.

Consider a free operation ℰ∈𝒪S→S′\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime}} that transforms ρS→ρS′′\rho_{S}\to\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}. Let γ~S∈𝒮S\tilde{\gamma}_{S}\in\mathcal{S}_{S} be a free state that achieves the infimum in the definition of ℙ⁡(ρS)\mathbb{P}(\rho_{S}), such that ℙ(ρS)=𝔻(ρS∥γ~S)\mathbb{P}(\rho_{S})=\mathbb{D}(\rho_{S}\|\tilde{\gamma}_{S}). Then by the data-processing inequality, we have

ℙ(ρS)≥𝔻(ρS∥γ~S)≥𝔻(ℰ(ρS)∥ℰ(γ~S)).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\rho_{S})\geq\mathbb{D}(\rho_{S}\|\tilde{\gamma}_{S})\geq\mathbb{D}(\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S})\|\mathcal{E}(\tilde{\gamma}_{S})). (10)

The golden rule guarantees that ℰ⁡(γ~S)∈𝒮S′\mathcal{E}(\tilde{\gamma}_{S})\in\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}} and thus

𝔻(ℰ(ρS)∥ℰ(γ~S))=𝔻(ρS′′∥ℰ(γ~S))≥infγS′∈𝒮S′𝔻(ρS′′∥γS′),\displaystyle\mathbb{D}(\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S})\|\mathcal{E}(\tilde{\gamma}_{S}))=\mathbb{D}(\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}\|\mathcal{E}(\tilde{\gamma}_{S}))\geq\inf_{\gamma_{S^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}}}\mathbb{D}(\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}\|\gamma_{S^{\prime}}), (11)

which proves the monotonicity of ℙ\mathbb{P}. The faithfulness arises from that of the divergence. The proof for ℙ\mathbb{P} follows the same argument. ∎

Finally, we introduce several examples of resource monotones that will be used in the subsequent chapters of this thesis.

Example 1.2.

When divergences are adapted as resource monotones, we denote them with the symbol RR in place of DD in the original notation.

  • •

    R(ρS)\coloneqinfγS∈𝒮SD(ρS∥γS)R(\rho_{S})\coloneq\inf_{\gamma_{S}\in\mathcal{S}_{S}}D(\rho_{S}\|\gamma_{S}) is the relative entropy of resource.

  • •

    Rmax⁡(min)(ρS)\coloneqinfγS∈𝒮SDmax⁡(min)(ρS∥γS)R_{\max(\min)}(\rho_{S})\coloneq\inf_{\gamma_{S}\in\mathcal{S}_{S}}D_{\max(\min)}(\rho_{S}\|\gamma_{S}) is the max (min) relative entropy of resource.

  • •

    R𝕄(ρS)\coloneqinfγS∈𝒮SD𝕄(ρS∥γS)R_{\mathbb{M}}(\rho_{S})\coloneq\inf_{\gamma_{S}\in\mathcal{S}_{S}}D_{\mathbb{M}}(\rho_{S}\|\gamma_{S}) is the measured relative entropy of resource.

Section 2 Catalysis

Catalysis is a process involving an auxiliary system that returns to its original state at the end. Fascinatingly, the very presence of such an auxiliary system, dubbed a catalyst, often enables transformations that would otherwise be impossible. Within the framework of resource theories and the →\to relation, we can formally define strict catalysis as follows:

Definition 2.1 (strict catalysis).

Strict catalysis is a process defined by a free operation ℰ∈𝒪S​C→S′​C\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{SC\to S^{\prime}C}, initial state ρS∈𝒟S\rho_{S}\in\mathcal{D}_{S}, and a catalyst τC∈𝒟C\tau_{C}\in\mathcal{D}_{C}, such that

ℰ⁡(ρS⊗τC)=ρS′⊗τC.\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})=\rho^{\prime}_{S}\otimes\tau_{C}. (12)

We use the term strict catalysis following Ref. [38] to distinguish this version of catalysis from other more generalised ones. Note that if ρS′′=ℱ⁡(ρS)\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}=\mathcal{F}(\rho_{S}) with some free operation ℱ∈𝒪S→S′\mathcal{F}\in\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime}}, it is always possible to find a catalysis ℰ⁡(ρS⊗τC)=ρS′′⊗τC\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})=\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}\otimes\tau_{C} with any catalyst state τC∈𝒟C\tau_{C}\in\mathcal{D}_{C}. This can be achieved by choosing a free operation ℰ=ℱ⊗idC∈𝒪S​C→S′​C\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{F}\otimes\id_{C}\in\mathcal{O}_{SC\to S^{\prime}C}.

However, only the non-trivial catalysis where ρS↛ρS′′\rho_{S}\not\to\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}} but ρS⊗τC→ρS′⊗τC\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C}\to\rho_{S^{\prime}}\otimes\tau_{C} are usually of interest. If we choose ℰ\mathcal{E} in Eq. (12) to be a tensor product ℰ1⊗ℰ2\mathcal{E}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{E}_{2} with ℰ1∈𝒪S→S′\mathcal{E}_{1}\in\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime}} and ℰ2∈𝒪C→C\mathcal{E}_{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{C\to C} both free, it is impossible to get a non-trivial catalysis. This is because ℰ1​(ρS)=ρS′′\mathcal{E}_{1}(\rho_{S})=\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}} without the help of a catalyst. Therefore, finding a catalysis necessitates the study of composite free operations 𝒪S​C→S′​C\mathcal{O}_{SC\to S^{\prime}C} that are not merely derived from the tensor product structure (Definition 1.4). Another layer of difficulty in studying catalysis arises from the freedom of choosing the system CC and the catalyst state τC\tau_{C}. Practically, these choices must be constrained by considerations regarding the difficulty of preparing and operating on the catalyst state τC\tau_{C}. Nonetheless we are often interested in the ultimate limit of catalysis and would like to learn whether a desired transformation is feasible with the help of some catalyst τC\tau_{C}, regardless of its size or complexity. This goal corresponds to the characterisation of a new binary relation →sc\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sc}} defined as

ρS→scρ′S′⇔∃τC,s.t.ρS⊗τC→ρ′S′⊗τC.\displaystyle\rho_{S}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sc}}\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\exists\tau_{C},\ \text{s.t.}\ \rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C}\to\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}\otimes\tau_{C}. (13)

This new relation →sc\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sc}} again defines a preorder. The reflexivity ρ→scρ\rho\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sc}}\rho follows from ρ→ρ\rho\to\rho. The transitivity can be proven explicitly: if ℰ⁡(ρS⊗τC)=ρS′′⊗τC\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})=\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}\otimes\tau_{C} for some free operation ℰ∈𝒪S​C→S′​C\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{SC\to S^{\prime}C} and ℱ⁡(ρS′′⊗τC′′)=ρS′′′′⊗τC′′\mathcal{F}(\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}\otimes\tau^{\prime}_{C^{\prime}})=\rho^{\prime\prime}_{S^{\prime\prime}}\otimes\tau^{\prime}_{C^{\prime}} for some free operation ℱ∈𝒪S′​C′→S′′​C′\mathcal{F}\in\mathcal{O}_{S^{\prime}C^{\prime}\to S^{\prime\prime}C^{\prime}}, the concatenation gives

[ℱ⊗idC]∘[ℰ⊗idC′]​(ρS⊗τC⊗τC′′)=ρS′′′′⊗τC⊗τC′′.\displaystyle[\mathcal{F}\otimes\id_{C}]\circ[\mathcal{E}\otimes\id_{C^{\prime}}](\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C}\otimes\tau^{\prime}_{C^{\prime}})=\rho^{\prime\prime}_{S^{\prime\prime}}\otimes\tau_{C}\otimes\tau^{\prime}_{C^{\prime}}. (14)

Furthermore, if the preorder defined with →\to relation is convex, i.e. ρ→ρ′\rho\to\rho^{\prime} and ρ→ρ′′\rho\to\rho^{\prime\prime} implies ρ→λ​ρ′+(1−λ)​ρ′′\rho\to\lambda\rho^{\prime}+(1-\lambda)\rho^{\prime\prime} for any λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1], the preorder defined with →sc\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sc}} also inherits the convexity.

Catalysis is also constrained by some of the monotones. ρ→scρ′\rho\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sc}}\rho^{\prime} is equivalent to ρ⊗τ→ρ′⊗τ\rho\otimes\tau\to\rho^{\prime}\otimes\tau for some τ\tau, which in turn implies ℙ⁡(ρ⊗τ)≥ℙ⁡(ρ′⊗τ)\mathbb{P}(\rho\otimes\tau)\geq\mathbb{P}(\rho^{\prime}\otimes\tau) for any resource monotone ℙ\mathbb{P}. If ℙ\mathbb{P} is additive and if ℙ⁡(τ)≠∞\mathbb{P}(\tau)\neq\infty, the monotone for the usual →\to relation also respects the preorder defined by →sc\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sc}}, i.e.

ρ→scρ′⇒ℙ⁡(ρ)≥ℙ⁡(ρ′).\displaystyle\rho\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sc}}\rho^{\prime}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mathbb{P}(\rho)\geq\mathbb{P}(\rho^{\prime}). (15)

In many theories, there are additive resource monotones. Consequently, strict catalysis cannot enhance the resource (as quantified by these monotones), but it can facilitate transitions from states possessing at least the same amount of resource to states with less resource by relaxing other constraints.

Indeed, the advantage of using strict catalysis has been reported in theories of entanglement [40, 120, 121, 41], coherence [122, 123, 124], thermodynamics [125, 126], and magic [127]. Yet, the origin of such advantages is still not understood clearly, despite having the full characterisation of →sc\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sc}} in some cases [41, 125]. The main motivation for the results in Chapters 3 and 4 is this absence of understanding that hinders more systematic studies on catalysis.

Nonetheless, one conceptual connection between catalysis and composite state transformation has been established. Suppose that a multi-copy transformation

ρ⊗nS1⋯Sn→σ⊗nS1⋯Sn\displaystyle\rho^{\otimes n}_{S_{1}\cdots S_{n}}\to\sigma^{\otimes n}_{S_{1}\cdots S_{n}} (16)

with some finite nn is feasible. Then there is a catalyst τC\tau_{C}, such that

ρS⊗τC→σS⊗τC,\displaystyle\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C}\to\sigma_{S}\otimes\tau_{C}, (17)

i.e. ρS→scσS\rho_{S}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sc}}\sigma_{S}, if one can conditionally apply the free operation, conditioned on the state of some ancillary system AA. That is, if one can measure the system AA by some basis {|i⟩​⟨i|}i\{|{i}\rangle\!\langle{i}|\}_{i} and depending on the result, apply a free operation ℰS(i)∈𝒪S→S′\mathcal{E}^{(i)}_{S}\in\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime}}, and then forget the measurement outcome ii. The necessity of the conditional free operation would become clear after we explain the protocol below.

This state τ\tau is called the Duan state [43], and it is a mixture of (n−1)(n-1) copies of initial and final states

τ=1n∑i=1nρS2⋯Si⊗i−1⊗σSi+1⋯Sn⊗n−i⊗|i⟩⟨i|A.\displaystyle\tau=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\rho^{\otimes i-1}_{S_{2}\cdots S_{i}}\otimes\sigma^{\otimes n-i}_{S_{i+1}\cdots S_{n}}\otimes|{i}\rangle\!\langle{i}|_{A}. (18)

Here, system AA represents the classical flag, where |i⟩​⟨i|A→|j⟩​⟨j|A|{i}\rangle\!\langle{i}|_{A}\to|{j}\rangle\!\langle{j}|_{A} for any i,ji,j by mere relabelling. The free operation is as follows:

  1. 1.

    measure AA system in a basis {|i⟩​⟨i|A}i\{|{i}\rangle\!\langle{i}|_{A}\}_{i}; when the outcome is nn, apply a free operation that achieves the transformation in Eq. (16) to ρS1⊗τ\rho_{S_{1}}\otimes\tau, which yields a state

    1n∑i=1n−1ρS1⋯Si⊗i⊗σSi+1⋯Sn⊗n−i⊗|i⟩⟨i|A+σS1⋯Sn⊗n⊗|n⟩⟨n|A,\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\rho^{\otimes i}_{S_{1}\cdots S_{i}}\otimes\sigma^{\otimes n-i}_{S_{i+1}\cdots S_{n}}\otimes|{i}\rangle\!\langle{i}|_{A}+\sigma^{\otimes n}_{S_{1}\cdots S_{n}}\otimes|{n}\rangle\!\langle{n}|_{A}, (19)
  2. 2.

    apply permutation Si→Si+1S_{i}\to S_{i+1} and Sn→S1S_{n}\to S_{1} to obtain

    1n∑i=1n−1σS1⊗ρS2⋯Si+1⊗i⊗σSi+2⋯Sn⊗n−i−1⊗|i⟩⟨i|A+σS1⋯Sn⊗n⊗|n⟩⟨n|A,\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\sigma_{S_{1}}\otimes\rho^{\otimes i}_{S_{2}\cdots S_{i+1}}\otimes\sigma^{\otimes n-i-1}_{S_{i+2}\cdots S_{n}}\otimes|{i}\rangle\!\langle{i}|_{A}+\sigma^{\otimes n}_{S_{1}\cdots S_{n}}\otimes|{n}\rangle\!\langle{n}|_{A}, (20)
  3. 3.

    apply relabelling |i⟩​⟨i|A→|i+1⟩​⟨i+1|A|{i}\rangle\!\langle{i}|_{A}\to|{i+1}\rangle\!\langle{i+1}|_{A} and |n⟩​⟨n|A→|1⟩​⟨1|A|{n}\rangle\!\langle{n}|_{A}\to|{1}\rangle\!\langle{1}|_{A}, which yields σS1⊗τC\sigma_{S_{1}}\otimes\tau_{C}, as desired.

Essentially, the catalyst allows us to ‘conceal’ multiple copies of the initial and final states within it. However, it is known that the converse is not always true [45], at least for exact state transformation cases. This also reveals that the power of catalytic processes is no less powerful than the alternative composite approaches that rely on the collective processing of multiple copies.

In the beginning, we loosely defined catalysis to be the process where a catalyst returns to its original state. For strict catalysis, this return is interpreted strictly; that is, it must be uncorrelated to the system of interest as in the beginning of the process. Sometimes, this strict recovery may not be necessary. We define another type of catalysis.

Definition 2.2 (correlated catalysis).

Correlated catalysis is a process defined by a free operation ℰ∈𝒪S​C→S′​C\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{SC\to S^{\prime}C}, initial state ρS∈𝒟S\rho_{S}\in\mathcal{D}_{S}, and a catalyst τC∈𝒟C\tau_{C}\in\mathcal{D}_{C}, such that

ℰ⁡(ρS⊗τC)=ϱS′​C,TrS′⁡[ϱS′​C]=τC,\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})=\varrho_{S^{\prime}C},\quad\Tr_{S^{\prime}}[\varrho_{S^{\prime}C}]=\tau_{C}, (21)

which achieves the transformation ρS→ccρS′′​\coloneq​TrC​[ϱS′​C]\rho_{S}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{cc}}\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}\coloneq\Tr_{C}[\varrho_{S^{\prime}C}].

Note that in Eq. (21), only the reduced state of the catalyst needs to be recovered, but it must be recovered exactly without any error. The binary relation →cc\xrightarrow{\mathrm{cc}} corresponding to the correlated catalytic transformation is defined analogously to →sc\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sc}}. Despite the correlation established between SS and CC, this catalyst can be reused for the same process when an identical but independent copy of the initial state is given. Observe that

(ℰS¯​C⊗idS′)​(ρS¯⊗ϱS′​C)=ςS′​S¯′​C,\displaystyle(\mathcal{E}_{\bar{S}C}\otimes\id_{S^{\prime}})(\rho_{\bar{S}}\otimes\varrho_{S^{\prime}C})=\varsigma_{S^{\prime}\bar{S}^{\prime}C}, (22)

where TrS′​S¯′⁡[ςS′​S¯′​C]=τC\Tr_{S^{\prime}\bar{S}^{\prime}}[\varsigma_{S^{\prime}\bar{S}^{\prime}C}]=\tau_{C} and TrS¯′​C⁡[ςS′​S¯′​C]=TrS′​C⁡[ςS′​S¯′​C]\Tr_{\bar{S}^{\prime}C}[\varsigma_{S^{\prime}\bar{S}^{\prime}C}]=\Tr_{S^{\prime}C}[\varsigma_{S^{\prime}\bar{S}^{\prime}C}]. Yet, the correlation can be problematic if the system S′S^{\prime} or S¯′\bar{S}^{\prime} are used afterwards. As a result of this accumulated correlation, manipulating system S′S^{\prime} might affect both S¯′\bar{S}^{\prime} and CC, potentially spoiling the desired final state in the other system or the catalyst. While this correlation can be made arbitrarily small, it typically requires a catalyst with diverging resources [128].

By definition, a strict catalysis is also a correlated catalysis, and ρ→scρ′\rho\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sc}}\rho^{\prime} implies ρ→ccρ′\rho\xrightarrow{\mathrm{cc}}\rho^{\prime}. Hence, correlated catalysis is usually adopted to consider the maximal advantage that can be obtained from catalysis. In Chapter 4, we mostly work with correlated catalyses, because if the no-go theorems can be established there, they are automatically valid for weaker definitions such as strict catalysis.

Correlated catalysis is typically far more powerful than its strict counterpart. First, it imposes strong constraints on all relevant monotones, because it is always possible to have a transformation [38]

ϱS1​S2→ccTrS2⁡[ϱS1​S2]⊗TrS1⁡[ϱS1​S2].\displaystyle\varrho_{S_{1}S_{2}}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{cc}}\Tr_{S_{2}}\left[\varrho_{S_{1}S_{2}}\right]\otimes\Tr_{S_{1}}\left[\varrho_{S_{1}S_{2}}\right]. (23)

To see this, let the catalyst state in system S¯2\bar{S}_{2} have the same density matrix as TrS1⁡[ϱS1​S2]\Tr_{S_{1}}[\varrho_{S_{1}S_{2}}]. Then, a simple swap operation between S2S_{2} and S¯2\bar{S}_{2} outputs a state ςS1​S2​S¯2=ϱS1​S¯2⊗TrS1⁡[ϱS1​S2]\varsigma_{S_{1}S_{2}\bar{S}_{2}}=\varrho_{S_{1}\bar{S}_{2}}\otimes\Tr_{S_{1}}[\varrho_{S_{1}S_{2}}], such that TrS¯2⁡[ςS1​S2​S¯2]=TrS2⁡[ϱS1​S2]⊗TrS1⁡[ϱS1​S2]\Tr_{\bar{S}_{2}}[\varsigma_{S_{1}S_{2}\bar{S}_{2}}]=\Tr_{S_{2}}[\varrho_{S_{1}S_{2}}]\otimes\Tr_{S_{1}}[\varrho_{S_{1}S_{2}}] and TrS1​S2⁡[ςS1​S2​S¯2]=TrS1⁡[ϱS1​S¯2]\Tr_{S_{1}S_{2}}[\varsigma_{S_{1}S_{2}\bar{S}_{2}}]=\Tr_{S_{1}}[\varrho_{S_{1}\bar{S}_{2}}], satisfying Definition 2.2. Therefore, it must always be true that

ℙ⁡(ϱS1​S2)≥ℙ⁡(TrS2⁡[ϱS1​S2]⊗TrS1⁡[ϱS1​S2]),\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\varrho_{S_{1}S_{2}})\geq\mathbb{P}\left(\Tr_{S_{2}}\left[\varrho_{S_{1}S_{2}}\right]\otimes\Tr_{S_{1}}\left[\varrho_{S_{1}S_{2}}\right]\right), (24)

for ℙ\mathbb{P} to be a monotone for correlated catalytic transformations.

A similar connection to multi-copy can also be established for correlated catalysis. In fact, correlated catalysis allows a broader class of multi-copy transformation, namely the approximate multi-copy transformation:

ρ⊗nS1⋯Sn→ςS1⋯Sn∼ϵσ⊗nS1⋯Sn,\displaystyle\rho^{\otimes n}_{S_{1}\cdots S_{n}}\to\varsigma_{S_{1}\cdots S_{n}}\overset{\epsilon}{\sim}\sigma^{\otimes n}_{S_{1}\cdots S_{n}}, (25)

where the symbol ∼ϵ\overset{\epsilon}{\sim} indicates that two operators have a trace distance smaller than ϵ\epsilon. Then, the transformation ρ→ccσϵ\rho\xrightarrow{\mathrm{cc}}\sigma^{\epsilon} for some σϵ​∼ϵ​σ\sigma^{\epsilon}\overset{\epsilon}{\sim}\sigma can be achieved when the permutation between identical systems and classical conditioning are free. The catalyst state needed is similar to the Duan state Eq. (18), with multiple copies of the final state σ⊗n−iSi+1⋯Sn\sigma^{\otimes n-i}_{S_{i+1}\cdots S_{n}} replaced by TrS1⋯Si[ςS1⋯Sn]\Tr_{S_{1}\cdots S_{i}}[\varsigma_{S_{1}\cdots S_{n}}] [129]. A few remarks are in order. Firstly, although this process implements an approximate multi-copy transformation, the catalyst reduced state is always recovered exactly, without any approximation. Secondly, approximate multi-copy transformations are qualitatively different from their exact counterparts; even when ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0, the approximate transformation reaches a vastly larger set of states [130, 131, 132, 133]. Furthermore, when nn can be arbitrarily large, the setting becomes that of the usual approximate asymptotic transformation. The equivalence between correlated catalysis and asymptotic has been demonstrated in many resource theories [133, 134, 135], which leads to the characterisation of →cc\xrightarrow{\mathrm{cc}} with a single complete monotone [136, 137, 138, 132, 129, 139], usually given by the relative entropy of resource in Example 1.2.

Despite all such positive results accumulated for catalytic processes, the framework has some serious issues to be used in practice. First, the preparation of catalysts is typically hard, e.g. when the Duan state construction Eq. (18) is used, which requires a catalyst system whose size is comparable to multiple copies of the original system and whose state already includes multiple copies of the desired final state. Another problem is the fragility of catalysis in the presence of noise due to its fine-tuned nature. We discuss and (partially) resolve these problems in Chapters 3 and 4.

Chapter 3 Overcoming Markovianity in thermal processes using catalysts

In this chapter, we investigate catalytic processes in resource theories modelling quantum thermodynamics. In particular, we focus on the theories with certain degree of Markovian restrictions. As described in Definition 2.2, Markovianity is closely related to the decomposability of the operations. Leveraging the decomposability, we identify the memory effect that catalysis provides. Furthermore, we prove that catalysis completely negates the additional restrictions imposed by Markovianity in thermodynamic resource theories, showcasing the power of catalysts as a non-Markovian auxiliary.

My original results in this section include Theorems 2.1, 3.1, 3.2 and Figures 2, 4, 5, 6, 7.

Section 1 Background: a hierarchy of thermodynamic resource theories

There are several classes of thermal processes studied in thermodynamic resource theories. These classes form a hierarchy: smaller classes are strictly contained within larger ones. Because choosing a different class in this hierarchy yields distinct descriptions of thermodynamic processes, it has been an active open problem whether there exists a setting in which all classes become equivalent. In the following subsections, the catalytic setting is considered as a potential candidate. This subsection gives a brief introduction to these classes of thermal processes, summarising results from the literature; it contains no original results.

Subsection 1 Free operations

Thermodynamic resource theories, also known as resource theories of athermality, are motivated by the typical thermodynamic settings, where the system of interest is embedded in a thermal environment with a single fixed temperature. In these settings, a natural free operation is the full thermalisation channel mapping the system to a thermal equilibrium state. For quantum systems with Hamiltonian HSH_{S}, the thermal equilibrium state at the inverse temperature β\beta is the Gibbs state

γSβ​\coloneq​1ZS​e−β​HS,\displaystyle\gamma^{\beta}_{S}\coloneq\frac{1}{Z_{S}}e^{-\beta H_{S}}, (1)

where the partition function ZS​\coloneq​Tr⁡[e−β​HS]Z_{S}\coloneq\Tr[e^{-\beta H_{S}}].

Gibbs states are special for several reasons. Firstly, when the entropy is defined as the von Neumann entropy S⁡(ρ)​\coloneq−Tr⁡[ρ​log⁡ρ]S(\rho)\coloneq-\Tr[\rho\log\rho], the free energy

F⁡(ρS)​\coloneq​Tr⁡[ρS​HS]−β−1​S​(ρS),\displaystyle F(\rho_{S})\coloneq\Tr[\rho_{S}H_{S}]-\beta^{-1}S(\rho_{S}), (2)

is minimised when ρS=γSβ\rho_{S}=\gamma^{\beta}_{S}. Secondly, Gibbs states can be uniquely identified by a few physical axioms. Passive states are defined as the states from which no energy can be extracted unitarily; if nn copies of the state ρ⊗n\rho^{\otimes n} is also passive for all nn, the state ρ\rho is completely passive. Gibbs states of inverse temperature 0≤β≤∞0\leq\beta\leq\infty are the only states that are completely passive [140]. Alternatively, Gibbs states are the only passive states that are structurally stable and consistent, i.e. small perturbations in Hamiltonians only give small perturbations in Gibbs states, and Gibbs states of a composite system is the tensor product of Gibbs states of each subsystem [141].

Therefore, Gibbs state, with respect to the environment inverse temperature (or ambient inverse temperature) β\beta, is the most natural choice for a free state. Indeed, if we assume that the full thermalisation is a free operation, Gibbs state is always the free state by Definition 1.2. Resource theories of athermality are then a family of theories sharing the same set of free states 𝒮S={γSβ}\mathcal{S}_{S}=\{\gamma^{\beta}_{S}\}, but with different free operations. We introduce five notable sets of thermodynamic free operations that form a hierarchy. For simplicity, we only discuss operations from SS to itself, with a fixed ambient inverse temperature β\beta and a fixed Hamiltonian HSH_{S}.

Definition 1.1 (Gibbs-preserving operations (GP) [110]).

Given a system SS and its Hamiltonian HSH_{S}, the set of Gibbs-preserving operations from SS to itself is defined as

𝒪S→SGP​\coloneq​{ℰ∈CPTPS→S|ℰ⁡(γSβ)=γSβ}.\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{GP}}\coloneq\left\{\mathcal{E}\in\mathrm{CPTP}_{S\to S}\,|\,\mathcal{E}(\gamma^{\beta}_{S})=\gamma^{\beta}_{S}\right\}. (3)

This set is by definition an RNG and in fact also a CRNG; see Definitions 1.5 and 1.6. The measure of resourcefulness most familiar to thermodynamicsts is the non-equilibrium free energy defined as in Eq. (2) [142, 143]. Interestingly, it is easy to show that [144] non-equilibrium free energy corresponds directly to the relative entropy of resource (Example 1.2), a resource measure popular in the resource theory community. The two are related by the factor β−1\beta^{-1} as

R⁡(ρS)=β−1​F​(ρS)−β−1​F​(γSβ)​\eqcolon​β−1​Δ​F​(ρS).\displaystyle R(\rho_{S})=\beta^{-1}F(\rho_{S})-\beta^{-1}F(\gamma^{\beta}_{S})\eqcolon\beta^{-1}\Delta F(\rho_{S}). (4)

Therefore, Δ​F\Delta F is monotonic under GP, and this monotonicity extends to all subsets of GP that will be introduced below.

GP, however, can be too general to capture all thermodynamic restrictions. In fact, any (C)RNG free operations with respect to singleton free state sets can be regarded as GP with some temperature and Hamiltonian, as β​HS=log⁡(γSβ)\beta H_{S}=\log(\gbs_{S}).

To capture another aspect of thermodynamics, let us consider coherence between different energy levels. The resource theory of asymmetry with respect to U(1) group generated by the Hamiltonian precisely tackles that problem. There, the set of free operations are covariant operations [111]

𝒪S→SCOV\coloneq{ℰ∈CPTPS→S|ℰ(e−i​θ​HS(⋅)ei​θ​HS)=e−i​θ​HSℰ(⋅)ei​θ​HS,∀θ∈ℝ}.\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{COV}}\coloneq\left\{\mathcal{E}\in\mathrm{CPTP}_{S\to S}\,|\,\mathcal{E}(e^{-i\theta H_{S}}(\cdot)e^{i\theta H_{S}})=e^{-i\theta H_{S}}\mathcal{E}(\cdot)e^{i\theta H_{S}},\quad\forall\theta\in\mathbb{R}\right\}. (5)

Covariant operations also correspond to the CRNG of symmetric states

𝒟SSYM\coloneq{ρS∈𝒟S|U(θ)ρSU(θ)†=ρS,∀θ∈ℝ}.\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{S}^{\mathrm{SYM}}\coloneq\left\{\rho_{S}\in\mathcal{D}_{S}\,|\,U(\theta)\rho_{S}U(\theta)^{\dagger}=\rho_{S},\ \forall\theta\in\mathbb{R}\right\}. (6)

For the U(1) group with the representation U⁡(θ)=e−i​θ​HSU(\theta)=e^{-i\theta H_{S}}, Eq. (6) is equivalent to 𝒟SSYM​\coloneq​{ρS∈𝒟S|[ρS,HS]=0}\mathcal{D}_{S}^{\mathrm{SYM}}\coloneq\{\rho_{S}\in\mathcal{D}_{S}\,|\,[\rho_{S},H_{S}]=0\}.

Covariant operations also have an operational meaning: 𝒪S→SCOV\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{COV}} is exactly the set of operations that can be written with a dilation

ℰ(⋅)=TrR[U(⋅⊗γR)U†],\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\cdot)=\Tr_{R}[U(\cdot\otimes\gamma_{R})U^{\dagger}], (7)

with some system RR with a Hamiltonian HRH_{R}, free ancilla state γR∈𝒮R\gamma_{R}\in\mathcal{S}_{R}, and energy-preserving unitary UU, satisfying

[U,HS⊗𝟙ℝ+𝟙𝕊⊗ℍℝ]=𝟘.\displaystyle[U,H_{S}\otimes\mathmybb{1}_{R}+\mathmybb{1}_{S}\otimes H_{R}]=0. (8)

Eq. (8) has a physical interpretation that UU strictly preserves the energy of any energy eigenstate of S​RSR. This also implies that the energy statistics of the S​RSR state before and after the unitary are identical. Note that the energy of each subsystem can change after an energy-preserving unitary.

To incorporate this global energy-preserving behaviour, we impose covariance (sometimes called time-translation symmetry), Eq. (5), in addition to the existing Gibbs-preserving condition.

Definition 1.2 (Gibbs-preserving covariant operations (GPC) [145, 146]).

Gibbs-preserving covariant operations from SS to itself is defined as

𝒪S→SGPC​\coloneq​𝒪S→SGP∩𝒪S→SCOV.\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{GPC}}\coloneq\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{GP}}\cap\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{COV}}. (9)

This set is also known as enhanced thermal operations or thermal processes. Note that 𝒪S→SGPC\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{GPC}} is a strict subset of 𝒪S→SGP\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{GP}} in general: a simple example of a GP that creates asymmetric state from a symmetric state is found in Ref. [110]. In fact, there exist GP channels that can be implemented with GPC channels only with the injection of infinite coherence auxiliaries [147].

Both GP and GPC are defined axiomatically; because the axioms only concern mathematical structure of the channels, the implementation of them are not considered. The remaining three sets of operations are defined bottom-up: these are the channels that can be constructed from implementation recipes. We first introduce the one defined as the set of operations with free dilations, similar to Eq. (7). However, the set of free states for the theory of athermality is a singleton including only the Gibbs state; hence, the free ancilla is also fixed to be the Gibbs state γRβ\gamma^{\beta}_{R}.

Definition 1.3 (thermal operations (TO) [148]).

Consider a set of channels ℰ\mathcal{E} satisfying

ℰ(⋅)=TrR[U(⋅⊗γRβ)U†],\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\cdot)=\Tr_{R}\left[U\left(\cdot\otimes\gamma^{\beta}_{R}\right)U^{\dagger}\right], (10)

for some system RR with some Hamiltonian HRH_{R} and some energy-preserving unitary UU with the condition Eq. (8). Thermal operations from SS to itself 𝒪S→STO\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{TO}} is defined as the closure of this set.

In some literature, the set without the closure is denoted TO and the closure of it is separately named as CTO, but in this thesis, we always define TO following Definition 1.3.

TO is a subset of GPC, as γRβ∈𝒟RSYM\gamma^{\beta}_{R}\in\mathcal{D}_{R}^{\mathrm{SYM}} and thus channel in the form Eq. (10) is a covariant channel. The converse is true when SS is a qubit system [145], but not in general: for dimension larger than 2, there exists a GPC that is not a TO; in fact there even exists a state transformation that is feasible in GPC but not in TO [149].

Although TO is operationally motivated, implementing arbitrary energy-preserving unitaries between system and (potentially infinitely large) environment is not realistic [150]. Another hindrance arises from the structure of the theoretical development, which tends to focus on the possibility of state transformations, instead of providing a construction of concrete, simple heat baths together with corresponding interaction Hamiltonians underlying the process.11 1 See Refs. [151, 152, 153] for rare examples where the concrete construction of TO has been investigated. As a result, even when a transformation is known to be possible, it remains non-trivial to construct the protocol that implements it, obscuring the dynamical description of the process. Hence, restrictions of TO inspired by more experimentally accessible setups have been defined.

Definition 1.4 (elementary thermal operations (ETO) [154]).

Let 𝒪S→STO2\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{TO}_{2}} be a subset of 𝒪S→STO\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{TO}} that can be written with the dilation Eq. (10), where the energy-preserving unitary UU acts non-trivially on at most two energy eigenstates of SS, i.e. there exists an energy-eigenbasis {|i⟩S}S\{|{i}\rangle_{S}\}_{S}, such that

⟨i|S​U|i⟩S=𝟙ℝ,\displaystyle\langle{i}|_{S}U|{i}\rangle_{S}=\mathmybb{1}_{R}, (11)

for all ii except at most two. Then, 𝒪S→SETO\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{ETO}} is defined as the closed convex hull of all concatenations of channels in 𝒪S→STO2\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{TO}_{2}}.

ETO by definition has a decomposition that offers a natural way to prescribe a process to the experimenter. Furthermore, any extreme point of 𝒪S→STO2\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{TO}_{2}} can be realised with a single bosonic mode bath and the intensity-dependent Jaynes-Cummings interaction [155]. With the addition of a pure dephasing operation, any 𝒪S→STO2\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{TO}_{2}} can be implemented [151]. A good portion of these operations can also be achieved via more experiment-friendly models [154, 151], such as the collision model [156] or the Jaynes-Cummings model [157]. Compared to the baths proposed in Refs. [158, 152], using a single-mode bath for each step is much more feasible.

Since 𝒪S→STO\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{TO}} is a set closed under concatenation and convex combination, ETO is a subset of TO; in fact it is a strict subset, i.e. 𝒪S→SETO​\subsetneq​𝒪S→STO\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{ETO}}\subsetneq\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{TO}} except when SS is a qubit system or β=0\beta=0 [154]. This is rather surprising, given the universality achieved in nn-qubit unitaries into two-qubit ones [159], nn-level unitaries into two-level ones [160], or nn-mode Gaussian unitaries into two-mode ones [160, 161].22 2 We note that another type of unexpected non-universality has been observed: when kk-local and symmetric operations are composed together, some of the global symmetric operations cannot be achieved [162, 163, 164, 165]. Moreover, a seemingly much easier task of decomposing TO into series of TOd-1—defined as a subset of TO involving at most all but one system levels at a time—is also shown to be impossible [166].

Another realistic restriction is requiring Markovianity of the bath. Similarly to ETO, Markovianity introduces the decomposition, providing a pathway to implement an operation with smaller and easier steps. In particular, when the full Markovianity is imposed, these steps can be infinitesimally small and continuous.

Definition 1.5 (Markovian thermal operations (MTO) [167]).

A channel ℰ∈𝒪S→STO\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{TO}} is an MTO if it is Markovian in the sense of Definition 2.2, i.e. if it can be written as a concatenation of TO channels that are ϵ\epsilon-close to the identity channel with arbitrarily small ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

This is equivalent to the condition that there exists a Markovian master equation, such that the evolution from t=0t=0 to t=Tt=T yields the channel ℰ\mathcal{E}, while for any time slices 0≤t1≤t2≤T0\leq t_{1}\leq t_{2}\leq T, the evolution from t=t1t=t_{1} to t=t2t=t_{2} is TO. Note that Refs. [168, 169] first considered such Markovian restrictions, but they considered a Markovian version of GPC not TO.

By definition, MTO is a subset of TO, and it is indeed a strict subset even for qubit systems [168]. The simplest example is the cooling of a qubit excited state |1⟩​⟨1|S|{1}\rangle\!\langle{1}|_{S}. With TO, it is known that the transformation |1⟩​⟨1|S→|0⟩​⟨0|S|{1}\rangle\!\langle{1}|_{S}\to|{0}\rangle\!\langle{0}|_{S} is possible even when the ambient inverse temperature β<∞\beta<\infty, i.e. a complete cooling is attainable. When Markovianity is imposed, |1⟩​⟨1|S|{1}\rangle\!\langle{1}|_{S} must be evolved into |0⟩​⟨0|S|{0}\rangle\!\langle{0}|_{S} continuously. Since TO is covariant, the state always remain incoherent, i.e. it is described by a one-parameter evolution of ρ⁡(t)=p⁡(t)​|1⟩​⟨1|S+(1−p⁡(t))|0⟩​⟨0|S\rho(t)=p(t)|{1}\rangle\!\langle{1}|_{S}+(1-p(t))|{0}\rangle\!\langle{0}|_{S} with p⁡(0)=1p(0)=1 and p⁡(T)=0p(T)=0. However, as soon as ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) reaches the Gibbs state, it cannot evolve to any other state via TO. Hence, if γSβ≠|0⟩​⟨0|S\gamma^{\beta}_{S}\neq|{0}\rangle\!\langle{0}|_{S}, i.e. if β<∞\beta<\infty, MTO cannot completely cool down an excited state.

We summarise the hierarchy among these free operations; see also Figure 1.

Remark 1.1 (Hierarchies of thermodynamic resource theories).

Suppose that SS has dimension higher than two. Then,

𝒪S→SMTO,𝒪S→SETO​\subsetneq​𝒪S→STO​\subsetneq​𝒪S→SGPC​\subsetneq​𝒪S→SGP.\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{MTO}},\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{ETO}}\subsetneq\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{TO}}\subsetneq\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{GPC}}\subsetneq\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{GP}}. (12)

Subsection 2 State transformations

A hierarchy can also be formed at the level of state transformations. The inclusion relations in Remark 1.1 would again hold for state transformations, yet the strict inclusions may not necessarily hold. For example, when the initial states for the state transformations are restricted, the gap between different free operations may not manifest in the set of reachable final states.

Hence, we restrict the initial states to be symmetric states in 𝒟SSYM\mathcal{D}_{S}^{\mathrm{SYM}}. This choice brings a huge simplification. With the exception of the largest set GP, all free operations are covariant; that is, if the initial state is in 𝒟SSYM\mathcal{D}_{S}^{\mathrm{SYM}}, the final state must also be in 𝒟SSYM\mathcal{D}_{S}^{\mathrm{SYM}}. Thus both initial and final states are block-diagonal in the energy-eigenbasis, with each block corresponding to degenerate-energy subspaces. It is therefore more convenient to represent states not as d×dd\times d-dimensional density matrices, but as dd-dimensional vectors whose elements are the energy-eigenvalues of those density matrices.

Definition 1.6 (population vectors).

Suppose that ρS∈𝒟SSYM\rho_{S}\in\mathcal{D}_{S}^{\mathrm{SYM}}, i.e. [ρS,HS]=0[\rho_{S},H_{S}]=0. Then, there exists an energy-eigenbasis {|i⟩S}i\{|{i}\rangle_{S}\}_{i}, such that H​|i⟩S=Ei​|i⟩SH|{i}\rangle_{S}=E_{i}|{i}\rangle_{S} and ρS​|i⟩S=pi​|i⟩S\rho_{S}|{i}\rangle_{S}=p_{i}|{i}\rangle_{S} for all ii. The ordering is given by Ei≤EjE_{i}\leq E_{j} whenever i≤ji\leq j. We define a population vector corresponding to ρS\rho_{S} as 𝐩\mathbf{p}, where its ithi_{\text{th}} element is defined as (𝐩)i=pi(\mathbf{p})_{i}=p_{i}. We denote a set of all dd-dimensional probability vectors as 𝒱d\mathcal{V}_{d}.

There might exist multiple density matrices corresponding to one population vector 𝐩\mathbf{p} when the Hamiltonian has degeneracy. However, these density matrices are connected by energy-preserving unitary operations, because they all have the same energy eigenvalues. Since energy-preserving unitary is free in any set of free operations we consider, all density matrices with the same population vector are fully equivalent in the preorder given by thermodynamic resource theories. This means that we can define the preorder 𝐩→𝐪\mathbf{p}\to\mathbf{q} using the one defined with the corresponding density matrices ρS→ρS′\rho_{S}\to\rho^{\prime}_{S} and vice versa. We sometimes denote different binary relations stemming from the set of free operations XX as →𝑋\xrightarrow{X}.

Since state transformations between symmetric states are of interest, we define the set of population vectors that can be reached from a given initial population vectors.

Definition 1.7 (set of reachable states).

The set of reachable states from 𝐩\mathbf{p} via some class of operation XX is defined as

𝒯X​(𝐩)​\coloneq​{𝐪|𝐩→𝑋𝐪},X=GPC,TO,ETO,MTO.\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{X}(\mathbf{p})\coloneq\left\{\mathbf{q}\,|\,\mathbf{p}\xrightarrow{X}\mathbf{q}\right\},\quad X=\mathrm{GPC},\mathrm{TO},\mathrm{ETO},\mathrm{MTO}. (13)

We denote the extreme points of this set as extr⁡[𝒯X​(𝐩)]\extr[\mathcal{T}_{X}(\mathbf{p})].

Analogously to the mapping of density matrices into population vectors, any GPC channel can be represented as a d×dd\times d-dimensional matrix that preserves the Gibbs population vector and the sum of probability vector elements.

Definition 1.8 (Gibbs-stochastic matrices).

A d×dd\times d-dimensional matrix EE is Gibbs-stochastic, if

𝐞\transp​E=𝐞\transp,E​γβ=γβ,\displaystyle\mathbf{e}^{\transp}E=\mathbf{e}^{\transp},\quad E\gamma^{\beta}=\gamma^{\beta}, (14)

for the uniformly distributed probability vector 𝐞=(1d,⋯,1d)\mathbf{e}=(\frac{1}{d},\cdots,\frac{1}{d}) and the population vector γβ\gamma^{\beta} corresponding to the Gibbs state γSβ\gamma^{\beta}_{S}.

The set of Gibbs-stochastic matrices is well-characterised with explicit recipes to find all extreme points, using the techniques developed for transportation matrices [170].

Now we establish the correspondence between GPC and TO channels with Gibbs-stochastic matrices.

Proposition 1.1 (Ref. [148], Theorems 5 and 6).

Suppose that ℰ∈𝒪S→SGPC\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{GPC}} for dd-dimensional system SS. Then there exists a d×dd\times d-dimensional Gibbs-stochastic matrix EE, such that

ℰ(ρS)=ρS′⇔E𝐩=𝐪,\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S})=\rho^{\prime}_{S}\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad E\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{q}, (15)

for any ρS,ρS′∈𝒟SSYM\rho_{S},\rho^{\prime}_{S}\in\mathcal{D}_{S}^{\mathrm{SYM}}, where 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐪\mathbf{q} are population vectors corresponding to ρS\rho_{S} and ρS′\rho^{\prime}_{S}, respectively.

Furthermore, for any Gibbs-stochastic matrix EE, there exists a TO channel ℰ∈𝒪S→STO\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{TO}}, satisfying Eq. (15).

This proposition also implies that 𝒯TO​(𝐩)=𝒯GPC​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}}(\mathbf{p})=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{GPC}}(\mathbf{p}) for all population vectors 𝐩∈𝒱d\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{V}_{d}.

For ETO and MTO, a special class of Gibbs-stochastic matrices assumes such a role. To construct them, we first consider how 𝒪S→STO2\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{TO}_{2}} operations effectively act on population vectors. Suppose that ρS\rho_{S} and ρS′\rho^{\prime}_{S} have corresponding population vectors 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐪\mathbf{q}. If there exists ℰ∈𝒪S→STO2\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{TO}_{2}} acting on energy levels j≤kj\leq k, such that ℰ⁡(ρS)=ρS′\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S})=\rho^{\prime}_{S}, then there exists a Gibbs-stochastic matrix Mλ(j,k)M^{(j,k)}_{\lambda} defined as

Mλ(j,k)​\coloneq​(1−λ​Δj​kλλ​Δj​k1−λ)⊕𝟙∖(j,k),Δj​k​\coloneq​γkβγjβ,\displaystyle M^{(j,k)}_{\lambda}\coloneq\begin{pmatrix}1-\lambda\Delta_{jk}&&\lambda\\ \lambda\Delta_{jk}&&1-\lambda\end{pmatrix}\oplus\mathbb{1}_{\setminus(j,k)},\quad\Delta_{jk}\coloneq\frac{\gamma^{\beta}_{k}}{\gamma^{\beta}_{j}}, (16)

such that 𝐪=Mλ(j,k)​𝐩\mathbf{q}=M^{(j,k)}_{\lambda}\mathbf{p}. When the order between jj and kk is not certain, we may write Mλ(j,k)M^{(j,k)}_{\lambda} even if k<jk<j; in such cases, Mλ(j,k)M^{(j,k)}_{\lambda} must be understood as Mλ(k,j)M^{(k,j)}_{\lambda}. For Mλ(j,k)M^{(j,k)}_{\lambda} to be Gibbs-stochastic the parameter λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1].

When λ=0\lambda=0, the matrix M0(j,k)=𝟙M^{(j,k)}_{0}=\mathmybb{1}. The other extremal case of λ=1\lambda=1 is named a β\beta-swap (sometimes we refer to it simply as a swap),

β(j,k)​\coloneq​M1(j,k)=(1−Δj​k1Δj​k0)⊕𝟙∖(j,k).\displaystyle\beta^{(j,k)}\coloneq M^{(j,k)}_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}1-\Delta_{jk}&1\\ \Delta_{jk}&0\end{pmatrix}\oplus\mathbb{1}_{\setminus(j,k)}. (17)

Another notable special case is the full two-level thermalisation swap (or T-swap for short) corresponding to λ=11+Δ\lambda=\frac{1}{1+\Delta}, denoted as

T(j,k)​\coloneq​M11+Δ(j,k).\displaystyle T^{(j,k)}\coloneq M^{(j,k)}_{\frac{1}{1+\Delta}}. (18)

As the name suggests,

(T(j,k)​𝐩)k(T(j,k)​𝐩)j=Δj​k,\displaystyle\frac{(T^{(j,k)}\mathbf{p})_{k}}{(T^{(j,k)}\mathbf{p})_{j}}=\Delta_{jk}, (19)

for any initial population vector 𝐩\mathbf{p} i.e. two levels jj and kk are fully thermalised relative to each other.

Finally, we define an ordering of energy eigenbasis labels for each population vector. Intuitively, this ordering shows which levels are more populated, compared to the Gibbs state. It is thus a special case of dd-majorisation (also known as relative majorisation) where the weight vector is the Gibbs state population.

Definition 1.9 (β\beta-ordering).

Given 𝐩∈𝒱d\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{V}_{d} and a Gibbs population vector γβ∈𝒱d\gamma^{\beta}\in\mathcal{V}_{d}, we define the element-wise ratio of the two vectors as

𝐠​(𝐩)i​\coloneq​piγiβ.\displaystyle\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{p})_{i}\coloneq\frac{p_{i}}{\gamma^{\beta}_{i}}. (20)

We define the β\beta-order π𝐩\pi_{\mathbf{p}} as a permutation of (1,⋯,d)(1,\cdots,d), such that the ratios according to this ordering is non-increasing, i.e.

𝐠​(𝐩)π𝐩​(k)≥𝐠​(𝐩)π𝐩​(k+1),∀k≤d−1,\displaystyle\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{p})_{\pi_{\mathbf{p}}(k)}\geq\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{p})_{\pi_{\mathbf{p}}(k+1)},\quad\forall k\leq d-1, (21)

where we omit γβ\gamma^{\beta} in the argument when it is obvious from context. We also denote π𝐩\pi_{\mathbf{p}} as a vector (π𝐩​(1),⋯,π𝐩​(d))(\pi_{\mathbf{p}}(1),\cdots,\pi_{\mathbf{p}}(d)).

Note that the β\beta-ordering of a population vector 𝐩\mathbf{p} is not unique when there are two identical element-wise ratios. We accept all possible β\beta-orderings of a vector as valid β\beta-orders.

Previous results on state transformation characterisations and our new improvements for the ETO case is in Appendix 9.

Section 2 Unravelling catalytic operations with small catalysts and step-wise operations

One great advantage of ETO is that it opens up the opportunity to analyse intermediate states, which are found by partially applying the swap sequence—providing a time-resolved description of the system dynamics, rarely possible in other resource theories.

For example, see Figure 2, which displays the real time evolution of the state during ETO transitions. By construction, only two levels of the state undergo change in time, i.e. all the other populations are fixed during that period, imposing the system to follow the straight lines in the barycentric representation as in (a). In (b), dashed lines correspond to the free energies during the evolution. Suppose we apply β(j,k)\beta^{(j,k)} to a state 𝐩\mathbf{p}. The state evolves as 𝐪⁡(λ⁡(t))=Mλ⁡(t)(j,k)​𝐩\mathbf{q}(\lambda(t))=M^{(j,k)}_{\lambda(t)}\mathbf{p}, where 𝐪⁡(λ=1)=β(j,k)​𝐩\mathbf{q}(\lambda=1)=\beta^{(j,k)}\mathbf{p} with some monotonic function λ⁡(t)\lambda(t) reaching 11 at some t=Tt=T. Since the evolution is continuous, the system passes through a state 𝐪⁡(λ∗)=T(j,k)​𝐩\mathbf{q}(\lambda^{*})=T^{(j,k)}\mathbf{p} during the evolution. This state is the closest to being thermal, and achieves minimal generalised free energies—minima of dashed lines in (b)—among states 𝐪⁡(λ⁡(t))\mathbf{q}(\lambda(t)). In other words, during a single β\beta-swap, free energy decreases until the minimum point 𝐪⁡(λ∗)\mathbf{q}(\lambda^{*}) is reached, and then increases until the end of the β\beta-swap. On the other hand, if only the endpoints values are considered (solid lines of (b)), free energy cannot increase after each ETO step. These intermediate increases within a single swap evince the non-Markovian effect of thermal reservoirs at each step, differentiating ETO from MTO.

Subsection 1 Qubit catalysts

Now we move on to the catalytic case. When the system is symmetric and two-dimensional, thermal operations do not benefit from strict catalysis [171]. Hence, we consider the simplest non-trivial case: qutrit system and qubit catalyst. The composite state 𝐩⊗𝐜\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{c} lives in a six-dimensional probability space 𝒱6\mathcal{V}_{6}. Our goal is to construct a set attainable by catalytic elementary thermal operations with a qubit catalyst (CETO2)

𝒯CETO(2)(𝐩)\coloneq{𝐪|∃𝐜∈𝒱2s.t.𝐩⊗𝐜→ETO𝐪⊗𝐜}.\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CETO}}^{(2)}(\mathbf{p})\coloneq\{\mathbf{q}\,|\,\exists\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{V}_{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{c}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{ETO}}\mathbf{q}\otimes\mathbf{c}\}. (22)

It is easy to show that 𝒯ETO​(𝐩)⊂𝒯CETO(2)​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p})\subset\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CETO}}^{(2)}(\mathbf{p}), but qubit catalytic advantage exists if and only if 𝒯CETO(2)​(𝐩)⊄𝒯ETO​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CETO}}^{(2)}(\mathbf{p})\not\subset\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}). For a number of limited cases, given a fixed catalyst state 𝐜=(c1,1−c1)\mathbf{c}=(c_{1},1-c_{1}), some parts of the set

𝒯CETO​(𝐩,𝐜)​\coloneq​{𝐪|𝐩⊗𝐜→ETO𝐪⊗𝐜}\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CETO}}(\mathbf{p};\mathbf{c})\coloneq\{\mathbf{q}\,|\,\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{c}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{ETO}}\penalty\ \mathbf{q}\otimes\mathbf{c}\} (23)

can be evaluated analytically. Nonetheless, 𝒯CETO​(𝐩,𝐜)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CETO}}(\mathbf{p};\mathbf{c}) is in general constructed by numerically finding the extreme points of 𝒯ETO​(𝐩⊗𝐜)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{c}) and imposing exact catalyst recovery conditions. The set 𝒯CETO(2)​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CETO}}^{(2)}(\mathbf{p}) is then given by iterating the process for different values of c1c_{1}. In this section, we focus on the strict catalysis, where SS remains uncorrelated to CC to affirm that catalytic advantages exist even in the most conservative setting.

In Figure 3, we present two 𝒯CETO(2)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CETO}}^{(2)} sets corresponding to two different initial states that have distinct β\beta-orders. The sets are displayed in comparison with non-catalytic sets of reachable states 𝒯ETO\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}} and 𝒯TO\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}}. Notice that in Figure 3 (a), where the initial state is set to have π=(2,1,3)\pi=(2,1,3), we observe that 𝒯TO​\subsetneq​𝒯CETO(2)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}}\subsetneq\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CETO}}^{(2)}. This feature persists for a number of randomly chosen initial states with β\beta-orders π=(2,1,3)\pi=(2,1,3) and (3,1,2)(3,1,2). When this happens, we can on one hand reproduce every TO transition using ETO with a single qubit catalyst; and on the other hand, combat some of the finite-size effects and enable a larger set of transitions than previously allowed by an arbitrary TO. Likewise, consider Figure 3 (b), for an initial state π=(1,2,3)\pi=(1,2,3). Here, 𝒯CETO(2)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CETO}}^{(2)} overlaps almost entirely with 𝒯TO\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}}, but neither is fully contained by the other. This qualitative characteristic is again present for different initial states with the same β\beta-ordering.

In Figure 3, the set of states that go beyond 𝒯TO\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}} (yellow) highlights the additional advantage brought forward by CETO2. In addition, the set of states between 𝒯TO\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}} and 𝒯ETO\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}} (pink) also has operational merits—there exist states which require genuine multi-level TO to achieve, but can be obtained by an alternative pathway that involves only basic, Jaynes-Cummings-like interactions needed for ETO, when a catalyst is present.

Now that we have established the existence of the catalytic advantage, we leverage the decomposability of ETO and track changes in the system free energy throughout the catalytic process. Specifically, we analyse a simple series of ETO swaps that leads to the transformation of an initial state 𝐩\mathbf{p} into an extreme point of 𝒯CETO(2)​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CETO}}^{(2)}(\mathbf{p}).

We tackle the problem by the following procedure:

  1. 1.

    Construction of 𝒯ETO​(𝐩⊗𝐜)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{c}) for each 𝐜\mathbf{c}. Given the initial state 𝐩∈𝒱3\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{V}_{3}, we choose a qubit catalyst 𝐜∈𝒱2\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{V}_{2}. Furthermore, the catalyst Hamiltonian is assumed to be degenerate33 3 It is believed that any catalytic transformation can be done with some catalyst with a degenerate Hamiltonian. For example, Ref. [172] shows that any large enough catalyst can be universal for any transformation (approximately). The same assumption has been made in Refs. [173]., meaning that a choice of the population 𝐜=(c1,1−c1)\mathbf{c}=(c_{1},1-c_{1}) completely determines the catalyst. The set 𝒯ETO​(𝐩⊗𝐜)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{c}) is found by identifying all its extreme points extr⁡[𝒯ETO​(𝐩⊗𝐜)]\extr[\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{c})] by using necessary and sufficient conditions for ETO state transformations described in Appendix 9.

  2. 2.

    Finding 𝒯CETO(2)​(𝐩,𝐜)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CETO}}^{(2)}(\mathbf{p};\mathbf{c}) from 𝒯ETO​(𝐩⊗𝐜)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{c}). The resulting set 𝒯ETO​(𝐩⊗𝐜)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{c}) also includes states p′∈𝒱6p^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}_{6} that are correlated. The above example showcases a typical strategy for constructing catalytic transformations:

  1. 1.

    exploits expanded dimensionality to swap a particular energy level with more numbers of levels, storing free energy in the form of i) temporary correlations and ii) local variations on catalyst;

  2. 2.

    resolves correlations by mixing in the degenerate energy subspace; and

  3. 3.

    recovers original catalyst distribution while increasing system local free energy.

The most striking observation from this example is the increase of system non-equilibrium free energy in the later steps of the process. This behaviour of increasing free energy after swaps is strictly forbidden in non-catalytic setting, and allowed in this case by sacrificing correlation and catalyst free energy stored from previous operations.

Since strict catalysis, the most conservative form of catalysis, is assumed, catalyst local free energy goes back to its original level, and mutual information also returns to zero, as shown in (b) and (d) of Figure 5. Hence, the catalyst’s role is restricted to temporary free energy storages. Furthermore, the total free energy always decreases after each swap, obeying the monotonicity of free energies under ETO.

Similar behaviours are observed for other monotones, such as generalised free energies with α≠1\alpha\neq 1 constructed from the α\alpha-Rényi divergence (Definition 3.5) as ΔFα(𝐩)\coloneqβDα(𝐩∥γβ)\Delta F_{\alpha}(\mathbf{p})\coloneq\beta D_{\alpha}(\mathbf{p}\|\gamma^{\beta}). In Figure 6, α=0.5\alpha=0.5 and 22 are presented as representative examples. In both cases, FαF_{\alpha} for a system reduced state (see (c) and (d) of Figure 6) shares the decreasing/increasing trend, albeit with different slopes.

Subsection 2 Intermediate-size catalysts

After examining qubit catalysis, a natural question follows: how does the gap between CETOd and ETO change with dd being the dimension of the allowed catalyst? In general, identifying the whole set of reachable states 𝒯CETO(d)​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CETO}}^{(d)}(\mathbf{p}) with dd-dimensional catalysts is highly challenging, even when 𝐩\mathbf{p} is three-dimensional and d=3d=3, because constructing the set 𝒯ETO​(𝐩⊗𝐜)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{c}) requires calculating (3​d)2​(3​d)!(3d)^{2(3d)!} different final states in the worst case. However, by developing a theoretical tool, namely Theorem 2.1, we show that the numerical cost is dramatically reduced for initial states 𝐩\mathbf{p} whose β\beta-orders are monotonic in energy levels, i.e. 𝐩\mathbf{p} such that π𝐩=(1,2,⋯,d)\pi_{\mathbf{p}}=(1,2,\cdots,d) or (d,d−1,⋯,1)(d,d-1,\cdots,1). The extreme state of 𝒯ETO​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}) corresponding to each β\beta-ordering is uniquely determined by Theorem 2.1, hence reducing (m​d)2​(m​d)!(md)^{2(md)!} potential candidates for extreme points into (m​d)!(md)! for mm-dimensional catalyst and dd-dimensional system. See Theorem 9.B.1 in Appendix 9 for the reiteration of the theorem and its proof.

Theorem 2.1 (original result).

If π𝐩\pi_{\mathbf{p}} is monotonic in energy, extreme points of 𝒯ETO​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}) are achieved if and only if the corresponding β\beta-swap series that produce them are

  1. 1.

    always acting on two consecutive energy levels of the β\beta-ordering,

  2. 2.

    containing no repetition of each swap.

Furthermore, when β→1​𝐩,β→2​𝐩∈extr⁡[𝒯ETO​(𝐩)]\vec{\beta}_{1}\mathbf{p},\vec{\beta}_{2}\mathbf{p}\in\extr[\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p})] and πβ→1​𝐩=πβ→2​𝐩\pi_{\vec{\beta}_{1}\mathbf{p}}=\pi_{\vec{\beta}_{2}\mathbf{p}} for such 𝐩\mathbf{p}, the two series are identical (β→1=β→2\vec{\beta}_{1}=\vec{\beta}_{2}).

A particularly important class of states that satisfy this property is the set of Gibbs states with temperatures different from the ambient temperature β−1\beta^{-1}. When βh<β\beta_{h}<\beta, the state γβh\gamma^{\beta_{h}} is hotter than the environment with temperature β−1\beta^{-1}, and the β\beta-order πγβh=(d,d−1,⋯,1)\pi_{\gamma^{\beta_{h}}}=(d,d-1,\cdots,1). Similarly, colder states with βc>β\beta_{c}>\beta have the order πγβc=(1,2,⋯,d)\pi_{\gamma^{\beta_{c}}}=(1,2,\cdots,d). If we further employ a catalyst 𝐜\mathbf{c} from the set of states which are sufficiently thermal, the monotonicity of β\beta-order would be preserved, i.e. π𝐩⊗𝐜\pi_{\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{c}} is again monotonic in the total energy. In such cases, the analysis of higher-dimensional catalysts becomes computationally tractable. We will refer to such catalyst states as minimally-disturbing catalysts, in the sense that they do not disturb the β\beta-ordering of the system-catalyst composite. This setup has an additional merit that catalysts are low-resource states, as they are chosen to be closer to the thermal state.

To demonstrate the benefit of this reduction, let us consider the cooling process via (C)ETO starting from a high temperature thermal state γβh\gamma^{\beta_{h}} with βh<β\beta_{h}<\beta to a colder thermal state γβc\gamma^{\beta_{c}}. For any temperature βh−1\beta_{h}^{-1}, it is always possible to reach βc=β\beta_{c}=\beta by a full thermalisation with the environment. However, with ETO and TO, colder temperatures βc>β\beta_{c}>\beta can be achieved. To corroborate the effectiveness of small catalysts with practicable procedures and investigate the scaling of catalytic advantage with respect to catalyst size, we apply Theorem 2.1 to find the limits of the cooling performance for a qutrit when using catalysts of varying dimensions, ranging from two to thirty. The catalyst Hamiltonian is again set to be trivial for simplicity.

Figure 7 shows the coldest achievable βc\beta_{c} from minimally-disturbing catalysts, where the worst and the best cases are marked with purple circles and blue diamonds, respectively. Even with qubit catalysts, almost half of the gap between the TO limit (dashed line) and the ETO limit (dim(𝐜)=1\dim(\mathbf{c})=1) is covered. The maximal catalytic advantage (blue solid line) gradually increases with the catalyst size, and at dim(𝐜)=16\dim(\mathbf{c})=16, best catalysts among the sample surpass TO limit, whilst at dim(𝐜)=30\dim(\mathbf{c})=30, most of the samples perform better than TO.

Note that we have limited the range of catalyst distributions to fix the initial composite state β\beta-order; hence there might exist (not minimally-disturbing) catalyst states that activate a better cooling process than the ones marked in Figure 7. Also, even the worst case catalysts provide some advantage for the same reason. Usually, if the catalyst is pure or almost pure, catalytic advantage vanishes, but minimally-disturbing ones are typically far from pure. Nevertheless, our results give an efficiently computable lower bound to the achievable amount of cooling when any dd-dimensional catalyst is allowed.

One heuristic approach for exploring catalyst distributions that are not minimally-disturbing, is to search over sequences of β\beta-swaps satisfying the conditions of Theorem 2.1. This method is computationally efficient and yields a subset of 𝒯ETO​(𝐩⊗𝐜)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}\otimes\mathbf{c}), typically strictly smaller than the full set. Nonetheless, we have observed instances where catalytic advantage is still present even within this restricted set.

Overall, the results in this section demonstrate that small catalysts do provide substantial advantage in the setting of ETO, where simple two-level swaps are sufficient to execute the procedure. Furthermore, we leverage the step-wise structure of ETO to track and analyse catalytic evolutions, by capturing snapshots of states after each ETO step. This approach opens up a new avenue for understanding the underlying origins of catalytic advantage. In our example, the catalyst’s role was to receive the free energy flowing out from the system, either through reduced state population changes or correlations with the system. Without the catalyst, all changes in system free energy would dissipate into the surrounding bath, which thermalises after each swap. This interpretation could potentially be extended to catalysts in different resource theories. For instance, it would be intriguing to further investigate the snapshots of correlated catalysis in ETO to observe whether the memory effect is still the primary reason behind the catalytic advantage.

Section 3 A hierarchy of thermodynamic resource theories collapses under catalysis

Interestingly, regardless of the catalyst dimension, the worst catalysts in Figure 7 are given by maximally mixed states which are the Gibbs states for the trivial Hamiltonian that is assumed. This is striking because Gibbs states are free states in thermodynamic resource theories. In GP, GPC, and TO, appending any free state is free, i.e. ρS→ρS⊗γRβ\rho_{S}\to\rho_{S}\otimes\gamma^{\beta}_{R}. Hence, catalytic operations using γRβ\gamma^{\beta}_{R} as a catalyst can be done without using it catalytically, as it can be used freely.

However, MTO assumes that the bath is fully Markovian, i.e. the bath loses its memory much faster than the timescale of the system dynamics. In such cases, Gibbs states can activate state transitions as a catalyst by providing additional non-Markovianity, as studied in Refs. [169, 173]. This is reminiscent of the discussion in the qubit catalyst case, where the catalyst functions as a temporary storage during the evolution.

In general, ETO is not fully Markovian and thus distinct from MTO; nevertheless, an innate Markovianity is also embedded in the definition of ETO. ETO is written as sequences of two-level operations ℰi∈𝒪S→STO2\mathcal{E}_{i}\in\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{TO}_{2}} (and their convex combinations), where each two-level operation is implemented with a fresh bath γRiβ\gamma^{\beta}_{R_{i}}. Intuitively, the irreversible loss of information into bath RiR_{i} in each channel ℰi\mathcal{E}_{i} produces an in-built Markovian behaviour, although each bath γRiβ\gamma^{\beta}_{R_{i}} goes out of equilibrium during individual evolutions ℰi\mathcal{E}_{i} as can be seen in Figure 2 (b). We understand the inclusion 𝒯ETO​(ρ)​\subsetneq​𝒯TO​(ρ)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\rho)\subsetneq\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}}(\rho) with a strict gap from this in-built Markovianity of ETOs.

Is the gap between thermal operations and its simpler counterparts solely attributed to their Markovianity? If this were the case, the injection of sufficient memory states should enable the implementation of any complex, multi-level thermal operation using only sequential two-level operations. We answer this question affirmatively—indeed, any thermal operation can be accomplished with this strategy. In other words, we discover that the use of Gibbs catalysts is the decisive factor in closing the gap between thermal operations and their elementary counterparts (Theorem 3.1). More significantly, we show that Gibbs catalysts also close the gap between catalytic versions of TO and ETO (Theorem 3.2).

To address the irreversible loss of information to the bath after each step in ETO, we must be able to retrieve the information from the bath. This necessitates the controllability over certain parts of the used baths. We do so by modelling such parts of the baths as catalysts; we thus retain the baths throughout the process without tracing them out midway. This naturally leads to the formulation of operations supplemented with Gibbs state catalysts, i.e. controllable thermal baths; see Figure 8 for the GC-ETO illustration.

Definition 3.1 (Gibbs-catalytic operations).

A transformation ρS→σS\rho_{S}\rightarrow\sigma_{S} is achievable by Gibbs-catalytic X (GC-X) if there exists a Gibbs state γCβ\gamma^{\beta}_{C} such that

ρS⊗γCβ→XσS⊗γCβ\displaystyle\rho_{S}\otimes\gamma^{\beta}_{C}\xrightarrow{\text{X}}\sigma_{S}\otimes\gamma^{\beta}_{C} (39)

for X = TO, ETO, MTO. In other words, the existence of the catalyst Hamiltonian HCH_{C} such that σS⊗γCβ∈𝒯X​(ρS⊗γCβ)\sigma_{S}\otimes\gamma^{\beta}_{C}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{X}}(\rho_{S}\otimes\gamma^{\beta}_{C}) is equivalent to σS∈𝒯GC−X​(ρS)\sigma_{S}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{GC-X}}(\rho_{S}).

Note that Gibbs-catalytic ETO or MTO are different from the usual ETO or MTO, because ρS\rho_{S} cannot be freely transformed into ρS⊗γCβ\rho_{S}\otimes\gamma^{\beta}_{C} even though γCβ\gamma^{\beta}_{C} is a free state; see Definition 1.2.

Importantly, the full thermalisation can be performed by a sequence of ETO (or MTO), with the aid of an additional bath. Since the full thermalisation channel transforms every density matrix into a single fixed-point, it also eliminates any correlation between the catalyst and the system. Therefore, whenever a Gibbs state is used, the fulfilment of the strict catalytic condition is free, i.e.

ρS​C→TrC⁡[ρS​C]⊗γCβ\displaystyle\rho_{SC}\to\Tr_{C}[\rho_{SC}]\otimes\gamma^{\beta}_{C} (40)

via ETO or MTO, for any potentially correlated final state ρS​C\rho_{SC}.

We already established that TO does not benefit from using Gibbs states as a catalyst. In other words, GC-TO is exactly equivalent to TO. Since ETO is a subset of TO, any transformation ρS⊗γCβ→ETOσS⊗γCβ\rho_{S}\otimes\gamma^{\beta}_{C}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{ETO}}\sigma_{S}\otimes\gamma^{\beta}_{C} implies that ρS⊗γCβ→TOσS⊗γCβ\rho_{S}\otimes\gamma^{\beta}_{C}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{TO}}\sigma_{S}\otimes\gamma^{\beta}_{C}. This in turn means that

𝒯GC−ETO​(ρS)⊂𝒯TO​(ρS),\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{GC-ETO}}(\rho_{S})\subset\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}}(\rho_{S}), (41)

for any input state ρS\rho_{S}. Similarly, we can establish the relation 𝒯GC−MTO​(ρS)⊂𝒯TO​(ρS)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{GC-MTO}}(\rho_{S})\subset\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}}(\rho_{S}) for any input state ρS\rho_{S}.

Our first result shows that the converse of Eq. (41) is also true. We emphasise that this theorem holds for arbitrary asymmetric initial states that may not commute with the system Hamiltonian, as opposed to other majorisation-based approaches that are only valid for symmetric state transitions.
