Such generality is achieved thanks to the emulation of TO channels themselves via Gibbs-catalytic operations.

Theorem 3.1 (original result).

𝒯TO​(ρS)=𝒯GC−ETO​(ρS)=𝒯GC−MTO​(ρS)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}}(\rho_{S})=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{GC-ETO}}(\rho_{S})=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{GC-MTO}}(\rho_{S}) for all states ρS∈𝒟S\rho_{S}\in\mathcal{D}_{S}.

Proof.

For the proof, we only need to show that any TO channel can be recast into a GC-ETO (or GC-MTO) channel. Consider a TO channel ℰ∈𝒪S→STO\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{TO}} that admits the dilated form ℰ⁡(ρS)=TrR⁡[U⁡(ρS⊗γRβ)​U†]\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S})=\Tr_{R}[U(\rho_{S}\otimes\gamma^{\beta}_{R})U^{\dagger}], with some bath Hamiltonian HR∈ℒRH_{R}\in\mathcal{L}_{R} and an energy-preserving unitary U∈ℒS​RU\in\mathcal{L}_{SR}, such that [U,H0]=0[U,H_{0}]=0, where we denote the non-interacting Hamiltonian H0=HS⊗𝟙ℝ+𝟙𝕊⊗ℍℝH_{0}=H_{S}\otimes\mathmybb{1}_{R}+\mathmybb{1}_{S}\otimes H_{R}.

The language of Lie group and Lie algebra, briefly summarised in Appendix 10, is useful for our proof. The set of all energy-preserving unitaries GG given the Hamiltonian H0H_{0} [Eq. (1) in Appendix 10] forms a compact connected Lie group, where the corresponding Lie algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is the set of energy preserving Hamiltonians (times −i-i). Let us choose a set of linearly independent anti-Hermitian operators {K1,K2,⋯,KL}\{K_{1},K_{2},\cdots,K_{L}\} that generates the Lie algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g}. Then from Lemma 10..1 in Appendix 10, any energy-preserving unitary UU is a product of a finite number of exponentials of the form exp⁡(K​t)\exp(Kt), where K∈{K1,K2,⋯,KL}K\in\{K_{1},K_{2},\cdots,K_{L}\} and t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}.

Now we show that each KiK_{i} in the set can be chosen as an operator acting on at most two levels. Any Hermitian operator Hint∈ℒS​CH_{\mathrm{int}}\in\mathcal{L}_{SC} can be expanded in the energy eigenbasis as

Hint=∑k,l,E,E′,g,g′H(k​l​E​E′​g​g′),H_{\mathrm{int}}=\sum_{k,l,E,E^{\prime},g,g^{\prime}}H^{(klEE^{\prime}gg^{\prime})}, (42)

with each term being H(k​l​E​E′​g​g′)∝|k⟩⟨l|S⊗|E,g⟩⟨E′,g′|CH^{(klEE^{\prime}gg^{\prime})}\propto|{k}\rangle\!\langle{l}|_{S}\otimes|{E,g}\rangle\!\langle{E^{\prime},g^{\prime}}|_{C}, where {|k⟩S}k\{|{k}\rangle_{S}\}_{k} is the eigenbasis of HSH_{S}, such that HS​|k⟩S=Ek​|k⟩SH_{S}|{k}\rangle_{S}=E_{k}|{k}\rangle_{S} and {|E,g⟩C}E,g\{|{E,g}\rangle_{C}\}_{E,g} that of HCH_{C} with HC|E,g⟩C=E|E,g⟩CH_{C}|{E,g}\rangle_{C}=E|{E,g}\rangle_{C}. Here, we have chosen the catalyst to be the Gibbs state γCβ\gamma^{\beta}_{C} with Hamiltonian HCH_{C} identical to the bath Hamiltonian HRH_{R}. Now observe that

[H(k​l​E​E′​g​g′),H0]=(Ek+E−El−E′)​H(k​l​E​E′​g​g′).[H^{(klEE^{\prime}gg^{\prime})},H_{0}]=(E_{k}+E-E_{l}-E^{\prime})H^{(klEE^{\prime}gg^{\prime})}. (43)

Eq. (43) vanishes only when Ek+E=El+E′E_{k}+E=E_{l}+E^{\prime}, i.e. when |k⟩S|E,g⟩C|{k}\rangle_{S}|{E,g}\rangle_{C} and |l⟩S|E′,g′⟩C|{l}\rangle_{S}|{E^{\prime},g^{\prime}}\rangle_{C} are in the same energy subspace. The energy-preserving condition [Hint,H0]=0[H_{\mathrm{int}},H_{0}]=0 indicates that Eq. (43) is zero for all terms in Eq. (42), as H(k​l​E​E′​g​g′)H^{(klEE^{\prime}gg^{\prime})} for different superscripts are all linearly independent.

As a result, any energy-preserving Hamiltonian HintH_{\mathrm{int}} is a linear combination of (genuine) two-system-level terms

|k⟩​⟨l|S\displaystyle|{k}\rangle\!\langle{l}|_{S} ⊗|E−Ek,g⟩⟨E−El,g′|C+h.c.,\displaystyle\otimes|{E-E_{k},g}\rangle\!\langle{E-E_{l},g^{\prime}}|_{C}+\mathrm{h.c.}, (44)
i​|k⟩​⟨l|S\displaystyle i|{k}\rangle\!\langle{l}|_{S} ⊗|E−Ek,g⟩⟨E−El,g′|C+h.c.,\displaystyle\otimes|{E-E_{k},g}\rangle\!\langle{E-E_{l},g^{\prime}}|_{C}+\mathrm{h.c.}, (45)

with k≠lk\neq l and one-system-level terms with g≠g′g\neq g^{\prime},

|j⟩​⟨j|S\displaystyle|{j}\rangle\!\langle{j}|_{S} ⊗|E−Ej,g⟩⟨E−Ej,g′|C+h.c.,\displaystyle\otimes|{E-E_{j},g}\rangle\!\langle{E-E_{j},g^{\prime}}|_{C}+\mathrm{h.c.}, (46)
i​|j⟩​⟨j|S\displaystyle i|{j}\rangle\!\langle{j}|_{S} ⊗|E−Ej,g⟩⟨E−Ej,g′|C+h.c.,\displaystyle\otimes|{E-E_{j},g}\rangle\!\langle{E-E_{j},g^{\prime}}|_{C}+\mathrm{h.c.}, (47)
|j⟩​⟨j|S\displaystyle|{j}\rangle\!\langle{j}|_{S} ⊗|E−Ej,g⟩⟨E−Ej,g|C.\displaystyle\otimes|{E-E_{j},g}\rangle\!\langle{E-E_{j},g}|_{C}. (48)

By collecting each of these terms (times −i-i), we obtain the basis set {K1,K2,⋯,KL}\{K_{1},K_{2},\cdots,K_{L}\} of the Lie algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g}. Basis set is also a generating set; therefore, any energy-preserving unitary can be written as a finite product of at-most-two-level unitaries.

Since we regard the Gibbs state as a catalyst in GC-ETO framework, a unitary channel with the unitary operator exp⁡(Ki​t)\exp(K_{i}t) is itself an ETO channel; the product of these unitaries is then an ETO sequence. After this sequence the resulting intermediate state is σS​C\sigma_{SC}, whose reduced state on SS is already the target state σS\sigma_{S}. Another ETO sequence that implements the fully thermalising channel on CC yields the final product state σS⊗γCβ\sigma_{S}\otimes\gamma^{\beta}_{C}. This concludes the proof of 𝒯TO​(ρS)⊂𝒯GC−ETO​(ρS)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}}(\rho_{S})\subset\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{GC-ETO}}(\rho_{S}).

We remark that the rank-1 projectors of the form Eq. (48), which act on a single system-catalyst level instead of two, generate valid ETO channels, according to the definition of ETO allowing at most two energy levels to be manipulated simultaneously.44 4 In addition, it is always possible to choose a different generating set {K1′,K2′,⋯,KL′}\{K^{\prime}_{1},K^{\prime}_{2},\cdots,K^{\prime}_{L}\}, where all elements are rank-2 operators

Finally, note that the same energy-preserving unitary channels generated by KiK_{i} are also MTO channels since the system-catalyst composite is regarded as a controllable system. Furthermore, fully thermalising channel is also in MTO. Therefore, we also conclude that 𝒯TO​(ρS)⊂𝒯GC−MTO​(ρS)∩𝒯GC−ETO​(ρS)⊂𝒯GC−MTO​(ρS)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}}(\rho_{S})\subset\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{GC-MTO}}(\rho_{S})\cap\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{GC-ETO}}(\rho_{S})\subset\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{GC-MTO}}(\rho_{S}). ∎

This proof can be easily generalised to other subsets of thermal operations besides ETO and MTO. Suppose that a set X consists of step-wise operations and in each step within an operation, the system and the bath are coupled via an interaction Hamiltonian HjH_{j}, selected from some restricted set X={Hi}i\mathrm{X}=\{H_{i}\}_{i}, whose elements commute with the total Hamiltonian H0H_{0} (e.g. for ETO, this set is the set of interaction Hamiltonians that act non-trivially on at most two system energy levels). Because the operation is step-wise decomposable, the bath is rethermalised after each interaction by HjH_{j}. Then, the same proof employed for Theorem 3.1 can be used to prove 𝒯TO​(ρS)=𝒯GC−X​(ρS)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}}(\rho_{S})=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{GC-X}}(\rho_{S}) for any ρS\rho_{S}.

Lemma 10..1 in Appendix 10 provides a powerful tool for the decomposition of energy-preserving unitary operators. When a target Hamiltonian HintH_{\mathrm{int}} can be generated by linear combinations and commutations of the accessible Hamiltonians {Hi}\{H_{i}\}, it is possible to exactly decompose e−i​t​Hinte^{-itH_{\mathrm{int}}} into a finite product of unitaries e−i​ti​Hie^{-it_{i}H_{i}} generated from individual Hamiltonians HiH_{i}. Therefore, we obtain the desired result 𝒯TO​(ρS)⊂𝒯GC−X​(ρS)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}}(\rho_{S})\subset\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{GC-X}}(\rho_{S}). The condition imposed on X={Hi}i\mathrm{X}=\{H_{i}\}_{i} in Lemma 10..1 can also be understood as X achieving universality (for energy-preserving unitaries). ETO corresponds exactly to the case where X is the set of two-system-level interaction Hamiltonians.

Due to the rethermalisation, even when the set X achieves universality for all energy-preserving interactions, concatenations (and even convex combinations) of X channels cannot achieve a general TO channel. Remarkably, even with the freedom of choosing a bath different from the one used for the thermal operation, some TO channels are still not decomposable into X channels. The main idea of our proof is that employing Gibbs states as catalysts simplifies the problem of decomposing TO channels into that of decomposing energy-preserving unitary operators. As long as such X operations still allow for full thermalisation, one can use Gibbs states catalytically, i.e. they can be restored to their original state by the use of additional thermal baths.

The above Theorem 3.1 states that for any TO channel, there always exists a GC-X process that emulates it, yet the explicit construction is not granted by the proof. Nevertheless, an exact and explicit construction can be established for the decomposition by GC-ETO. In Ref. [160], a decomposition of generic d×dd\times d unitary operator into a product of length d⁡(d−1)2\frac{d(d-1)}{2} two-level unitaries is given. We observe that the argument also translates to energy-preserving unitaries. This is true, because any energy-preserving unitary can be first written as a direct sum of unitaries ⨁iUi\bigoplus_{i}U_{i} with each UiU_{i} acting on a fully degenerate energy subspace. Using the construction for generic unitaries, we can decompose each UiU_{i} into a series of two-level unitaries. Each of these two-level unitaries would be energy-preserving, and therefore the full decomposition corresponds to an ETO sequence.

Building on Theorem 3.1, we formulate our second main result of this section: when arbitrary catalysts are allowed, the hierarchy of thermodynamic free operations—MTO, ETO, and TO, which were previously studied independently—collapses. Such a statement can be subtle due to the various types of catalysis [38], leading to significantly different state transition conditions. In particular, without the exact emulation of TO in Theorem 3.1, there is no guarantee that the catalyst can be exactly recovered, even when the GC-ETO or GC-MTO approximates TO arbitrarily well. Nevertheless, since our result provides a direct and exact decomposition of the unitary corresponding to TO, it holds for any catalytic type (strict or correlated), as long as the definition remains consistent across different thermodynamic free operations.

Theorem 3.2 (original result).

𝒯CTO​(ρS)=𝒯CETO​(ρS)=𝒯CMTO​(ρS)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CTO}}(\rho_{S})=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CETO}}(\rho_{S})=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CMTO}}(\rho_{S}) for all ρS∈𝒟S\rho_{S}\in\mathcal{D}_{S}, where CX may stand for either strict or correlated catalytic X operations.

Proof.

By the inclusion in Remark 1.1, we immediately have 𝒯CETO​(ρS),𝒯CMTO​(ρS)⊂𝒯CTO​(ρS)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CETO}}(\rho_{S}),\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CMTO}}(\rho_{S})\subset\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CTO}}(\rho_{S}). For the other direction, consider σS∈𝒯CTO​(ρS)\sigma_{S}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CTO}}(\rho_{S}): this implies the existence of a catalyst state τC\tau_{C}, such that σS​C∈𝒯TO​(ρS⊗τC)\sigma_{SC}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C}) and TrC⁡[σS​C]=σS\Tr_{C}[\sigma_{SC}]=\sigma_{S}. Furthermore, the catalyst recovery condition, which depends on the definition of catalysis, is imposed; see Definitions 2.1 and 2.2. Using Theorem 3.1, we find that σS​C∈𝒯GC−ETO​(ρS⊗τC)\sigma_{SC}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{GC-ETO}}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C}), or equivalently, σS​C​C′​\coloneq​σS​C⊗γC′β∈𝒯ETO​(ρS⊗τC⊗γC′β)\sigma_{SCC^{\prime}}\coloneq\sigma_{SC}\otimes\gamma^{\beta}_{C^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C}\otimes\gamma^{\beta}_{C^{\prime}}) for some HC′H_{C^{\prime}}. Any catalyst recovery condition imposed on σS​C\sigma_{SC} is satisfied by σS​C​C′\sigma_{SCC^{\prime}}. Therefore, we have that σS∈𝒯CETO​(ρS)\sigma_{S}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CETO}}(\rho_{S}), and hence 𝒯CTO​(ρS)⊂𝒯CETO​(ρS)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CTO}}(\rho_{S})\subset\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CETO}}(\rho_{S}). The same proof strategy applies to MTO. ∎

The equivalence for correlated catalysis is significant for the programme of using correlating catalysis to make thermodynamic resource theories reversible [174]. First, it is known that GP with correlated catalysis achieves reversibility, i.e. state transformation is always determined by a single complete monotone [129].

In addition, GPC with correlated catalysis is shown to be almost reversible [175]. To be precise, suppose that HS=∑iEi​|i⟩​⟨i|SH_{S}=\sum_{i}E_{i}|{i}\rangle\!\langle{i}|_{S} with all energy eigenvalues EiE_{i} being commensurable. Then there exists 𝖤\mathsf{E}, such that all EiE_{i} are integer multiples of 𝖤\mathsf{E}. In such cases, for each quantum state ρS\rho_{S} there is a set of durations, called period, such that the state returns to itself after these durations, i.e. τ\tau is a period of ρS\rho_{S} if e−i​τ​HS​ρS​ei​τ​HS=ρSe^{-i\tau H_{S}}\rho_{S}e^{i\tau H_{S}}=\rho_{S}. For symmetric states, any τ\tau works; for any asymmetric state, τ=2​π𝖤\tau=\frac{2\pi}{\mathsf{E}} is a period. If the smallest such period for ρS\rho_{S} is 2​π𝖤\frac{2\pi}{\mathsf{E}}, we have 𝒯CGPC​(ρS)=𝒯CGP​(ρS)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CGPC}}(\rho_{S})=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CGP}}(\rho_{S}), which is the set of all states with the free energy smaller than that of ρS\rho_{S}.

On the other hand, the other part of the hierarchy, namely 𝒪S→SMTO,𝒪S→SETO​\subsetneq​𝒪S→STO\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{MTO}},\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{ETO}}\subsetneq\mathcal{O}_{S\to S}^{\mathrm{TO}} collapses by Theorem 3.2. If, furthermore, 𝒯CTO​(ρS)=𝒯CGPC​(ρS)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CTO}}(\rho_{S})=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{CGPC}}(\rho_{S}) can be shown for correlated catalysis, all thermodynamic resource theories in the hierarchy Remark 1.1 would (almost) become catalytically equivalent and reversible.

Section 4 Concluding remarks

We have demonstrated catalytic advantages in action within various resource theories of thermodynamics. Furthermore, fulfilling our initial objective, we identified the memory-effect as a key mechanism underpinning auxiliary system assistance. This insight arises from two key observations: firstly, snapshots of the catalytic evolution, and secondly, our proof that catalysis enables memory-restricted operations to achieve the full scope of thermodynamic transformations.

The collapse of a hierarchy (or part of the full hierarchy stated in Remark 1.1) has been an important open problem in quantum thermodynamics, particularly for those adopting resource-theoretic approaches. This stems from the fact that the choice of free operations yields inequivalent thermodynamic theories, especially in cases involving energy coherence, i.e. beyond the semi-classical setting. Hence, finding a setting in which these discrepancies vanish amounts to reconciling different paradigms of quantum thermodynamics. Interestingly, the other part of the hierarchy (between GP and GPC) is also (almost) resolved using catalysts [175], leaving only the gap between TO and GPC unaddressed.

One understated feature of our results is that GC-ETO and GC-MTO implement TO channels catalytically, not merely TO state transformations. In other words, the emulation of TO by GC-ETO (or GC-MTO) works regardless of the input system state. By contrast, GPC achieves GP state transformations catalytically but cannot implement GP channels themselves. This impossibility is most apparent from a recent result [147] showing that some GP channels require an infinite amount of energy coherence in the ancilla, even when that ancilla need not be catalytic. The distinction between catalytic channels and catalytic state transformations is a central topic in Chapter 4.

In Chapter 7, we identify other underlying mechanisms of catalysis and leverage these to design a novel algorithmic paradigm for quantum computing. The memory-effects investigated in this chapter will prove particularly instructive, as our paradigm employs auxiliaries as a memory—storing the operations performed upon them—much like catalysis within ETO and MTO.

Chapter 4 The importance of fine-tuning and catalysts as a resource broadcasting seed

In this chapter we identify two additional factors that explain catalytic advantages, i.e. how catalysts can enable state transformations or channels that are impossible without them. These factors correspond to two paradigms of catalysis: processes that implement state transformations and processes that implement channels. Section 1 introduces these two paradigms. A catalytic implementation of a channel always yields a catalytic state transformation, but not vice versa. The main result of Section 1 shows that the converse—that every catalytic state transformation implements a catalytic channel—holds if we impose an additional noise-robustness requirement. This demonstrates that one source of catalytic power is the ability to fine-tune the catalyst state based on exact knowledge of the system state, a capability that can make catalytic state transformations strictly stronger than catalytic channels. In Section 2 we show that catalytic channels (under certain assumptions) necessarily enable resource broadcasting: the catalyst acts as a seed that can be broadcast, which constitutes the second power of catalyst we identified. This connection to resource broadcasting also serves as a critical technical tool for establishing main theorems in the next section. Section 3 then presents a no-go theorem for resource broadcasting—and thereby for catalytic channels—in one class of resource theories and an existence theorem in another. To obtain these results we develop a new perspective on resource theories that focuses on composing the subsystem resource theories into a theory for the composite system. This viewpoint lets us prove the no-go and existence theorems in a very general setting, independent of the specific physical resource. We close the chapter with concluding remarks in Section 4.

My original results in this section are: Theorems 1.1, 2.1, 3.3, 3.6, Remarks 2.1, 3.1, Lemma 3.2, Observation 3.1, and Proposition 3.5.

Section 1 Fragility of catalysis and catalytic channels

So far, catalysis is defined as catalytic transformations as in Definitions 2.1 and 2.2, i.e., as a process with three interconnected elements: initial system state ρS\rho_{S}, catalyst τC\tau_{C}, and a free channel ℰ∈𝒪S​C→S′​C\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{SC\to S^{\prime}C}, which output the final state with the catalyst state intact. For example, consider strict catalysis in Definition 2.1 which outputs ρS′⊗τC=ℰ⁡(ρS⊗τC)\rho^{\prime}_{S}\otimes\tau_{C}=\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C}). Although the final catalyst state τC\tau_{C} is retrieved as an independent system, tensored with ρS′\rho^{\prime}_{S}, the process ℰ\mathcal{E} generally acts non-trivially and collectively on both systems SS and CC. That is because the operation of the form ℰ=ℰS⊗ℰC\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{E}_{S}\otimes\mathcal{E}_{C} can only prepare ρS′=ℰS​(ρS)\rho^{\prime}_{S}=\mathcal{E}_{S}(\rho_{S}) regardless of the catalyst state used. This intricacy of the process renders catalysis sensitive to the noise affecting the initial setup. The effective operation acting on the catalyst reads

τC↦ℰC​(τC)​\coloneq​TrS′​[ℰ⁡(ρS⊗τC)],\displaystyle\tau_{C}\mapsto\mathcal{E}_{C}(\tau_{C})\coloneq\Tr_{S^{\prime}}\left[\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})\right], (1)

and the process can be made catalytic by choosing the catalyst state τC\tau_{C} to be the fixed-point of the map ℰC\mathcal{E}_{C} [176, 177, 178, 8]. Since ℰ\mathcal{E} is not decomposable into local operations, Eq. (1) is affected by any change in any of the three elements in the initial setup: initial system state ρS\rho_{S}, catalyst τC\tau_{C}, and the operation ℰ\mathcal{E}.

We can upper-bound the error in the final catalyst state using the linearity of quantum channels. The desired outcome is TrS′⁡[ℰ⁡(ρS⊗τC)]=τC\Tr_{S^{\prime}}[\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})]=\tau_{C}, for an initial system state ρS\rho_{S}, catalyst state τC\tau_{C}, and a free operation ℰ∈𝒪S​C→S′​C\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{SC\to S^{\prime}C}. Now consider the case where a noisy channel is used instead of ℰ\mathcal{E}, which corresponds to panel (b) in Figure 1. Suppose that ℰϵ∈CPTPS​C→S′​C\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}\in\mathrm{CPTP}_{SC\to S^{\prime}C} is a channel such that 12​‖ℰ−ℰϵ‖Tr≤ϵ\frac{1}{2}\|\mathcal{E}-\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}\|_{\Tr}\leq\epsilon for some ϵ>0\epsilon>0, i.e. the one that is ϵ\epsilon-close to ℰ\mathcal{E}. Here, we use the trace norm ∥⋅∥Tr\|\cdot\|_{\Tr}, but any other channel norm, including the diamond norm ∥⋅∥⋄\|\cdot\|_{\diamond}, may alternatively be used; see Definition 3.3 for definitions. Then, the upper bound

12​‖TrS′​[ℰ⁡(ρS⊗τC)]−TrS′​[ℰϵ​(ρS⊗τC)]‖≤12​‖ℰ⁡(ρS⊗τC)−ℰϵ​(ρS⊗τC)‖1≤ϵ,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\Tr_{S^{\prime}}\left[\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})\right]-\Tr_{S^{\prime}}\left[\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})\right]\right\|\leq\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})-\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})\right\|_{1}\leq\epsilon, (2)

follows from the data-processing inequality for the trace norm. The LHS of Eq. (2) is the trace distance between the initial (ideal) catalyst state τC\tau_{C} and the final state obtained after applying the noisy channel ℰϵ\mathcal{E}_{\epsilon}, and it is upper-bounded by the noise in the channel itself. This scenario appears somewhat hopeless to salvage. Even with the simplest noise model—small, independent noise occurring after the ideal channel ℰ\mathcal{E}—the catalyst state inevitably suffers disturbance. Furthermore, without appropriate error correction, this disturbance tends to accumulate over multiple uses, eventually rendering the catalyst ineffective. Currently, there is no generally applicable method to prevent this error propagation.

Next, consider a catalytic process starting from a faulty catalyst τCϵ\tau^{\epsilon}_{C} [panel (d) in Figure 1], such that 12​‖τC−τCϵ‖1≤ϵ\frac{1}{2}\|\tau_{C}-\tau^{\epsilon}_{C}\|_{1}\leq\epsilon. Data-processing inequality gives

12​‖TrS′​[ℰ⁡(ρS⊗τC)]−TrS′​[ℰ⁡(ρS⊗τCϵ)]‖1≤12​‖τC−τCϵ‖1,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\Tr_{S^{\prime}}\left[\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})\right]-\Tr_{S^{\prime}}\left[\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau^{\epsilon}_{C})\right]\right\|_{1}\leq\frac{1}{2}\left\|\tau_{C}-\tau^{\epsilon}_{C}\right\|_{1}, (3)

by considering TrS′[ℰ(ρS⊗⋅)]\Tr_{S^{\prime}}[\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\cdot)] as the data-processing process. Again, the final error is upper-bounded by the initial error. However, compared to the noisy channel ℰ\mathcal{E}, this noisy initial catalyst scenario is easier to handle. The key difference lies in the fact that when catalysis is repeated, the same catalyst system is reused without a fresh source of noise. After one round of catalysis, the initial noisy catalyst state τCϵ\tau^{\epsilon}_{C} is transformed into a new state τ~Cϵ\tilde{\tau}^{\epsilon}_{C}, and the latter is no noisier than the former, by Eq. (3). If the new catalysis begins with τ~Cϵ\tilde{\tau}^{\epsilon}_{C}, the resulting catalyst state would still be at least as good as the initial one. In other words, the error does not accumulate, and after each round of catalysis, the final system state can be obtained with ϵ\epsilon error without further degradation. Therefore, even without additional measures, catalysis is robust against initial error in the catalyst state.

Finally, when the initial system state is noisy as in panel (c) of Figure 1, data-processing inequality can again be used to yield

12​‖TrS′​[ℰ⁡(ρS⊗τC)]−TrS′​[ℰ⁡(ρSϵ⊗τC)]‖1≤ϵ,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\Tr_{S^{\prime}}\left[\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})\right]-\Tr_{S^{\prime}}\left[\mathcal{E}(\rho^{\epsilon}_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})\right]\right\|_{1}\leq\epsilon, (4)

for any ρSϵ\rho^{\epsilon}_{S}, such that 12​‖ρS−ρSϵ‖1≤ϵ\frac{1}{2}\|\rho_{S}-\rho^{\epsilon}_{S}\|_{1}\leq\epsilon, which implies that the noise in the system state translates to the catalyst state.

This last scenario is the most interesting. In this case, the catalyst state effectively experiences a channel TrS′[ℰ(ρSϵ⊗⋅)]\Tr_{S^{\prime}}[\mathcal{E}(\rho^{\epsilon}_{S}\otimes\cdot)] at each round of catalysis, and the error accumulates, potentially driving the catalyst far from its original state. In the worst case, the accumulated error on the catalyst may grow linearly with the number of repetitions, leading to eventual breakdown of catalysis.

Example 1.1 (accumulating errors on the catalyst).

It suffices to demonstrate that catalyst continues to degrade after the first round of catalysis. Consider a qutrit system and a qubit catalyst undergoing a joint unitary evolution. Denote the eigenvalues of the system and catalyst to be:

pS=(p1,p2,p3),qC=(q1,q2).p_{S}=(p_{1},p_{2},p_{3}),\qquad q_{C}=(q_{1},q_{2}). (5)

The unitary swaps the eigenstates corresponding to p1​q1↔p2​q2p_{1}q_{1}\leftrightarrow p_{2}q_{2} and p2​q1↔p3​q2p_{2}q_{1}\leftrightarrow p_{3}q_{2}. This operation is catalytic whenever (p1+p2)​q1=(p2+p3)​q2(p_{1}+p_{2})q_{1}=(p_{2}+p_{3})q_{2}. Such toy examples are useful for illustrations, and have been used, e.g. in Appendix B of [176].

Now, suppose that in the first round, we have a noisy system state pε=(p1−ε,p2,p3+ε)p_{\varepsilon}=(p_{1}-\varepsilon,p_{2},p_{3}+\varepsilon) for some ε>0\varepsilon>0. This leads to a final degraded catalyst q′=(q1′,q2′)q^{\prime}=(q_{1}^{\prime},q_{2}^{\prime}), such that

q1′=p2​q2+(p3+ε)​q2+(p3+ε)​q1=q1+ε.q_{1}^{\prime}=p_{2}q_{2}+(p_{3}+\varepsilon)q_{2}+(p_{3}+\varepsilon)q_{1}=q_{1}+\varepsilon. (6)

From normalisation, we also have that q2′=q2−εq_{2}^{\prime}=q_{2}-\varepsilon. In other words, the full amount of error ε\varepsilon has propagated into the catalyst. Next, suppose that in a second round, we have another noisy system state p−ε=(p1+ε,p2,p3−ε)p_{-\varepsilon}=(p_{1}+\varepsilon,p_{2},p_{3}-\varepsilon). Under the action of the same catalytic unitary, the catalyst further degrades into qC′′=(q1′′,q2′′)q^{\prime\prime}_{C}=(q^{\prime\prime}_{1},q^{\prime\prime}_{2}), where

q1′′=p2​q2′+(p3−ε)​q2′+(p3−ε)​q1′\displaystyle q^{\prime\prime}_{1}=p_{2}q_{2}^{\prime}+(p_{3}-\varepsilon)q_{2}^{\prime}+(p_{3}-\varepsilon)q_{1}^{\prime} =q1−ε⁡(p2+p3+q2+q1−p3)\displaystyle=q_{1}-\varepsilon(p_{2}+p_{3}+q_{2}+q_{1}-p_{3})
=q1−ε⁡(1+p2).\displaystyle=q_{1}-\varepsilon(1+p_{2}). (7)

In summary, the error accumulated almost linearly during two rounds of catalysis, as we anticipated.

To prevent this error accumulation, a robustness condition needs to be established and imposed. We define robust catalysis as a catalytic process that is robust against small system-preparation noise, which is the most relevant and interesting type of noise, as explained above. The formal definition is as follows.

Definition 1.1 (robust catalysis).

Given an initial state ρS\rho_{S} and a robustness parameter ϵ>0\epsilon>0, a channel ℰ∈𝒪S​C→S′​C\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{SC\to S^{\prime}C} implements (ρ,ϵ)(\rho,\epsilon)-robust catalysis if there exists a catalyst state τC∈𝒟C\tau_{C}\in\mathcal{D}_{C} such that, for all system states σS\sigma_{S} with 12​‖σS−ρS‖1≤ϵ\frac{1}{2}\|\sigma_{S}-\rho_{S}\|_{1}\leq\epsilon, the catalyst is recovered exactly, i.e. TrS′⁡[ℰ⁡(σS⊗τC)]=τC\Tr_{S^{\prime}}[\mathcal{E}(\sigma_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})]=\tau_{C}. We say that (ρ,ϵ)(\rho,\epsilon)-robust catalysis is strict when no correlation is established between the system and the catalyst, i.e., ℰ⁡(σS⊗τC)=σ~S′⊗τC\mathcal{E}(\sigma_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})=\tilde{\sigma}_{S^{\prime}}\otimes\tau_{C}.

Definition 1.1 relaxes the catalyst’s fine-tuned dependence on the initial system state, addressing a key conceptual weakness in the theory of catalysis. The definition makes no assumption about the system’s state after the process, although we already know that it will be at most ϵ\epsilon-far from the desired final state. Notably, the robustness parameter ϵ\epsilon, capturing the degree of initial state preparation errors, can be arbitrarily small. The only truly stringent requirement is that the catalyst be returned to its initial state without error. This is a common requirement in the literature on catalytic transformations, necessary to prevent embezzlement [37, 179, 180].

The extreme case of the (ρ,ϵ)(\rho,\epsilon)-robust catalysis in Definition 1.1 is when ϵ=1\epsilon=1, which becomes completely agnostic to the input state ρ\rho. This input-agnostic approach fundamentally transforms how catalysis is defined, i.e. from catalytic transformations to catalytic channels. In other words, we can define a set of catalytically free operations similarly to the set of free operations, unlike catalytic transformations, which must be investigated only at the level of state transformation, i.e. pairs of states (ρ,ρ′)(\rho,\rho^{\prime}) such that ρ→ρ′\rho\to\rho^{\prime}. The concept of catalytic channels has been studied in the literature for a setting where the set of free operations 𝒪S​C→S​C\mathcal{O}_{SC\to SC} is the set of all unitary operations [181, 182, 183]. Here, we generalise this notion to any set of free operations 𝒪S​C→S′​C\mathcal{O}_{SC\to S^{\prime}C}.

Definition 1.2 (catalytic channel).

A channel ℰ~∈CPTPS→S′\tilde{\mathcal{E}}\in\mathrm{CPTP}_{S\to S^{\prime}} is a catalytic channel if there exists a dilation ℰ∈𝒪S​C→S′​C\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{SC\to S^{\prime}C} and a catalyst state τC∈𝒟C\tau_{C}\in\mathcal{D}_{C}, such that

TrC⁡[ℰ⁡(ρS⊗τC)]\displaystyle\Tr_{C}[\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})] =ℰ~​(ρS),\displaystyle=\tilde{\mathcal{E}}(\rho_{S}), (8)
TrS′⁡[ℰ⁡(ρS⊗τC)]\displaystyle\Tr_{S^{\prime}}[\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})] =τC,\displaystyle=\tau_{C}, (9)

for all input states ρS∈𝒟S\rho_{S}\in\mathcal{D}_{S}.

Surprisingly, this extreme limit in Definition 1.2 turns out to be equivalent to a seeming much less stringent definition of robust catalysis with any ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

Theorem 1.1 (original result).

For any ρS∈𝒟S\rho_{S}\in\mathcal{D}_{S} and any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, a channel ℰ∈𝒪S​C→S′​C\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{SC\to S^{\prime}C} implements a (ρ,ϵ)(\rho,\epsilon)-robust catalysis with catalyst’s state τC\tau_{C}, if and only if ℰ~(⋅S)=TrC[ℰ(⋅S⊗τC)]\tilde{\mathcal{E}}(\cdot_{S})=\Tr_{C}[\mathcal{E}(\cdot_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})] is a catalytic channel.

Proof.

If ℰ~\tilde{\mathcal{E}} is a catalytic channel, it implements a robust catalysis, for any state ρS\rho_{S} and any robustness parameter ϵ>0\epsilon>0. We thus only need to prove the converse, and we do it by contradiction. Suppose that ℰ\mathcal{E} implements a (ρ,ϵ)(\rho,\epsilon)-robust catalysis, but ℰ~\tilde{\mathcal{E}} is not a catalytic channel. This means that there exists at least one state, say ηS∈𝒟S\eta_{S}\in\mathcal{D}_{S}, such that

τC=TrS′​[ℰ⁡(ρS⊗τC)]≠TrS′​[ℰ⁡(ηS⊗τC)]​\eqcolon​τC′.\displaystyle\tau_{C}=\Tr_{S^{\prime}}[\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})]\neq\Tr_{S^{\prime}}[\mathcal{E}(\eta_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})]\eqcolon\tau_{C}^{\prime}. (10)

Let us then consider the state ρ~S​\coloneq​(1−ϵ)​ρS+ϵ​ηS\tilde{\rho}_{S}\coloneq(1-\epsilon)\rho_{S}+\epsilon\eta_{S}. By construction, we have 12​‖ρ~S−ρS‖1=12​‖ϵ​ηS−ϵ​ρS‖1≤ϵ\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{\rho}_{S}-\rho_{S}\|_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\|\epsilon\eta_{S}-\epsilon\rho_{S}\|_{1}\leq\epsilon. Nevertheless, by linearity, TrS′⁡[ℰ⁡(ρ~S⊗τC)]=(1−ϵ)​τC+ϵ​τC′≠τC\Tr_{S^{\prime}}[\mathcal{E}(\tilde{\rho}_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})]=(1-\epsilon)\tau_{C}+\epsilon\tau^{\prime}_{C}\neq\tau_{C}, contradicting the assumption that ℰ\mathcal{E} implements an ϵ\epsilon-robust catalysis for ρS\rho_{S}. ∎

Theorem 1.1 clarifies that all forms of catalysis, other than catalytic channels, are inevitably fine-tuned to a very specific initial state of the system, and risk degrading the catalyst whenever the system’s state is not prepared with strictly infinite precision. It also offers a mathematically streamlined pathway towards robust catalysis, as one may directly examine the structure of catalytic channels rather than inspect different catalyst states and fine-tuned strategies for state transformations.

Even though both catalytic channels and universal catalysts share universality with respect to input system states, they should not be conflated. The latter concept refers to a catalyst state that can be used for any catalytic transformation, assuming the operation can be appropriately fine-tuned. The intuition behind such catalysts is simple: the universal state just needs to subsume all catalyst states that may be required. Specifically, one can coarse-grain over all catalytic transformations and collect all associated catalysts into a single, large universal catalyst [184]. Alternatively, the asymptotic reversibility of a resource theory—if it exists—can be leveraged. By selecting sufficiently many copies of some quantum state to be a universal catalyst, this catalyst can be pre-processed into many copies of the initial system state, transformed into many copies of the desired final state, and post-processed back into the original catalyst state, all without dissipating (almost) any resources [172]. In both approaches, however, the process is not robust against noise in the preparation of the initial system state.11 1 To make such universal catalysts robust, one may envisage a protocol where the initial state can be known by some free operations. In Refs. [185, 186], an interesting protocol is presented. Given asymptotically many copies of the initial state unknown to us, an optimal resource extraction can be performed by measuring some of the copies to learn the initial state and extracting the resource from the rest of the copies. This process is indeed independent of different choices of the initial state. However, the measurement sampling cost is negligible only when working within the asymptotic setting, which negates the need of catalysis in asymptotically reversible theories that these universal catalysts are considered. Once the operation is fixed, any deviation from the intended input can break the catalytic behaviour. Catalytic channels are therefore anticipated to be more reliably implementable, as they guarantee reusability of the catalyst even in the presence of such errors.

Theorem 1.1 prompts us to examine whether catalytic channels can provide any meaningful advantage. Indeed, special cases have been studied in the literature. Initially, catalytic channels were defined and analysed for the unitary theory, i.e. when 𝒪X→X\mathcal{O}_{X\to X} is the set of unitary channels for system XX [181, 182, 183]. In this setting, the most straightforward catalytic channels are mixed unitary channels. Suppose that the catalyst τC=∑ipi​|i⟩​⟨i|C\tau_{C}=\sum_{i}p_{i}|{i}\rangle\!\langle{i}|_{C} for some basis {|i⟩C}i\{|{i}\rangle_{C}\}_{i}. By choosing the unitary operator U=∑iUi⊗|i⟩​⟨i|CU=\sum_{i}U_{i}\otimes|{i}\rangle\!\langle{i}|_{C}, the catalytic channel

TrC⁡[U⁡(ρS⊗τC)​U†]=∑ipi​Ui​ρS​Ui†,\displaystyle\Tr_{C}\left[U\left(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C}\right)U^{\dagger}\right]=\sum_{i}p_{i}U_{i}\rho_{S}U_{i}^{\dagger}, (11)

is obtained with the guarantee of the exact recovery TrS⁡[U⁡(ρS⊗τC)​U†]=τC\Tr_{S}[U(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})U^{\dagger}]=\tau_{C} for any ρS∈𝒟S\rho_{S}\in\mathcal{D}_{S}. In other words, any mixed unitary channel (i.e. a channel that can be written as a convex combination of unitary channels) can be implemented using a catalyst state with its eigenvalues coinciding with the convex coefficients.

It turns out that catalytic channels can also implement channels that are not in the form of Eq. (11) [187]. They form a set that is strictly larger than the set of mixed unitaries and strictly smaller than the set of strongly factorisable channels (also known as noisy operations [188]).22 2 Interestingly, the free unitary U∈𝒪S​C→S​CU\in\mathcal{O}_{SC\to SC} can implement a catalytic channel if and only if its partial transpose U\transpSU^{\transp_{S}} is also unitary. When the dimensions for SS and CC are the same, this class of unitary is equivalent to dual unitaries (multiplied by a SWAP operator) [189], or sometimes called Γ\Gamma-dual unitaries [190], which are actively studied in the context of chaos and operator spreading.

Catalytic channels similar to Eq. (11) can be constructed more generally; if the set of free operations is not convex but not necessarily unitary, and if controlled operations are free, catalysts can be used as a source of randomness that is encoded in its spectrum; see Ref. [118] for more general discussion on this topic.

Alternatively, catalytic channels also emerge naturally when the catalyst is a free state; in fact, this catalysis is also strict. By Definition 1.2, there always exists a free operation ℱ∈𝒪C→C\mathcal{F}\in\mathcal{O}_{C\to C}, which prepares a fixed free state γC∈𝒮C\gamma_{C}\in\mathcal{S}_{C}. By applying ℱ\mathcal{F} to the catalyst after any operation on system and catalyst, the resulting operation becomes catalytic, i.e. (idS⊗ℱ)∘ℰ⁡(ρS⊗γC)=ρS′⊗γC(\id_{S}\otimes\mathcal{F})\circ\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\gamma_{C})=\rho^{\prime}_{S}\otimes\gamma_{C} for any ρS∈𝒟S\rho_{S}\in\mathcal{D}_{S}. Typically, the catalytic channel ℰ(⋅⊗γC)\mathcal{E}(\cdot\otimes\gamma_{C}) is a free channel when γC∈𝒮C\gamma_{C}\in\mathcal{S}_{C} is a free state and ℰ∈𝒪S​C→S​C\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{SC\to SC} is a free operation. However, this is not always the case, as observed in some resource theories of athermality [169, 173, 1, 2]; see Section 3 how even Gibbs states can expand the set of free operations. In such cases, catalytic channels exploit the memory effect of the catalyst, overcoming the inherent Markovianity of the resource theory.

Section 2 Resource broadcasting and catalytic channels

To study more intricate advantages from catalytic channels, beyond the aforementioned special cases of catalytic randomness and non-Markovianity boost, a few additional axioms are imposed on resource theories of interest. {kaobox}[frametitle = Axioms for convex resource theories with free tensor product and partial trace]

  1. (A1)

    ρA⊗ρB∈𝒮A​B\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B}\in\mathcal{S}_{AB} is a free state whenever ρA∈𝒮A\rho_{A}\in\mathcal{S}_{A} and ρB∈𝒮B\rho_{B}\in\mathcal{S}_{B} are free states

  2. (A2)

    If ρA​B∈𝒮A​B\rho_{AB}\in\mathcal{S}_{AB} is a free state, then TrB⁡[ρA​B]∈𝒮A\Tr_{B}[\rho_{AB}]\in\mathcal{S}_{A} and TrA⁡[ρA​B]∈𝒮B\Tr_{A}[\rho_{AB}]\in\mathcal{S}_{B} are free states

  3. (A3)

    the set of free states 𝒮X\mathcal{S}_{X} is a convex set for any system XX

(A1) and (A2) set basic rules for composing free state sets in larger spaces. (A2) is implied by the tensor product structure of resource theories: it follows from the third axiom in the definition of free operations (Definition 1.1) and the second axiom in the tensor product structure (Definition 1.4). (A1) serves to exclude a phenomenon known as (super-)activation [191, 192, 193], whereby even free states can activate catalytic channels. Similarly, the convexity assumption (A3) ensures that any classical randomness is already incorporated into the definition of free operations, negating the need for catalytic randomness.

These axioms do not uniquely characterise the composite free states 𝒮A​B\mathcal{S}_{AB} given the subsystem sets 𝒮A\mathcal{S}_{A} and 𝒮B\mathcal{S}_{B}. Nevertheless, they are standard assumptions that hold in a broad range of quantum resource theories, including those of entanglement, athermality, coherence, asymmetry, and magic. Furthermore, these axioms leave considerable flexibility in the choice of free operations, the only constraint being the golden rule (Definition 1.3). A canonical way of defining free operations from free states is via completely resource non-generating (CRNG) operations (Definition 1.6), which comprise the full set of channels that cannot generate any resource from free states, even when acting on a marginal state of a larger free state. An additional merit of CRNG operations is that they are maximal under assumptions (A1)–(A3) and the golden rule. For these reasons, we will focus of CRNG operations from now on.

Since catalysis refers to the activation of processes that would otherwise be impossible, robust catalysis must implement a catalytic channel ℰ~∈CPTPS→S′\tilde{\mathcal{E}}\in\mathrm{CPTP}_{S\to S^{\prime}} that is not free. To ascertain that ℰ~\tilde{\mathcal{E}} is not free, it suffices to find a process that maps a free state γS\gamma_{S} into a resourceful state ℰ~​(γS)∉𝒮S′\tilde{\mathcal{E}}(\gamma_{S})\notin\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}}. Conversely, if ℰ~\tilde{\mathcal{E}} maps free states 𝒮S\mathcal{S}_{S} to free states 𝒮S′\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}}, it is resource non-generating (RNG). Furthermore, if every catalytic channel ℰ~\tilde{\mathcal{E}} is RNG, so are their extensions idA⊗ℰ~\id_{A}\otimes\tilde{\mathcal{E}}, as these are themselves catalytic channels. This in turn implies that all ℰ~\tilde{\mathcal{E}} are completely resource non-generating. In this case, if the set of free operations is chosen to be CRNG, catalytic channels offer no advantage.

To examine the power of catalytic channels, let us introduce a related concept with the name resource broadcasting. The name broadcasting comes from the fact that the channel propagates some resource from one system to another system, while leaving the original one completely intact. This notion is inspired by, but not identical to, quantum state broadcasting (Theorem 2.2); see also Refs. [194, 195, 196, 197, 198]. Resource broadcasting is an interesting phenomenon that has attracted attention from the community [199, 200, 201, 202, 203]. Nevertheless, in this thesis, this concept is introduced primarily as a technical tool for establishing results for robust catalysis; the connection between the two will become more apparent in Theorem 2.1 below.

There are variations in how resource broadcasting is defined in the literature. Here, we take the most lenient one as our definition.

Definition 2.1 (resource broadcasting).

A broadcasting channel ℬ∈𝒪A→A​B\mathcal{B}\in\mathcal{O}_{A\to AB} is a free operation such that

TrB⁡[ℬ⁡(ρA)]\displaystyle\Tr_{B}[\mathcal{B}(\rho_{A})] =ρA,\displaystyle=\rho_{A}, (12)
TrA⁡[ℬ⁡(ρA)]\displaystyle\Tr_{A}[\mathcal{B}(\rho_{A})] ∉𝒮B,\displaystyle\notin\mathcal{S}_{B}, (13)

i.e. producing a non-free state in system BB for some state ρA∈𝒟A\rho_{A}\in\mathcal{D}_{A}.

Setting AA as the catalyst system CC and BB as the system of interest SS highlights the similarity to catalytic channels. Consider the application of the catalytic channel ℰ~\tilde{\mathcal{E}} to a free system state γS∈𝒮S\gamma_{S}\in\mathcal{S}_{S}, yielding a resourceful state ℰ~​(γS)=TrC​[ℰ⁡(γS⊗τC)]∉𝒮S′\tilde{\mathcal{E}}(\gamma_{S})=\Tr_{C}[\mathcal{E}(\gamma_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})]\notin\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}}; this process can be viewed as broadcasting the catalyst τC\tau_{C}. We establish that, under some assumptions, the two concepts accompany one another.

Theorem 2.1 (original result).

Suppose that a resource theory having all CRNG operations as the free operation satisfies axioms (A1)–(A3). If there exists a non-free catalytic channel ℰ~∉𝒪S→S′\tilde{\mathcal{E}}\notin\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime}} with some catalyst τC\tau_{C}, there must exist a free broadcasting channel ℬ∈𝒪C→S′​C\mathcal{B}\in\mathcal{O}_{C\to S^{\prime}C} defined as in Definition 2.1. Conversely, given a broadcasting channel ℬ∈𝒪C→S′​C\mathcal{B}\in\mathcal{O}_{C\to S^{\prime}C}, it is possible to construct a non-free catalytic channel TrC∘ℬ∘TrS[⋅⊗τC]∉𝒪S→S′\Tr_{C}\circ\mathcal{B}\circ\Tr_{S}[\cdot\otimes\tau_{C}]\notin\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime}}.

Proof.

Suppose that ℰ~∉𝒪S→S′\tilde{\mathcal{E}}\notin\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime}} is a non-free catalytic channel with a dilation into free channel ℰ∈𝒪S​C→S′​C\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{SC\to S^{\prime}C} and a catalyst τC\tau_{C}. Since the set of free operations 𝒪S→S′\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime}} is defined to be CRNG, ℰ~\tilde{\mathcal{E}} must be able to transform a free state into a resourceful one, i.e. ∃γS∈𝒮S\exists\gamma_{S}\in\mathcal{S}_{S} such that the output ρS​C=ℰ⁡(γS⊗τC)\rho_{SC}=\mathcal{E}(\gamma_{S}\otimes\tau_{C}) satisfies the catalytic condition, TrS⁡[ρS​C]=τC\Tr_{S}[\rho_{SC}]=\tau_{C} and the resourcefulness of the final state TrC⁡[ρS​C]∉𝒮S′\Tr_{C}[\rho_{SC}]\notin\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}}. Now, define the free channel ℬ∈𝒪C→S′​C\mathcal{B}\in\mathcal{O}_{C\to S^{\prime}C} by ℬ(⋅)=ℰ(γS⊗⋅)\mathcal{B}(\cdot)=\mathcal{E}(\gamma_{S}\otimes\cdot). This construction makes ℬ\mathcal{B} a broadcasting channel that maps τC\tau_{C} into ρS​C\rho_{SC}.

For the converse direction, suppose that the free channel ℬ∈𝒪C→S′​C\mathcal{B}\in\mathcal{O}_{C\to S^{\prime}C} broadcasts τC\tau_{C}. Then the channel ℰ=ℬ∘TrS∈𝒪S​C→S′​C\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{B}\circ\Tr_{S}\in\mathcal{O}_{SC\to S^{\prime}C} is free, as it is a concatenation of two free operations. A catalytic channel can be constructed as ℰ~​(ρS)=TrC​[ℰ⁡(ρS⊗τC)]\tilde{\mathcal{E}}(\rho_{S})=\Tr_{C}[\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})] and it is not CRNG since ℰ~​(γS)=TrC​[ℬ⁡(τC)]∉𝒮S′\tilde{\mathcal{E}}(\gamma_{S})=\Tr_{C}[\mathcal{B}(\tau_{C})]\notin\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}} is not free. ∎

Despite the equivalence in the existences of two phenomena, catalytic channels and resource broadcasting exhibit subtle differences. In real experimental setups, implementing the broadcasting channel ℬ∈𝒪C→S′​C\mathcal{B}\in\mathcal{O}_{C\to S^{\prime}C} requires an auxiliary state γS′∈𝒮S′\gamma_{S^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}}, which is assumed to be fixed. Unlike catalytic channels, the broadcasting process may fail to preserve the original state τC\tau_{C} if the auxiliary state γS′\gamma_{S^{\prime}} is perturbed in any way. This point does not play a role in the proof of Theorem 2.1, because we assume that the channel ℬ∈𝒪C→S′​C\mathcal{B}\in\mathcal{O}_{C\to S^{\prime}C} can be implemented faithfully.

In fact, the implication from the existence of broadcasting channels to the existence of catalytic channels holds even without some of the assumptions.

Remark 2.1 (original result).

As long as the resource theory follows the Definitions 1.1 and 1.3, i.e. as long as it is a proper resource theory according to our definitions, given a broadcasting channel ℬ∈𝒪C→S′​C\mathcal{B}\in\mathcal{O}_{C\to S^{\prime}C}, it is possible to construct a non-free catalytic channel TrC∘ℬ∘TrS[⋅⊗τC]∉𝒪S→S′\Tr_{C}\circ\mathcal{B}\circ\Tr_{S}[\cdot\otimes\tau_{C}]\notin\mathcal{O}_{S\to S^{\prime}}.

This remark follows immediately from the construction of the non-free catalytic channel.

On the other hand, the implication from the existence of catalytic channels to that of resource broadcasting requires all assumptions in Theorem 2.1. As an example, suppose that the set of free operations is strictly smaller than the entire CRNG operations. Then, there may exist robust catalysis that implements a catalytic channel ℰ~\tilde{\mathcal{E}} that is not free, but still CRNG. The example below presents one such case.

Example 2.1.

Elementary thermal operations (ETO, Definition 1.4) and Markovian thermal operations (MTO, Definition 1.5) admit robust catalysis, with the Gibbs catalyst state γCβ\gamma^{\beta}_{C} as shown in Chapter 3. Both operations have the Gibbs state as the only free state, but it is known that ETO or MTO with any catalysis are bound to be Gibbs-preserving. The latter can be inferred from Theorem 3.2 and the fact that Gibbs-preserving operations (Definition 1.1) cannot broadcast. Hence, resource theories whose free operations are ETO and MTO do not have broadcasting channels.

Another subtle relationship emerges for robust catalysis in theories having free operations strictly smaller than CRNG versus the full CRNG set. Firstly, even if there exists robust catalysis in the latter, it is possible to construct a smaller set of free operations that excludes this process. On the other hand, even if the impossibility of robust catalysis is proved with the full set of CRNG operations, this result cannot be extended to its subsets. An example below shows the contrapositive of this statement.

Example 2.2.

Consider the theory where the set of free operations 𝒪S→S\mathcal{O}_{S\to S} is always the set of all unitary channels from SS to itself, regardless of the system SS. These sets are strict subsets of the CRNG operation, which is the set of unital channels (i.e. channels that preserve the identity 𝟙𝕊\mathmybb{1}_{S}). Eq. (11) shows that robust catalysis exists when 𝒪S→S\mathcal{O}_{S\to S} is defined in this way. However, it is known that catalytic channels implemented via unitary channels 𝒪S​C→S​C\mathcal{O}_{SC\to SC} are always unital [182]. Furthermore, from no-broadcasting of unital channels implies that there is no robust catalysis for the unital theory.

The full relationships between robust catalysis and resource broadcasting for theories having free operations strictly smaller than CRNG versus the full CRNG set are summarised in Figure 2.

Section 3 How composition of local resource theories determines the existence of resource broadcasting

As illustrated in Figure 2, the existence of resource broadcasting map can always probed by working with the set of free operations defined as all CRNG operations. Hence, for the rest of this chapter, we assume the set of free operations to be the set of CRNG operations.

Moreover, we impose the fourth axiom for the resource theories of our interest. {kaobox}[frametitle = Additional axioms for convex resource theories with free tensor product and partial trace]

  1. (A4)

    There always exists a full-rank free state γX∈𝒮X\gamma_{X}\in\mathcal{S}_{X} for any system XX

Axiom (A4) is introduced to eliminate the possibility of having a state with infinite resources. The below example demonstrates that when (A4) does not hold, i.e. when there exists a catalyst state that has infinite resources, any state can be obtained from broadcasting.

Observation 3.1 (limited subspace theories; original result).

Suppose that all free states are non-full rank, while axioms (A1)–(A3) still hold; we call such theories as limited subspace theories. Due to the convexity assumption (A3), the non-full rank condition implies the existence of a subspace orthogonal to the space spanned by free states. Then the non-zero projectors for each of these two subspaces can be defined: Π0\Pi_{0} is the projector onto the subspace spanned by free states ⋃γC∈𝒮Csupp⁡(γC)\bigcup_{\gamma_{C}\in\mathcal{S}_{C}}\supp(\gamma_{C}), and Π1=𝟙ℂ−Π𝟘\Pi_{1}=\mathmybb{1}_{C}-\Pi_{0}. Since Π1≠0\Pi_{1}\neq 0, a state τC\tau_{C} can be chosen in the latter space, i.e. τC​Π0=0\tau_{C}\Pi_{0}=0.

Then the robust catalysis mapping ρS→ρS′′\rho_{S}\to\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}} for any pair (ρS,ρS′′)(\rho_{S},\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}) can be constructed:

  1. 1.

    the catalyst CC is measured with effects Π0\Pi_{0} and Π1\Pi_{1};

  2. 2.

    if the outcome is 00 (corresponding to Π0\Pi_{0}), prepare a S′​CS^{\prime}C free state;

  3. 3.

    otherwise, prepare ρS′′⊗τC\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}\otimes\tau_{C}, where ρS′′\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}} is any resourceful system state and τC\tau_{C} is the initial catalyst state.

Combined, this measure-and-prepare channel is written as

ℰ⁡(ρS​C)=γS′​C​Tr⁡[ρS​C​(𝟙𝕊⊗Π𝟘)]+ρ𝕊′′⊗τℂ​Tr⁡[ρ𝕊​ℂ​(𝟙𝕊⊗Π𝟙)],\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\rho_{SC})=\gamma_{S^{\prime}C}\Tr[\rho_{SC}(\mathmybb{1}_{S}\otimes\Pi_{0})]+\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}\otimes\tau_{C}\Tr[\rho_{SC}(\mathmybb{1}_{S}\otimes\Pi_{1})], (14)

where γS′​C∈𝒮S′​C\gamma_{S^{\prime}C}\in\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}C} is some free state. When any S​CSC free state is input, this channel always outputs γS′​C\gamma_{S^{\prime}C}, i.e. ℰ∈𝒪S​C→S′​C\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{SC\to S^{\prime}C} is free. Furthermore, ℰ⁡(ρS⊗τC)=ρS′′⊗τC\mathcal{E}(\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})=\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}\otimes\tau_{C} for any ρS\rho_{S}, achieving the strict robust catalysis.

The broadcasting map can be constructed similarly as

ℬ⁡(ρC)=γS′​C​Tr⁡[ρC​Π0]+ρS′′⊗τC​Tr⁡[ρC​Π1],\displaystyle\mathcal{B}(\rho_{C})=\gamma_{S^{\prime}C}\Tr[\rho_{C}\Pi_{0}]+\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}\otimes\tau_{C}\Tr[\rho_{C}\Pi_{1}], (15)

for any ρS′\rho^{\prime}_{S}. Then ℬ⁡(τC)=ρS′′⊗τC\mathcal{B}(\tau_{C})=\rho^{\prime}_{S^{\prime}}\otimes\tau_{C}, as promised. Note that the broadcasting is also strict, i.e. the final state is uncorrelated.

This catalyst state τC\tau_{C} can be interpreted as the infinite resource state, because any state within the subspace spanned by free states cannot have a finite overlap with τC\tau_{C} after any free operation. Moreover, divergence-based monotones (Example 1.2) diverge for this state, as ℙ(τC∥γC)=∞\mathbb{P}(\tau_{C}\|\gamma_{C})=\infty, whenever supp⁡(τC)​\nsubset​supp⁡(γC)\supp(\tau_{C})\nsubset\supp(\gamma_{C}).

The simplest example is the resource theory of athermality at temperature T=0T=0, where the only free state is the ground state γX=|0⟩​⟨0|X\gamma_{X}=|{0}\rangle\!\langle{0}|_{X} for any XX. Suppose that CC is a qubit system with 𝟙ℂ=|𝟘⟩​⟨𝟘|ℂ+|𝟙⟩​⟨𝟙|ℂ\mathmybb{1}_{C}=|{0}\rangle\!\langle{0}|_{C}+|{1}\rangle\!\langle{1}|_{C}. Then by setting Π0=|0⟩​⟨0|C\Pi_{0}=|{0}\rangle\!\langle{0}|_{C} and Π1=|1⟩​⟨1|C\Pi_{1}=|{1}\rangle\!\langle{1}|_{C}, any final state can be generated from a free initial state using the catalytic channel with a catalyst state τC=|1⟩​⟨1|C\tau_{C}=|{1}\rangle\!\langle{1}|_{C}. A similar construction was used in Ref. [204].

We address the central question again with the additional axiom (A4): when does robust catalysis offer a net advantage? It turns out that the answer hinges on an additional degree of freedom that has not been explicitly considered before: how the set of free states 𝒮A​B\mathcal{S}_{AB} is composed given 𝒮A\mathcal{S}_{A} and 𝒮B\mathcal{S}_{B}. In typical resource theories, this composition is usually defined operationally, depending on the particular resource at hand. For instance, the subset of separable states (Definition 1.1) can be clearly defined for any set of density matrices, given a partition in entanglement theory; the set of symmetric states is determined by the unitary representation of the symmetry group in each Hilbert spaces in the theory of asymmetry; etc.

However, in abstract resource theories, where no operational definition exists a priori, any composition rule can be adopted, as long as it does not cause inconsistencies with the rest of the theory. In particular, we can establish lower and upper bound of the composition.

Remark 3.1 (minimal and maximal compositions; original result).

Define minimal and maximal compositions of free state sets

𝒮A⊗min𝒮B\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{min}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B} \coloneqconv{ρA⊗ρB|ρA∈𝒮A,ρB∈𝒮B},\displaystyle\coloneq\conv\left\{\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B}\,|\,\rho_{A}\in\mathcal{S}_{A},\ \rho_{B}\in\mathcal{S}_{B}\right\}, (16)
𝒮A⊗max𝒮B\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{max}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B} \coloneq{ρA​B|TrB[ρA​B]∈𝒮A,TrA[ρA​B]∈𝒮B}.\displaystyle\coloneq\left\{\rho_{AB}\,|\,\Tr_{B}[\rho_{AB}]\in\mathcal{S}_{A},\Tr_{A}[\rho_{AB}]\in\mathcal{S}_{B}\right\}. (17)

for given free state sets 𝒮A\mathcal{S}_{A} and 𝒮B\mathcal{S}_{B}. Then for any free state set 𝒮A​B\mathcal{S}_{AB} satisfying axioms (A1)-(A3),

𝒮A⊗min𝒮B⊂𝒮A​B⊂𝒮A⊗max𝒮B.\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{min}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B}\subset\mathcal{S}_{AB}\subset\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{max}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B}. (18)

We note that Ref. [205] defines 𝒮A⊗min𝒮B\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{min}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B} as their composition rule in the context of resource censorship.

The notations ⊗min\otimes_{\textrm{min}} and ⊗max\otimes_{\textrm{max}} are inspired by minimal and maximal tensor products of convex cones [206, 207, 208], often discussed in the context of general probabilistic theories [209, 210]. {kaobox}[frametitle = A digression on minimal and maximal tensor products] We define convex cones and their duals following Refs. [211, 212]. Let 𝒱\mathcal{V} be a vector space. A non-empty subset 𝒞⊂𝒱\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{V} is a convex cone if it is convex and closed under positive scalar multiplication. We also assume that 𝒞\mathcal{C} is closed and 𝒞∩(−𝒞)={0}\mathcal{C}\cap(-\mathcal{C})=\{0\}. Let 𝒱∗\mathcal{V}^{*} be the set of linear functionals on 𝒱\mathcal{V} with the duality ⟨,⟩:𝒱∗×𝒱→ℝ\langle,\rangle:\mathcal{V}^{*}\times\mathcal{V}\to\mathbb{R}. The dual cone of 𝒞\mathcal{C} is then given by 𝒞∗={x∗∈𝒱∗|⟨x∗,z⟩≥0​ for all ​z∈𝒞}\mathcal{C}^{*}=\Bqty{x^* \in\mV^*\,|\, \langle x^*, z \rangle\geq 0 \textrm{ for all } z \in\mathcal{C}}. The minimal and maximal tensor products of two cones 𝒞A\mathcal{C}_{A} and 𝒞B\mathcal{C}_{B} are defined as

𝒞A⊗min𝒞B\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{A}\!\otimes_{\textrm{min}}\!\mathcal{C}_{B} \coloneqconv{zA⊗zB|zA∈𝒞A,zB∈𝒞B},\displaystyle\coloneq\conv\left\{z_{A}\otimes z_{B}\,|\,z_{A}\in\mathcal{C}_{A},z_{B}\in\mathcal{C}_{B}\right\}, (19)
𝒞A⊗max𝒞B\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{A}\!\otimes_{\textrm{max}}\!\mathcal{C}_{B} \coloneq{z|⟨x∗⊗y∗,z⟩≥0,x∗∈𝒞A∗,y∗∈𝒞B∗}.\displaystyle\coloneq\left\{z\,|\,\langle x^{*}\otimes y^{*},z\rangle\geq 0,\,x^{*}\in\mathcal{C}^{*}_{A},\,y^{*}\in\mathcal{C}^{*}_{B}\right\}. (20)

Consider the case where cones are defined on the space of linear Hermitian operators acting on Hilbert spaces, with the duality ⟨,⟩\langle,\rangle given by the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product. We now observe that for each free state set 𝒮A\mathcal{S}_{A}, the associated cone can be defined as 𝒞⁡(𝒮A)=⋃λ≥0λ​𝒮A\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{S}_{A})=\bigcup_{\lambda\geq 0}\lambda\mathcal{S}_{A}. Then, it follows that 𝒞⁡(𝒮A)⊗min𝒞⁡(𝒮B)=𝒞⁡(𝒮A⊗min𝒮B)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{S}_{A})\!\otimes_{\textrm{min}}\!\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{S}_{B})=\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{min}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B}), i.e. the minimal tensor product is equivalent to the minimal composition in Eq. (16).

For the maximal counterparts, we have 𝒞⁡(𝒮A)⊗max𝒞⁡(𝒮B)⊂𝒞⁡(𝒮A⊗max𝒮B)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{S}_{A})\!\otimes_{\textrm{max}}\!\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{S}_{B})\subset\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{max}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B}). To see this, note that choosing x∗=𝟙𝔸∈𝒞∗​(𝒮𝔸)x^{*}=\mathmybb{1}_{A}\in\mathcal{C}^{*}(\mathcal{S}_{A}) in Eq. (20), ensures the BB marginal of γA​B∈𝒞⁡(𝒮A)⊗max𝒞⁡(𝒮B)\gamma_{AB}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{S}_{A})\!\otimes_{\textrm{max}}\!\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{S}_{B}) is always in 𝒞⁡(𝒮B)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{S}_{B}). Choosing y∗=𝟙𝔹∈𝒞∗​(𝒮𝔹)y^{*}=\mathmybb{1}_{B}\in\mathcal{C}^{*}(\mathcal{S}_{B}) implies the same for the AA marginal. The converse of this inclusion does not hold in general, as one can check by constructing counter-examples: consider qubit systems AA and BB with 𝒮A=𝒮B={𝟙2}\mathcal{S}_{A}=\mathcal{S}_{B}=\{\frac{\mathmybb{1}}{2}\}. The maximum tensor product turns out to be 𝒞⁡(𝒮A)⊗max𝒞⁡(𝒮B)={λ​𝟙𝔸⊗𝟙𝔹|λ≥𝟘}\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{S}_{A})\!\otimes_{\textrm{max}}\!\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{S}_{B})=\{\lambda\mathmybb{1}_{A}\otimes\mathmybb{1}_{B}\,|\,\lambda\geq 0\}, which is strictly smaller than 𝒞⁡(𝒮A⊗max𝒮B)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{max}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B}).

Minimal and maximal compositions encapsulate the limits of allowed correlations in free states. For instance, the resource theories of athermality, where the tensor product e−β⁡(HA+HB)ZA​B=e−β​HAZA⊗e−β​HBZB\frac{e^{-\beta(H_{A}+H_{B})}}{Z_{AB}}=\frac{e^{-\beta H_{A}}}{Z_{A}}\otimes\frac{e^{-\beta H_{B}}}{Z_{B}} of subsystem Gibbs states e−β​HAZA\frac{e^{-\beta H_{A}}}{Z_{A}} and e−β​HBZB\frac{e^{-\beta H_{B}}}{Z_{B}} is a free state, and coherence [213], where diagonal states are free, follow the minimal composition rule. On the other hand, the maximal composition of athermality includes the thermofield double state ∑ie−βEi/2Z​|i⟩A​|i⟩B\sum_{i}\frac{e^{-\beta E_{i}/2}}{\sqrt{Z}}|{i}\rangle_{A}|{i}\rangle_{B} [214] as a free state, when HA=HB=∑iEi​|i⟩​⟨i|H_{A}=H_{B}=\sum_{i}E_{i}|{i}\rangle\!\langle{i}|. While 𝒮A⊗max𝒮B\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{max}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B} may appear contrived, it can be interpreted as a theory concerned with local, rather than global, resources.

Perhaps the most problematic aspect of maximal composition is that entanglement between subsystems is considered free, which may seem counter-intuitive. We define another composition rule precisely to address this issue. Separable composition

𝒮A⊗sep𝒮B​\coloneq​(𝒮A⊗max𝒮B)∩SEP,\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{sep}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B}\coloneq(\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{max}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B})\cap\mathrm{SEP}, (21)

where SEP\mathrm{SEP} denotes all separable states across the A|BA|B partition, explicitly excluding entanglement between subsystems as a free resource.

These composition rules streamline the analysis by making the set of CRNG operations identical to RNG operations, eliminating the need to consider resource-generating effects on larger Hilbert spaces.

Lemma 3.2 (original result).

If the set of free state 𝒮A​B\mathcal{S}_{AB} is either 𝒮A⊗min𝒮B\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{min}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B}, 𝒮A⊗sep𝒮B\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{sep}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B}, or 𝒮A⊗max𝒮B\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{max}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B}, then RNG = CRNG.

Proof.

First consider the case 𝒮A​B=𝒮A⊗min𝒮B\mathcal{S}_{AB}=\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{min}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B}. For any system BB, a free state γA​B∈𝒮A​B\gamma_{AB}\in\mathcal{S}_{AB} can be written as γA​B=∑ipi​(γA(i)⊗γB(i))\gamma_{AB}=\sum_{i}p_{i}(\gamma^{(i)}_{A}\otimes\gamma^{(i)}_{B}), where γB(i)∈𝒮B\gamma^{(i)}_{B}\in\mathcal{S}_{B} is another free state. Let ℰ∈CPTPA→A′\mathcal{E}\in\mathrm{CPTP}_{A\to A^{\prime}} be an RNG channel. Then the extension

ℰ⊗idB⁡(γA​B)=∑ipi​(γ~A′(i)⊗γB(i)),\displaystyle\mathcal{E}\otimes\id_{B}(\gamma_{AB})=\sum_{i}p_{i}(\tilde{\gamma}^{(i)}_{A^{\prime}}\otimes\gamma^{(i)}_{B}), (22)

where each γ~A′(i)=ℰ⁡(γA(i))∈𝒮A′\tilde{\gamma}^{(i)}_{A^{\prime}}=\mathcal{E}(\gamma^{(i)}_{A})\in\mathcal{S}_{A^{\prime}} is a free state. This implies that ℰ⊗idB\mathcal{E}\otimes\id_{B} is an RNG channel and thus ℰ\mathcal{E} is a CRNG channel.

Next, we prove the case 𝒮A​B=𝒮A⊗max𝒮B\mathcal{S}_{AB}=\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{max}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B}. Let γA​B∈𝒮A​B\gamma_{AB}\in\mathcal{S}_{AB} be any free state and ℰ\mathcal{E} be any RNG channel from AA to A′A^{\prime}. The extension γ~A​B=ℰ⊗idB⁡(γA​B)\tilde{\gamma}_{AB}=\mathcal{E}\otimes\id_{B}(\gamma_{AB}) is also free if and only if its reduced states are free. Since ℰ\mathcal{E} is RNG, the AA reduced state TrB⁡[γ~]=ℰ⁡(TrB⁡[γA​B])\Tr_{B}[\tilde{\gamma}]=\mathcal{E}(\Tr_{B}[\gamma_{AB}]) is free. The BB reduced state TrA⁡[γ~]=TrA⁡[γA​B]\Tr_{A}[\tilde{\gamma}]=\Tr_{A}[\gamma_{AB}] is free because γA​B∈𝒮A​B\gamma_{AB}\in\mathcal{S}_{AB} is free. Therefore, ℰ\mathcal{E} is a CRNG channel.

The proof is very similar for 𝒮A​B=𝒮A⊗sep𝒮B\mathcal{S}_{AB}=\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{sep}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B}. The free state γA​B=∑ipi​(ξA(i)⊗ζB(i))\gamma_{AB}=\sum_{i}p_{i}(\xi_{A}^{(i)}\otimes\zeta_{B}^{(i)}) for ξA(i)∈𝒟A\xi_{A}^{(i)}\in\mathcal{D}_{A}, ζB(i)∈𝒟B\zeta_{B}^{(i)}\in\mathcal{D}_{B}, pi≥0p_{i}\geq 0 for all ii and ∑ipi​ξA(i)∈𝒮A\sum_{i}p_{i}\xi_{A}^{(i)}\in\mathcal{S}_{A}, ∑ipi​ζB(i)∈𝒮B\sum_{i}p_{i}\zeta_{B}^{(i)}\in\mathcal{S}_{B} are free. The final state after the extended channel becomes

ℰ⊗idB⁡(γA​B)=∑ipi​(ξ~A′(i)⊗ζB(i)),\displaystyle\mathcal{E}\otimes\id_{B}(\gamma_{AB})=\sum_{i}p_{i}(\tilde{\xi}^{(i)}_{A^{\prime}}\otimes\zeta^{(i)}_{B}), (23)

where ξ~A′(i)∈𝒟A′\tilde{\xi}^{(i)}_{A^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{D}_{A^{\prime}} for all ii. Furthermore, since ℰ\mathcal{E} is an RNG channel, we have that ∑ipi​ξ~A′(i)∈𝒮A′\sum_{i}p_{i}\tilde{\xi}_{A^{\prime}}^{(i)}\in\mathcal{S}_{A^{\prime}} is free. Hence, ℰ⊗idB⁡(γA​B)\mathcal{E}\otimes\id_{B}(\gamma_{AB}) is separable and its reduced states are free, making it a free state in 𝒮A′⊗sep𝒮B\mathcal{S}_{A^{\prime}}\!\otimes_{\text{sep}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B}. ∎

After establishing these composition rules for sets of free states, one might wonder whether composition rules for free operations can be constructed in a similar fashion. The minimal composite free operation can be defined straightforwardly: convex combinations of tensor products of free operations are natural candidates. Unfortunately, there is no inclusion between CRNG⁡(𝒮A⊗min𝒮B)\mathrm{CRNG}(\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{min}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B}) and CRNG⁡(𝒮A⊗max𝒮B)\mathrm{CRNG}(\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{max}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B}), and taking the union of the two (and concatenations within the union set) trivialises the theory, as all quantum channels can be constructed in this way. Therefore, a better method is needed to define the maximal composite free operation. We leave this problem for future work.

Subsection 1 The impossible: no-broadcasting in minimal composition and other theories

With this newly developed categorisation of compositions in quantum resource theories, we establish a no-go theorem for robust catalysis when the composition restricts correlations between partitions of free states, i.e. when the free state set is minimal.

Theorem 3.3 (original result).

Suppose that a resource theory satisfies axioms (A1)–(A4) and takes CRNG as its free operations. If the composite free state sets are minimal, i.e. 𝒮A​B=𝒮A⊗min𝒮B\mathcal{S}_{AB}=\mathcal{S}_{A}\!\otimes_{\text{min}}\!\mathcal{S}_{B} for any AA and BB, then the theory allows neither resource broadcasting nor robust catalysis.

While no-broadcasting has previously been established in specific theories, such as asymmetry under connected Lie groups [200, 201] and, more recently, stabilizer operations [203], our result provides the first known sufficient condition that guarantees no-broadcasting across generic classes of resource theories.

The proof boils down to constructing an inequality that resembles the strong super-additivity of resource monotones. The strategy is to show that resource broadcasting increases the total amount of resources, which must not be possible. If there exists a faithful, strongly super-additive resource monotone ℙ\mathbb{P} (see Definitions 1.9 and 1.10), it is easy to prove no-broadcasting; if the broadcasting channel ℬ∈𝒪A→A​B\mathcal{B}\in\mathcal{O}_{A\to AB} maps ρA\rho_{A} to ℬ⁡(ρA)=ϱA​B\mathcal{B}(\rho_{A})=\varrho_{AB} with TrB⁡[ϱA​B]=ρA\Tr_{B}[\varrho_{AB}]=\rho_{A}, the monotonicity and super-additivity of ℙ\mathbb{P} implies

ℙ⁡(ρA)≥ℙ⁡(ϱA​B)≥ℙ⁡(ρA)+ℙ⁡(TrA⁡[ϱA​B]).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\rho_{A})\geq\mathbb{P}(\varrho_{AB})\geq\mathbb{P}(\rho_{A})+\mathbb{P}(\Tr_{A}[\varrho_{AB}]). (24)

When ℙ⁡(ρA)<∞\mathbb{P}(\rho_{A})<\infty, which is imposed by axiom (A4), ℙ⁡(TrA⁡[ϱA​B])=0\mathbb{P}(\Tr_{A}[\varrho_{AB}])=0 and the faithfulness of ℙ\mathbb{P} dictates that TrA⁡[ϱA​B]∈𝒮B\Tr_{A}[\varrho_{AB}]\in\mathcal{S}_{B}, indicating the failure of broadcasting.

In some resource theories, the existence of such monotones is known. Entries in the upper right cell of Table 1, except for the theory of asymmetry with respect to connected Lie group symmetries, are the examples. The asymmetry theory is an interesting exception: it is proven that no faithful strongly super-additive resource monotone exists for the theory, yet broadcasting is still not possible. Hence, no-broadcasting does not imply the existence of faithful strongly super-additive monotones.

In general, the existence of a faithful and super-additive monotone is not known.33 3 For the theories satisfying the assumptions of Theorem 3.3, measured relative entropy is found to be faithful and strongly super-additive [215]. This result can provide a simpler alternative proof for Theorem 3.3. Nevertheless, our proof establishes an inequality similar to Eq. (24) for resource broadcasting. First, we introduce a lemma necessary for the proof.

Lemma 3.4 (Ref. [103], Thm. 1).

Suppose that assumptions (A2) and (A3) hold. Furthermore, assume that for any POVM ℳ={Mi}i\mathcal{M}=\{M_{i}\}_{i} on XX and for all γX​Y∈𝒮X​Y\gamma_{XY}\in\mathcal{S}_{XY}, the post-measurement YY marginal state TrX⁡[(Mi⊗𝟙𝕐)​γ𝕏​𝕐]Tr⁡[(Mi⊗𝟙𝕐)​γ𝕏​𝕐]∈𝒮Y\frac{\Tr_{X}[(M_{i}\otimes\mathmybb{1}_{Y})\gamma_{XY}]}{\Tr[(M_{i}\otimes\mathmybb{1}_{Y})\gamma_{XY}]}\in\mathcal{S}_{Y} is free for any effect MiM_{i}. Then, for any ρX​Y∈𝒟X​Y\rho_{XY}\in\mathcal{D}_{XY},

R⁡(ρX​Y)≥R𝕄​(TrY​[ρX​Y])+R⁡(TrX​[ρX​Y]),\displaystyle R(\rho_{XY})\geq R_{\mathbb{M}}(\Tr_{Y}[\rho_{XY}])+R(\Tr_{X}[\rho_{XY}]), (25)

where the relative entropy of resource RR and the measured relative entropy of resources R𝕄R_{\mathbb{M}} are defined in Example 1.2 with (measured) relative entropy defined in Definitions 3.6 and 3.7.

Intuitively, Eq. (25) establishes a quasi-strong-super-additivity for the monotone RR. In the original paper [103], Lemma 3.4 is proven for a more general case, where the measured relative entropy of resource is optimised over a set of measurements, not necessarily all POVMs. For our proof of Theorem 3.3, the canonical choice R𝕄R_{\mathbb{M}} of optimisation over all POVMs is sufficient.

Proof for Theorem 3.3.

First, we state some properties of R𝕄R_{\mathbb{M}}:

  1. 1.

    R𝕄​(ρX)≤R⁡(ρX)R_{\mathbb{M}}(\rho_{X})\leq R(\rho_{X}) for any ρX\rho_{X}, by the data-processing inequality for Umegaki relative entropy;

  2. 2.

    R𝕄R_{\mathbb{M}} is faithful, i.e. R𝕄​(ρX)≥0R_{\mathbb{M}}(\rho_{X})\geq 0 with the equality if and only if ρX∈𝒮X\rho_{X}\in\mathcal{S}_{X} is free;

  3. 3.

    R𝕄R_{\mathbb{M}} is a monotone, i.e. R𝕄​(ℰ⁡(ρX))≤R𝕄​(ρX)R_{\mathbb{M}}(\mathcal{E}(\rho_{X}))\leq R_{\mathbb{M}}(\rho_{X}) for any ρX\rho_{X} and any free operation ℰ∈𝒪X→Y\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{X\to Y}.

Now consider a catalyst τC\tau_{C} and a free operation ℰ∈𝒪S​C→S′​C\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{SC\to S^{\prime}C} inducing a catalytic channel ℰ~\tilde{\mathcal{E}}. For any free system state γS∈𝒮S\gamma_{S}\in\mathcal{S}_{S}, denote χS′​C=ℰ⁡(γS⊗τC)\chi_{S^{\prime}C}=\mathcal{E}(\gamma_{S}\otimes\tau_{C}), where TrC​[χS′​C]=ℰ~​(γS)\Tr_{C}[\chi_{S^{\prime}C}]=\tilde{\mathcal{E}}(\gamma_{S}) and TrS′⁡[χS′​C]=τC\Tr_{S^{\prime}}[\chi_{S^{\prime}C}]=\tau_{C}. By monotonicity of RR,

R⁡(τC)=R⁡(γS⊗τC)≥R⁡(χS′​C),\displaystyle R(\tau_{C})=R(\gamma_{S}\otimes\tau_{C})\geq R(\chi_{S^{\prime}C}), (26)

where the first equality follows from both appending and discarding a free state γS\gamma_{S} being a free operation.

To apply Lemma 3.4, set the set of free states 𝒮S′​C=𝒮S′⊗min𝒮C\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}C}=\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}}\!\otimes_{\text{min}}\!\mathcal{S}_{C}.

  • •

    The first requirement—assumptions (A2) and (A3)—are already assumed as the axioms.

  • •

    The second requirement follows from the structure of 𝒮S′⊗min𝒮C\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}}\!\otimes_{\text{min}}\!\mathcal{S}_{C}: note that any free state γS′​C∈𝒮S′⊗min𝒮C\gamma_{S^{\prime}C}\in\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}}\!\otimes_{\text{min}}\!\mathcal{S}_{C} can be written as

    γS′​C=∑ipi​(γS′(i)⊗γ~C(i)).\displaystyle\gamma_{S^{\prime}C}=\sum_{i}p_{i}(\gamma_{S^{\prime}}^{(i)}\otimes\tilde{\gamma}_{C}^{(i)}). (27)

    Then for any POVM effect MiM_{i} that acts on system S′S^{\prime},

    TrS′⁡[(Mi⊗𝟙ℂ)​γ𝕊′​ℂ]Tr⁡[(Mi⊗𝟙ℂ)​γ𝕊′​ℂ]=∑ipi​Tr⁡[Mi​γS′(i)]​γ~C(i)∑ipi​Tr⁡[Mi​γS′(i)]​\eqcolon​∑ip~i​γ~C(i),\displaystyle\frac{\Tr_{S^{\prime}}\left[(M_{i}\otimes\mathmybb{1}_{C})\gamma_{S^{\prime}C}\right]}{\Tr\left[(M_{i}\otimes\mathmybb{1}_{C})\gamma_{S^{\prime}C}\right]}=\frac{\sum_{i}p_{i}\Tr[M_{i}\gamma_{S^{\prime}}^{(i)}]\tilde{\gamma}_{C}^{(i)}}{\sum_{i}p_{i}\Tr[M_{i}\gamma_{S^{\prime}}^{(i)}]}\eqcolon\sum_{i}\tilde{p}_{i}\tilde{\gamma}_{C}^{(i)}, (28)

    where {p~i}i\{\tilde{p}_{i}\}_{i} are valid convex coefficients. By convexity of the free state set, the resulting state in Eq. (28) remains free.

Now we are ready to use Lemma 3.4, which gives

R⁡(χS′​C)≥R𝕄​(ℰ~​(ρS))+R⁡(τC).\displaystyle R(\chi_{S^{\prime}C})\geq R_{\mathbb{M}}(\tilde{\mathcal{E}}(\rho_{S}))+R(\tau_{C}). (29)

Combined with Eq. (26), it follows that

R⁡(τC)≥R𝕄​(ℰ~​(ρS))+R⁡(τC),\displaystyle R(\tau_{C})\geq R_{\mathbb{M}}(\tilde{\mathcal{E}}(\rho_{S}))+R(\tau_{C}), (30)

reminiscent of Eq. (24). Whenever R⁡(τC)<∞R(\tau_{C})<\infty, which is guaranteed by axiom (A4),

0≥R𝕄​(ℰ~​(γS)).\displaystyle 0\geq R_{\mathbb{M}}(\tilde{\mathcal{E}}(\gamma_{S})). (31)

The faithfulness of R𝕄R_{\mathbb{M}} leads to the conclusion ℰ~​(γS)∈𝒮S′\tilde{\mathcal{E}}(\gamma_{S})\in\mathcal{S}_{S^{\prime}} is free for any free state γS∈𝒮S\gamma_{S}\in\mathcal{S}_{S}. In other words, catalytic channels for resource theories with minimal composition are always free operations. By Theorem 2.1, this also proves the no-broadcasting statement. ∎

Note that in Ref. [44] it has been shown that the super-additive monotone, if exists, also restricts marginal or correlated catalysis that are not robust. Our result then implies that theories with the minimal composition cannot be trivialized via (fine-tuned) marginal or correlated catalysis.

Furthermore, many significant theories that lie beyond the minimal composition class also lack robust catalytic advantage and do not permit resource broadcasting. In Table 1, entanglement, PPT entanglement, magic, asymmetry (connected Lie groups) and optical nonclassicality are such examples. Particularly interesting cases are Gibbs-preserving covariant (GPC) operations (Definition 1.2) and thermal operations (Definition 1.3).

GPC operation is an example that is not itself full CRNG, but is an intersection of multiple CRNG sets for different resources; in GPC’s case, these are Gibbs-preserving operations (athermality) and covariant operations (asymmetry). In such cases, if each constituent CRNG set does not allow broadcasting of its respective resource, then their intersection also inherits the no-broadcasting property and yields no advantage from robust catalysis.

For thermal operations, the no-broadcasting result already follows from that of Gibbs-preserving operations. However, showing that no advantageous robust catalysis exists is a trickier problem that requires an entirely different set of techniques. This is done in Ref. [187].

Thus far, all our results apply to robust catalysis scenarios in which the catalyst may retain correlations with the system post-operation. A stricter condition can be imposed: the catalyst must be recovered without any correlation (strict robust catalysis, as defined in Definition 1.1). By definition, strict robust catalysis cannot offer any advantage whenever general robust catalysis fail to do so. We demonstrate that the strict setting indeed imposes even more stringent requirements for the existence of robust catalysis.

Proposition 3.5 (original result).

In any resource theory having all CRNG operations as the free operation satisfying axioms (A1)-(A4), there is no strict robust catalytic advantage if the catalyst state is full-rank, i.e. if ρS⊗τC→ρS′⊗τC\rho_{S}\otimes\tau_{C}\to\rho^{\prime}_{S}\otimes\tau_{C} with a full-rank τC\tau_{C}, then ρS→ρS′\rho_{S}\to\rho^{\prime}_{S} is always possible without catalysts.

Proof.

We begin by defining the reversed relative entropy of resource, first used in Ref. [222] in the context of entanglement theory,

R(ρS)\coloneqinfγS∈𝒮SD(γS∥ρS).\displaystyle\scalebox{-1}[1]{R}\pqty{\rho_{S}}\coloneq\inf_{\gamma_{S}\in\mathcal{S}_{S}}D(\gamma_{S}\|\rho_{S}). (32)

This is a special case of the measure defined in Eq. (9), with the choice 𝔻=D\mathbb{D}=D. Furthermore, Proposition 1.2 proves that it is faithful, and also it is finite, i.e. R​(ρS)<∞\scalebox{-1}[1]{R}\pqty{\rho_{S}}<\infty when ρS\rho_{S} is full rank.

Another important property is the additivity

R​(ρS⊗ωS′)=R​(ρS)+R​(ωS′),\displaystyle\scalebox{-1}[1]{R}\pqty{\rho_{S}\otimes\omega_{S'}}=\scalebox{-1}[1]{R}\pqty{\rho_{S}}+\scalebox{-1}[1]{R}\pqty{\omega_{S'}}, (33)

which is derived using the property of the quantum relative entropy: D(γS​S′∥ρS⊗ωS′)≥D(TrS′[γS​S′]∥ρS)+D(TrS[γS​S′]∥ωS′)D(\gamma_{SS^{\prime}}\|\rho_{S}\otimes\omega_{S^{\prime}})\geq D(\Tr_{S^{\prime}}[\gamma_{SS^{\prime}}]\|\rho_{S})+D(\Tr_{S}[\gamma_{SS^{\prime}}]\|\omega_{S^{\prime}}), with the equality if and only if γS​S′\gamma_{SS^{\prime}} is an uncorrelated state. Now, suppose a free state γS∈𝒮S\gamma_{S}\in\mathcal{S}_{S} can be transformed into another state σS′\sigma_{S^{\prime}} via strict robust catalysis with a full rank catalyst τC\tau_{C}. Then there exists a free channel ℰ∈𝒪S​C→S′​C\mathcal{E}\in\mathcal{O}_{SC\to S^{\prime}C}, such that
