Section 3 Concluding Remarks

Quantum recursion, as defined in Eqs. (1)–(3), is a natural extension of the recursive steps in classical computing; it is perhaps the most general form, when the computation is unitary and the recursion depends only on the immediately previous result. Nevertheless, relatively little effort has been dedicated to analysing quantum recursions as a distinct class of quantum algorithm, except for a few case studies [299, 259]. We suspect that a primary reason for this is the lack of effective implementation strategies for such state-dependent unitaries.

In this section, we have introduced a systematic way of implementing quantum recursions using techniques in Section 1 and the identity Eq. (6). We have also explicated the implementation with a specific example of quantum imaginary-time evolution in Section 2. Although it suffers from the exponential circuit growth, common to unfolding implementation as in Eq. (7), the performance guarantees suggest that the total circuit depth required for modestly good performance might not be unduly severe; see, e.g. Eq. (30). These findings provide strong motivation for further studies into quantum recursions.

Another motivation for quantum recursions comes from how we derive the recursion unitary Eq. (17) from the non-linear Schrödinger equation Eq. (13). The core idea is to discretise the continuous non-linear differential equation, akin to the Euler method used for numerically solving differential equations with classical computers. Similarly, any non-linear Schrödinger equation can be recast as quantum recursions, albeit with errors arising from discretisation. This observation vastly expands the potential use-cases of quantum recursions. However, there is a caveat: for each non-linear Schrödinger equation, the implementation error (from discretisation of the differential equation and from approximations needed for unfolding implementation) must be carefully managed.33 3 This is the same for classical numerical algorithms; see e.g. Ref. [289] for the example of classical double-bracket algorithm.

The performance guarantees presented in Section 2 achieve this for the imaginary-time evolution, leveraging the exponential convergence of the algorithm. Since the trajectory following the differential equation is exponentially converging, some deviations resulting from implementation errors do not significantly affect performance. Hence, studying exponentially converging non-linear Schrödinger equations from the perspective of quantum recursions is an especially promising avenue for future research.

We provide an even stronger motivation for such endeavours in the next chapter, by presenting a technique that can resolve the exponential circuit depth problem by employing (exponentially many) auxiliary systems as memory.

Chapter 7 Quantum dynamic programming

In this chapter, we develop an approach to quantum recursions that is complementary to unfolding in Chapter 6. In particular, while unfolding performs un-computation and re-computation to address memory calls, our approach makes use of auxiliary systems instead. The main result is the exponential circuit depth reduction that can be achieved for a certain class of recursions, thanks to these auxiliaries. However, the number of auxiliary systems must be large for this circuit depth reduction, making our result a form of trade-off between circuit depth and width. Intuitively, we use auxiliary systems as quantum memories. They evolve with the system of interest, while storing the operations applied to them, and later instruct the computation using the stored information.

Specifically, our technique is a quantum adaptation of memoisation [49], a type of dynamic programming [300, 301]. Memoisation utilises a small amount of memory to yield vastly shorter computation times by avoiding re-computations. We outline how it is done in classical computing with the example of the Fibonacci sequence.

Example 0.1 (memoisation for Fibonacci sequence evaluation).

Fibonacci sequence is defined by the recurrence relation

F⁡(k)=F⁡(k−1)+F⁡(k−2),k≥2,\displaystyle F(k)=F(k-1)+F(k-2),\quad k\geq 2, (1)

and its base cases F⁡(0)=0F(0)=0 and F⁡(1)=1F(1)=1. It is possible to define an algorithm directly in this recursive manner. In this case F⁡(⋅)F(\cdot) is a function that calls itself twice: F⁡(k)F(k) would call F⁡(k−1)F(k-1) and F⁡(k−2)F(k-2), and each of those two would call (F⁡(k−2)F(k-2), F⁡(k−3)F(k-3)) and (F⁡(k−3)F(k-3), F⁡(k−4)F(k-4)), respectively. We can already see the obvious redundancy of this algorithm that re-calculate the same entry, e.g. F⁡(k−2)F(k-2), multiple times. Indeed, the time complexity of this algorithm can be evaluated. If the time complexity for F⁡(k)F(k) is TkT_{k}, it must be larger than the sum of Tk−1T_{k-1} and Tk−2T_{k-2}. Setting the base complexities T0=T1=1T_{0}=T_{1}=1, we get the recurrence relation for TkT_{k}, identical to Eq. (1), with base cases corresponding to T0=F⁡(1)T_{0}=F(1) and T1=F⁡(2)T_{1}=F(2). Hence, the complexity

TN≥F⁡(N+1)=O⁡((1+52)N),\displaystyle T_{N}\geq F(N+1)=O\left(\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)^{N}\right), (2)

exponential to NN.

However, a better algorithm exists. Suppose that there exists a “memo pad” that records the results F⁡(k)F(k) for each kk after evaluation. Furthermore, when the function F⁡(k)F(k) is called, instead of immediately starting the recursive function calls, we look up the memo pad and retrieve the result there if it already exists. This way, F⁡(k)F(k) for each kk is calculated only once, making the time complexity of the algorithm for F⁡(N)F(N) linear, i.e. TN=O⁡(N)T_{N}=O(N). In other words, an exponential speedup is achieved with the cost of memory of the size O⁡(N)O(N).

The redundancy observed in the memoryless implementation without memoisation is reminiscent of the unfolding implementation in Section 1. In the unfolding implementation, the memory-call ei​t​ρke^{it\rho_{k}} needed for each recursion step kk is synthesised using Eq. (6), i.e. ei​t​ρk=U^[ρk−1]​ei​t​ρk−1​(U^[ρk−1])†e^{it\rho_{k}}=\hat{U}^{[\rho_{k-1}]}e^{it\rho_{k-1}}(\hat{U}^{[\rho_{k-1}]})^{\dagger}, every time it is called. This repetition is the source of exponential circuit depth growth for the unfolding implementation, just like the exponential time complexity of the memoryless implementation in Example 0.1.

Hence, we expect a solution for quantum recursions analogous to classical recursive algorithms. However, the memoisation technique as in Example 0.1 cannot be used straightforwardly because of quintessentially quantum challenges. Memory utilisation in memoisation consists of two steps: writing down the kkth result after evaluating it and reading it out from the memory when needed. In quantum recursions, the kkth result of the recursion is a quantum state ρk\rho_{k}.

This result can be stored in two ways: classically or quantumly. The classical way is what we call the tomography-based learning-and-compiling method. Learning a quantum state is a challenge because of the uncertainty principle of quantum mechanics. In this approach, the classical description of ρk\rho_{k} (i.e. its density matrix) is extracted via tomography [302, 303, 304]. This process requires a large number of copies of ρk\rho_{k}, scaling polynomially with the dimension of the system (2n2^{n} for an n-qubit system), as detailed in Eq. (13).

It is infeasible to go through this scaling for each step kk, and hence we must consider storing the result state quantumly, i.e. as a memory state ρk\rho_{k}. Now, the remaining problem is how to read out this quantum memory to synthesise the quantum recursion unitary U^[ρk]\hat{U}^{[\rho_{k}]}.

Counter-intuitively, our solution uses the memories without reading them out. Specifically, we use the techniques introduced in Section 2. Note that those techniques—density matrix exponentiation (DME) or Hermitian-preserving map exponentiation (HME)—also require multiple copies of the instruction state ρk\rho_{k} to approximate the recursion unitary to good precision. Nevertheless, the scaling is typically better: for example, DME requires M=1ϵM=\frac{1}{\epsilon} copies without the explicit dependence (Eq. (12)) on the system dimension, as opposed to Eq. (13).

In this sense, our approach belongs to a lineage of studies on circuits instructed by quantum states [250, 305, 306, 252, 307, 253, 254, 255, 308, 251, 309], where desired operations are implemented by injecting quantum instruction states that encode the operation, rather than by compiling circuits based on classical information. However, we use this technique not only with given (static) quantum states, but also with quantum memories that are dynamically evolving. We call this alternative algorithmic paradigm for quantum recursions quantum dynamic programming (QDP).

The main breakthrough of this work is the following observation: instead of unfolding the recursion (i.e. synthesising U^[ρk]\hat{U}^{[\rho_{k}]} with exponentially many queries to U^[ρ0]\hat{U}^{[\rho_{0}]}), we can evolve memory states from ρ0\rho_{0} to ρk\rho_{k} in parallel and directly implement U^[ρk]\hat{U}^{[\rho_{k}]} by injecting these memory states. In essence, QDP “folds up” the unfolded recursion step U^[ρk]\hat{U}^{[\rho_{k}]} into the memory state as it evolves to ρk\rho_{k}. By doing so, we achieve an exponential circuit depth reduction compared to the unfolding approach, as formalised in Theorems 1.1 and 2.1, on a par with the classic example of computing Fibonacci numbers. In the rest of this chapter, we introduce QDP in more detail and prove the exponential circuit depth reduction for two separate cases: pure state recursions and mixed state recursions.

My original results in this section include Theorems 1.1, 2.1 and Lemma 5.1.

Section 1 Pure state recursions

In this section, we consider quantum recursions with pure quantum states evolving as

|ψk⟩=U^[ψk−1]​|ψk−1⟩,\displaystyle|{\psi_{k}}\rangle=\hat{U}^{[\psi_{k-1}]}|{\psi_{k-1}}\rangle, (3)

with the notation for its density matrix ψk=|ψk⟩​⟨ψk|\psi_{k}=|{\psi_{k}}\rangle\!\langle{\psi_{k}}|. As in the unfolding implementation introduced in Section 1, we approximate the recursion unitary U^[ψ]\hat{U}^{[\psi]} by

U^[{fi}i,ψ]=VL​ei​fL​(ψ)​VL−1​…​V1​ei​f1​(ψ)​V0,\displaystyle\hat{U}^{[\{f_{i}\}_{i},\psi]}=V_{L}e^{if_{L}(\psi)}V_{L-1}\ldots V_{1}e^{if_{1}(\psi)}V_{0}, (4)

where {fi}i\{f_{i}\}_{i} is a collection of Hermitian-preserving (linear or polynomial) maps fif_{i}, while ViV_{i} are static unitaries independent of the instruction |ψ⟩|{\psi}\rangle. The quantum recursion unitary Eq. (4) contains LL memory-calls of the form ei​f​(ψ)e^{if(\psi)}. Recall that DB-QITE Eq. (21) introduced in Section 2 is one example of a pure state recursion with one memory-call ei​sk​ψke^{i\sqrt{s_{k}}\psi_{k}} and two constant unitaries e±i​sk​He^{\pm i\sqrt{s_{k}}H}.

To resolve the exponential depth of unfolded circuits discussed in Chapter 6, QDP invokes dynamically evolving memory states to directly instruct memory-calls. That is, instead of synthesising ei​fi​(ψk)e^{if_{i}(\psi_{k})} using multiple queries to U^[ψk−1]\hat{U}^{[\psi_{k-1}]} as in unfolding implementation (Proposition 1.2 followed by Eq. (6)), multiple copies of |ψk⟩|{\psi_{k}}\rangle and HME are used to implement ei​fi​(ψk)e^{if_{i}(\psi_{k})} directly. To reiterate the scheme, we first define Eq. (15) as a memory-usage query

ℰ^τ[f,ρ]​(σS)​\coloneq​TrS¯​[e−i​τ​F​(ρS¯⊗σS)​ei​τ​F].\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{[f,\rho]}_{\tau}(\sigma_{S})\coloneq\Tr_{\bar{S}}\left[e^{-i\tau F}\left(\rho_{\bar{S}}\otimes\sigma_{S}\right)e^{i\tau F}\right]. (5)

Here, F​\coloneq​d​(Cf)\transpS¯F\coloneq d(C_{f})^{\transp_{\bar{S}}}, where CfC_{f} is the Choi matrix of ff as defined in Definition 2.5, dd is the dimension of SS, and the partial transpose \transpS¯\transp_{\bar{S}} acts only on the system S¯\bar{S} that has the same size as the system SS. We call SS as the working register, upon which the operation acts, and S¯\bar{S} as the memory register, which contains the instruction state ρ\rho. Each memory-usage query invokes an error that scales quadratically with the duration τ\tau. By setting τ=1/M\tau=1/M and the same memory-usage queries (Eq. (5)) MM times, we obtain the channel (ℰ^1/M[f,ρ])M(\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{[f,\rho]}_{1/M})^{M}, which approximates the memory-call unitary ei​f​(ρ)e^{if(\rho)} with a total error O⁡(τ2/M)O(\tau^{2}/M). Therefore, the error in the memory-call approximation can be kept arbitrarily small by increasing MM.

To be explicit, we approximate the recursion unitary Eq. (4) by intialising the recursion with σ0=ψ0\sigma_{0}=\psi_{0} and define the QDP iteration as

σk+1=VL​(ℰ^1/M[fL,σk])M​VL−1​…​V1​(ℰ^1/M[fL,σk])M​V0,\displaystyle\sigma_{k+1}=V_{L}\left(\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{[f_{L},\sigma_{k}]}_{1/M}\right)^{M}V_{L-1}\ldots V_{1}\left(\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{[f_{L},\sigma_{k}]}_{1/M}\right)^{M}V_{0}, (6)

i.e. each memory-call is approximated by MM memory-usage queries, totalling M​LML memory-usage queries for a step. In general, memory states σk≠0\sigma_{k\neq 0} are no longer pure because the channel ℰ^1/M[fi,σk]\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{[f_{i},\sigma_{k}]}_{1/M} is not exactly unitary. However, we show in Theorem 1.1 that σN\sigma_{N} can be made arbitrarily close to the desired state |ψN⟩|{\psi_{N}}\rangle.

To prepare one copy of σ1\sigma_{1}, we make M​LML memory-usage queries with the memory state σ0\sigma_{0}. This requires (M​L+1)(ML+1) root state copies (M​LML in the memory register and one in the working register). Likewise, preparing σ2\sigma_{2} requires (M​L+1)2(ML+1)^{2} copies of σ0\sigma_{0}; thus, the iteration of Eq. (6) consumes (M​L+1)k(ML+1)^{k} copies of the root state for preparing one copy of σk\sigma_{k}. Meanwhile, the circuit depth remains linear: multiple instruction states can be prepared in parallel, resulting in a maximum depth of k​M​LkML memory-usage queries. Compare this to the unfolding scenario in Section 1, where a memory-call to |ψk⟩|{\psi_{k}}\rangle is executed by making (2​M​L+1)k(2ML+1)^{k} memory-calls to the root state (see Eq. (7)). In contrast, QDP folds all root state calls into the memory state σk\sigma_{k}, allowing a memory-call to be implemented with a fixed-depth circuit.

QDP inherently involves approximation errors at each step, which depend on MM, the number of memory-usage queries per memory-call. Setting M=O⁡(1/ϵ)M=O(1/\epsilon) in Eq. (6) ensures that the QDP prepared state σ1\sigma_{1} approximates the exact result |ψ1⟩|{\psi_{1}}\rangle within an error ‖σ1−ψ1‖1≤O⁡(ϵ)\|\sigma_{1}-\psi_{1}\|_{1}\leq O(\epsilon), in terms of the Schatten 1-norm ∥⋅∥1\|\cdot\|_{1} defined in Definition 3.2. However, subsequent steps may amplify this error, as σ1↦σ2\sigma_{1}\mapsto\sigma_{2} becomes instructed by the approximate state σ1\sigma_{1}, not the exact state |ψ1⟩|{\psi_{1}}\rangle. Indeed, the triangle inequality gives ‖σk+1−ψk+1‖1≤O⁡((M​L+1)​‖σk−ψk‖1)\|\sigma_{k+1}-\psi_{k+1}\|_{1}\leq O((ML+1)\|\sigma_{k}-\psi_{k}\|_{1}), which in principle allows the exponential error accumulation

‖σN−ψN‖1=O⁡((M​L+1)N),\displaystyle\|\sigma_{N}-\psi_{N}\|_{1}=O((ML+1)^{N}), (7)

indicating the failure of QDP.

To address this, we identify sufficient conditions to prevent such destructive error propagation. It turns out that if the first few steps are sufficiently accurate, then later steps benefit from stabilization properties of typical quantum recursions. In particular, recursions with fixed-points (e.g. via the Polyak-Łojasiewicz inequality in gradient descent iterations [296] or asymptotic stability in time-discrete dynamical systems [289]) typically exhibit exponential convergence. For quantum recursions, this implies ‖ψN−ψ∞‖1≤αN​‖ψ0−ψ∞‖1\|\psi_{N}-\psi_{\infty}\|_{1}\leq\alpha^{N}\|\psi_{0}-\psi_{\infty}\|_{1}, for some α<1\alpha<1. However, this relies on the assumption we call fast spectral convergence, whose formal definition is stated in Definition 5.1. Informally, fast spectral convergence can be understood as:

  1. (i)

    There exists a stable fixed-point |ψ∞⟩|{\psi_{\infty}}\rangle as N→∞N\rightarrow\infty.

  2. (ii)

    The fixed-point is unique for any initial state |ψ0⟩|{\psi_{0}}\rangle.

  3. (iii)

    The fixed-point is sufficiently strongly attracting.

Without (iii), recursions become unstable, suggesting limited physical relevance, as practically achievable protocols must withstand small perturbations. In such cases, quantum computation would require infinite precision and resources for a successful operation.

It is worth noting that unfolding is also subject to similar stability constraints: if U^[ψ0]\hat{U}^{[\psi_{0}]} is not compiled exactly, subsequent recursion unitaries U^[ψk]\hat{U}^{[\psi_{k}]}, which rely on exponentially many applications of U^[ψ0]\hat{U}^{[\psi_{0}]}, become exponentially unstable. Thus, whether using QDP or unfolding, quantum recursions must exhibit fast spectral convergence; otherwise, the computational task is ill-conditioned. When this condition is met, QDP delivers an exponential depth reduction compared to unfolding:

Theorem 1.1 (Exponential circuit depth reduction; original result).

Suppose a quantum recursion starting from |ψ0⟩|{\psi_{0}}\rangle satisfies fast spectral convergence. Then QDP combined with a mixedness reduction protocol yields a final state σN\sigma_{N} satisfying

‖σN−ψN‖1≤ϵ,\displaystyle\|\sigma_{N}-\psi_{N}\|_{1}\leq\epsilon, (8)

for any final error 0<ϵ<230<\epsilon<\frac{2}{3} and with any success probability 1−pth1-p_{\mathrm{th}}, using a circuit of depth O⁡(N​ϵ−1)O(N\epsilon^{-1}) and width ϵ−N​eO⁡(N)​log⁡(pth−1)\epsilon^{-N}e^{O(N)}\log(p_\mathrm{th}^{-1}). Here, ψN=|ψN⟩​⟨ψN|\psi_{N}=|{\psi_{N}}\rangle\!\langle{\psi_{N}}| is the exact solution to the recursion.

We prove this theorem in Section 5 by addressing two error types. Unitary errors are efficiently suppressed by fast spectral convergence; on the other hand, non-unitary errors destabilise convergence and require explicit mitigation. To suppress the latter, we employ an additional protocol (Proposition 3.1) designed to mitigate these non-unitary errors for pure states. This protocol is applied following each recursion step implemented through Eq. (6). The proof of Theorem 1.1 demonstrates this protocol incurs only a slightly faster exponential growth in circuit width. Moreover, this additional mixedness reduction protocol is probabilistic, rendering QDP for pure states probabilistic. However, it is possible to achieve an arbitrarily large success probability with overhead log⁡(pth−1)\log(p_\mathrm{th}^{-1}) where pthp_{\mathrm{th}} is the upper bound for the probability of failure.

Section 2 Mixed state recursions

Similarly to the pure state case in Section 1, we define the mixed state recursion starting from a mixed state ρ0\rho_{0} as

ρk↦ρk+1=𝐔^[ρk]​(ρk),\displaystyle\rho_{k}\mapsto\rho_{k+1}=\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho_{k}]}(\rho_{k}), (9)

where 𝐔^[ρk]\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho_{k}]} is the unitary channel corresponding to the recursion unitary U^[ρk]\hat{U}^{[\rho_{k}]} that depends on ρk\rho_{k}. Furthermore, the fast spectral convergence conditions in Section 1 need to be slightly refined to account for the mixed state cases. Specifically, we update the uniqueness of the fixed-point (condition (ii)) to be

  • (ii’)

    The fixed-point is spectrally unique, i.e. if the initial states ρ0\rho_{0} and ρ0′\rho^{\prime}_{0} have the same spectrum, they have the same fixed-point ρ∞=ρ∞′\rho_{\infty}=\rho^{\prime}_{\infty}.

For pure states, conditions (ii) and (ii’) are equivalent; the formal statement is in Definition 5.1.

The exponential circuit depth reduction established in Theorem 1.1 can also be achieved for mixed state recursions, albeit with lower efficiency.

Theorem 2.1 (Mixed state quantum dynamic programming; original result).

Suppose the quantum recursion satisfies fast spectral convergence. For any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, implementing NN recursion steps with each memory-call replaced by O⁡(N​ϵ−1)O(N\epsilon^{-1}) memory-usage queries, yields a final state σN\sigma_{N}, such that

‖σN−ρN‖1≤ϵ,\displaystyle\|\sigma_{N}-\rho_{N}\|_{1}\leq\epsilon, (10)

using a circuit of depth O⁡(N2​ϵ−1)O(N^{2}\epsilon^{-1}). Here, ρN\rho_{N} is the exact solution to the recursion.

This theorem is proved in Section 5. Note that we do not have an explicit exponential scaling of the circuit width in this case unlike Theorem 1.1. This is due to the lack of an additional protocol, corresponding to the mixedness reduction for the pure state case, that can preserve the spectrum of the density matrices. Hence, the non-unitary error from memory-usage queries must be suppressed by requiring each memory-usage query to be very close to a unitary channel. Unfortunately, the recently developed channel purification protocol [310], which is a quantum channel version of the state mixedness reduction protocols, also does not improve the scaling, as the number of copies needed for the channel purification is comparable to that of improving each memory-usage query. Hence, using our construction, the circuit width scales doubly exponentially in the worst case, which is highly impractical.

Section 3 Examples

We emphasise the potential impact of QDP by presenting examples of quantum recursions that can benefit from QDP.

Example 3.1 (nested fixed-point Grover search [259]).

The nested fixed-point Grover search [259], is a recursive version of the Grover search algorithm. The Grover search algorithm aims to transform a state |ψ0⟩|{\psi_{0}}\rangle into the one close to the unknown target state |τ⟩|{\tau}\rangle. This transformation is achieved by

|ψ0⟩↦|ψ1⟩=(∏i=1Le−i​αi​ψ0​e−i​βi​τ)​|ψ0⟩,\displaystyle|{\psi_{0}}\rangle\mapsto|{\psi_{1}}\rangle=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{L}e^{-i\alpha_{i}\psi_{0}}e^{-i\beta_{i}\tau}\right)|{\psi_{0}}\rangle, (11)

with density matrices ψ0=|ψ0⟩​⟨ψ0|\psi_{0}=|{\psi_{0}}\rangle\!\langle{\psi_{0}}|, τ=|τ⟩​⟨τ|\tau=|{\tau}\rangle\!\langle{\tau}|, and suitable angles {αi,βi}i\{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}\}_{i}. This transformation achieves

12​‖ψ1−τ‖1≃e−|⟨ψ0|τ⟩|​(2​L+1),\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\|\psi_{1}-\tau\|_{1}\simeq e^{-\lvert\langle{\psi_{0}}|{\tau}\rangle\rvert(2L+1)}, (12)

for large LL, which implies L=O⁡(|⟨ψ0|τ⟩|−1)L=O(\lvert\langle{\psi_{0}}|{\tau}\rangle\rvert^{-1}) achieving the quadratic advantage over the classical serach scaling as |⟨ψ0|τ⟩|−2\lvert\langle{\psi_{0}}|{\tau}\rangle\rvert^{-2}.

A recursive variant of this algorithm starts from the idea that, instead of setting a large LL for one round of the Grover search, we can choose small LL to obtain |ψ1⟩|{\psi_{1}}\rangle and re-initiate the Grover search with the new initial state |ψ1⟩|{\psi_{1}}\rangle and the reflection e−i​αi​ψ1e^{-i\alpha_{i}\psi_{1}}. Although |ψ1⟩|{\psi_{1}}\rangle is not very close to τ\tau due to small LL, the distance to τ\tau is decreased compared to |ψ0⟩|{\psi_{0}}\rangle, and the new round of the Grover search would transform it into a state that is even closer to τ\tau. An iteration of this process is called nested fixed-point Grover search, and it can be written as a quantum recursion

|ψk+1⟩=(∏i=1Le−i​αi​ψk​e−i​βi​τ)​|ψk⟩​\eqcolon​U^[ψk]​|ψk⟩.\displaystyle|{\psi_{k+1}}\rangle=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{L}e^{-i\alpha_{i}\psi_{k}}e^{-i\beta_{i}\tau}\right)|{\psi_{k}}\rangle\eqcolon\hat{U}^{[\psi_{k}]}|{\psi_{k}}\rangle. (13)

The performance of this algorithm is known to be equivalent to its non-recursive counterpart [259], that is, the circuit depth required for a desired final distance to τ\tau for non-recursive and recursive Grover search algorithms are almost equivalent. For the recursive version, the distance to the target final state |τ⟩|{\tau}\rangle evolves as

12​‖ψN−τ‖1≃e−|⟨ψ0|τ⟩|​(2​L+1)N,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\|\psi_{N}-\tau\|_{1}\simeq e^{-\lvert\langle{\psi_{0}}|{\tau}\rangle\rvert(2L+1)^{N}}, (14)

with (2​L+1)(2L+1) in the non-recursive version (Eq. (12)) replaced by (2​L+1)N(2L+1)^{N}. Nevertheless, when the recursion is implemented through unfolding as in Section 1, the total circuit depth scales exponentially as (2​L+1)N(2L+1)^{N}, annulling the improvement. This unfolding implementation and its analysis have been studied in Ref. [259], albeit with small differences in details.

Since Eq. (14) exhibits fast spectral convergence, the QDP implementation we developed in this chapter can be applied; this reduces the circuit depth to O⁡(N)O(N) but with the requirement of exponential copies of the initial state |ψ0⟩|{\psi_{0}}\rangle. Unfortunately, it is known that [252] there is no quantum advantage in sample-based Grover search algorithms, which include the QDP implementation. Nevertheless, this example serves as a valuable demonstration of QDP’s applicability for a historically significant quantum algorithm.

The second example is the double-bracket quantum imaginary-time evolution (DB-QITE) algorithm introduced in Chapter 6. There are two different ways to apply QDP for two different setups of implementing DB-QITE.

Example 3.2 (DB-QITE (Section 2)).

The recursion unitary is defined in Eq. (21), and Theorem 2.2 guarantees the fast spectral convergence of this recursion. Hence, it is possible to apply QDP to this algorithm by replacing the memory-call ei​sk​ψke^{i\sqrt{s_{k}}\psi_{k}} in the recursion unitary with the DME memory-usage query Eq. (5) with f=idf=\id. Since the recursion states |ψk⟩|{\psi_{k}}\rangle are pure, Theorem 1.1 can be applied, which implements NN steps of DB-QITE recursion with circuit depth linear to NN and width exponential to NN.

Interestingly, QDP can directly implement another recursion, which could not have been implemented via unfolding. Specifically, QDP can be applied to the QITE recursion Eq. (17), which we call QITE DBI. QITE DBI, which yields DB-QITE following a product formula approximation, exhibits a superior convergence rate to the ground state in terms of recursion steps when compared to DB-QITE (see Table II of Ref. [4]). However, its performance concerning circuit depth or width requires separate evaluation and warrants a dedicated study. This example is presented primarily to showcase QDP’s ability to unlock new quantum recursions for implementation.

Example 3.3 (QITE DBI).

The recursion Eq. (17) is known as QITE DBI in Ref. [4]. Furthermore a convergence theorem similar to Theorem 2.2 has been established in the same paper. Importantly, both algorithms converge to the ground state with the fidelity 1−qk1-q^{k} after kk steps, and QITE DBI typically has a larger lower bound for qq than DB QITE.

To apply QDP, we consider the sample-based Hamiltonian simulation setup [252]. In other words, instead of having access to evolutions e−i​t​He^{-itH}, multiple copies of the state Θ∝H\Theta\propto H that encodes the Hamiltonian are given. Multiple copies of Θ\Theta can indeed emulate the evolution e−i​t​He^{-itH} with DME. We also prepare copies of some pure state |ψ0⟩|{\psi_{0}}\rangle having non-zero overlap with the ground state. Using Θ\Theta and |ψ0⟩|{\psi_{0}}\rangle copies, recursions of the form

|ψk⟩↦|ψk+1⟩=es⁡[|ψk⟩​⟨ψk|,H]​|ψk⟩,\displaystyle|{\psi_{k}}\rangle\mapsto|{\psi_{k+1}}\rangle=e^{s[|{\psi_{k}}\rangle\!\langle{\psi_{k}}|,H]}|{\psi_{k}}\rangle, (15)

with some duration ss can be implemented oblivious to both HH and |ψk⟩|{\psi_{k}}\rangle with Proposition 2.3.

Finally, we introduce a novel algorithm that is natively dynamic.

Example 3.4 (oblivious Schmidt decomposition).

For pure bipartite states, the Schmidt decomposition (Definition 1.1) fully characterises their entanglement. Thus we may envision a protocol that unitarily transforms any unknown |ψ0⟩∈ℋA​B|{\psi_{0}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{AB} into a form where its Schmidt basis aligns with the computational basis: VA⊗VB​|ψ0⟩=∑k=1Dλk​|k⟩⊗|k⟩V_{A}\otimes V_{B}|{\psi_{0}}\rangle=\sum_{k=1}^{D}\sqrt{\lambda_{k}}|{k}\rangle\otimes|{k}\rangle with {λk}k\{\lambda_{k}\}_{k} denoting the Schmidt spectrum.

Traditionally, prior knowledge of |ψ0⟩|{\psi_{0}}\rangle is required to construct VAV_{A} and VBV_{B}. However, QDP enables this task while completely circumventing such a need. In this section, we demonstrate that this task is achievable by diagonalizing the reduced state of a given pure state ψ\psi via an adaptation of the double-bracket iteration [292], similar to Eq. (16).

We first describe how double-bracket iterations on the reduced system can be implemented with memory-usage queries using the entire bi-partite state. Suppose that multiple copies of the instruction state |ψk⟩A​B|{\psi_{k}}\rangle_{AB} are given. Let DD be a non-degenerate diagonal operator on subsystem AA. The recursion unitary is defined as

U^[f,ψk]=es⁡[D,TrB⁡[ψk]]⊗𝟙𝔹.\displaystyle\hat{U}^{[f,\psi_{k}]}=e^{s\left[D,\Tr_{B}[\psi_{k}]\right]}\otimes\mathmybb{1}_{B}\ . (16)

This is a single memory-call type recursion with f(ρA​B)=−is[D,TrB[ρA​B]]⊗𝟙𝔹f(\rho_{AB})=-is[D,\Tr_{B}[\rho_{AB}]]\otimes\mathmybb{1}_{B} that is Hermitian-preserving; hence, with copies of |ψk⟩|{\psi_{k}}\rangle, the recursion step |ψk⟩↦|ψk+1⟩=U^[ψk]​|ψk⟩|{\psi_{k}}\rangle\mapsto|{\psi_{k+1}}\rangle=\hat{U}^{[\psi_{k}]}|{\psi_{k}}\rangle can be approximated using HME. The fast spectral convergence of such a unitary is shown in Refs. [291, 290]. When ss is small, Theorem 1.1 applies and {|ψk⟩}\{|{\psi_{k}}\rangle\} exponentially converges to the fixed-point of the recursion Eq. (16). This fixed-point is the state that commutes with the matrix DD, i.e. a state diagonal to the computational basis. In other words, QDP effectively applies VA⊗𝟙𝔹​|ψ𝟘⟩V_{A}\otimes\mathmybb{1}_{B}|{\psi_{0}}\rangle. A similar procedure implements VBV_{B}, completing the oblivious Schmidt decomposition.

Let us discuss the implications of oblivious Schmidt decomposition in the context of quantum information processing. The replica method [311] extracts classical information λk\lambda_{k} but requires exponentially many swap operations. Similarly, we expect that oblivious Schmidt decomposition may also require a long runtime to converge. However, it not only enables sampling from the Schmidt spectrum but also provides the bipartite quantum state ∑kλk​|k⟩⊗|k⟩\sum_{k}\sqrt{\lambda_{k}}|{k}\rangle\otimes|{k}\rangle coherently in the computational basis. This is useful, e.g. for entanglement distillation of an unknown state ψ\psi, contrasting with standard settings [130] that require the knowledge about the initial state for compiling local operations. While oblivious Schmidt decomposition via QDP may not attain the optimal asymptotic rates as derived from Ref. [312], it provides a constructive approach to oblivious entanglement distillation with explicit circuit implementations.

Section 4 Concluding remarks: Implications of the depth-width trade-off

Theorems 1.1 and 2.1 establish the circuit depth-width trade-off. At its core, this trade-off is valuable because it exponentially reduces computational time, which can turn a practically impossible task into a feasible one. Beyond this immediate advantage, we focus on how QDP facilitates implementation.

One simple measure is the quantum circuit size, defined as the product of the maximum circuit depth and width [313, 314]. We illustrate how this measure benefits from the trade-off. Suppose that in each recursion step, LL memory-calls to ρ\rho are made, each approximated by MM black-box access to the evolution of the form e−i​t​ρe^{-it\rho}. The unfolding circuit size therefore scales as (2​M​L+1)N(2ML+1)^{N} for NN recursion steps as described in Eq. (7). Meanwhile, memory-usage queries directly implement each memory-call, but require M′M^{\prime} memory-usage queries to manage implementation error, i.e. M′​LM^{\prime}L memory-usage queries per recursion step. In this scenario, the QDP circuit width scales as (M′​L+1)N(M^{\prime}L+1)^{N}, which dominates the total circuit size for large NN. Whenever LL is large and M′<2​MM^{\prime}<2M, QDP approximately achieves a (2​M/M′)N(2M/M^{\prime})^{N}-fold improvement in circuit size compared to unfolding. For instance, in the most error-tolerant case of M=M′=1M=M^{\prime}=1, QDP significantly reduces the circuit size.

An interesting comparison arises from studies on quantum circuit complexity, which has been studied in contexts ranging from quantum circuit compilation to black holes [31, 315, 316, 317, 318]. Quantum circuit complexity of a state is defined as the minimum number of 2-local gates required to prepare that state from a fiducial state such as |0⟩|{0}\rangle. An implicit assumption in this definition is that the system is closed, without auxiliary systems. Ref. [319] explores the consequences of relaxing this assumption, investigating the depth-width trade-off when auxiliaries are employed. It demonstrates that using auxiliary systems enables the preparation of more complex states with shallower circuits, while the overall circuit size remains comparable (up to constant factors). Intriguingly, this advantage is gained by using the auxiliaries to effectively “fold up” the complexity within them, which is then transferred using the gate teleportation scheme [320]. This mechanism of using auxiliary systems to store and later deploy complexity closely parallels the way quantum memories are employed in QDP.

Beyond circuit size, QDP offers additional practical advantages: its local modularity is particularly well-suited for distributed quantum computing [321, 50, 322]. By localizing and decoupling circuits [323], QDP allows copies of |ψk⟩|{\psi_{k}}\rangle to be prepared independently before being injected into recursion steps U^[ψk]\hat{U}^{[\psi_{k}]}. As the recursion progresses, the circuit width decreases exponentially as most copies are consumed as memory and traced out during memory-usage queries. This enables greater flexibility in parallelization, since processors with shorter coherence times can be allocated for preparing |ψk⟩|{\psi_{k}}\rangle with smaller kk, optimizing the use of available quantum devices.

The flexibility of QDP is reinforced by a hybrid strategy. Realistically, quantum devices can neither execute exponentially many sequential gates nor operate on exponentially many qubits simultaneously. A practical approach is to initiate QDP after several rounds of unfolding, distributing the exponential factor between circuit depth and width to prevent either from becoming prohibitive. For example, one could begin with N1N_{1} unfolding steps, using a circuit of depth eO⁡(N1)e^{O(N_{1})}, nearing the device’s depth limit. These unfolding steps are performed in parallel, maximizing circuit width to produce MM copies of intermediate states |ψN1⟩|{\psi_{N_{1}}}\rangle. For many quantum recursions, this starting strategy also conveniently steers the system into a regime where the recursion starts to exhibit fast spectral convergence. This allows QDP to subsequently take over, executing an additional N2N_{2} recursions to attain the final state σN1+N2\sigma_{N_{1}+N_{2}}. This hybrid strategy fully utilises the device capacity, which is otherwise limited to producing either |ψN1⟩|{\psi_{N_{1}}}\rangle without QDP or σN2\sigma_{N_{2}} without unfolding.

Currently, we are unaware of quantum algorithms where QDP ensures a rigorous computational advantage over classical methods. These may appear in settings robust against imperfect unitary implementations, similar to those present in diagonalizing double-bracket iterations [291, 290, 292]. Furthermore, QDP allows us to add oblivious Schmidt decomposition to the quantum algorithmic toolkit. We hope that once it will be feasible to experimentally implement memory-usage queries with high fidelity, oblivious Schmidt decomposition and QDP in general will facilitate practical state preparations that will advance our knowledge of quantum properties in materials, e.g. magnets or superconductors.

Section 5 Proofs of exponential circuit depth reduction

We begin by formally defining fast spectral convergence for pure and mixed state recursions.

Definition 5.1 (Fast spectral convergence).

Consider a quantum recursion unitary channel 𝐔^[ρ]\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho]} that defines a fixed-point iteration

ρ↦𝐔^[ρ]​(ρ).\displaystyle\rho\mapsto\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho]}(\rho). (17)

This recursion defines sequences {ρ0}k=0∞\{\rho_{0}\}_{k=0}^{\infty} for each initial state ρ0\rho_{0}.

The recursion has the fast spectral convergence property if it satisfies the following conditions.

  1. 1.

    For any initial state ρ0\rho_{0}, the sequence must converge to a fixed-point τ\tau, i.e. the trace distance δk​\coloneq​12​‖τ−ρk‖1<δk−1\delta_{k}\coloneq\frac{1}{2}\|\tau-\rho_{k}\|_{1}<\delta_{k-1} and limk→∞δk=0\displaystyle\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\delta_{k}=0.

  2. 2.

    The fixed-point τ\tau must be the same for any two initial states ρ0\rho_{0} and ρ0~\tilde{\rho_{0}} (with the exception of states chosen from a measure zero set), with spec⁡(ρ0)=spec⁡(ρ~0)\spec(\rho_{0})=\spec(\tilde{\rho}_{0}).

  3. 3.

    The convergence must be fast, i.e. for any iso-spectral states ρ\rho and σ\sigma,

    ‖𝐔^[ρ]​(ρ)−𝐔^[σ]​(σ)‖≤r​‖ρ−σ‖\displaystyle\|\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho]}(\rho)-\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\sigma]}(\sigma)\|\leq r\|\rho-\sigma\| (18)

    for some r<1r<1.

Spectral convergence implies that the QDP implementation will also approach the same fixed-point, when the non-unitary error is not too large. Note that Theorem 2.2 guarantees the fast spectral convergence for DB-QITE algorithm.

We first prove Theorem 2.1 valid for mixed state recursions.

Proof of Theorem 2.1.

From Proposition 2.2, we are able to locally accurately implement the unitary channel 𝐔^[ρ]\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho]} by a non-unitary channel 𝒰^[ρ]\hat{\mathcal{U}}^{[\rho]}, such that

12​‖𝐔^[ρ]−𝒰^[ρ]‖Tr≤η,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho]}-\hat{\mathcal{U}}^{[\rho]}\right\|_{\Tr}\leq\eta, (19)

for any η>0\eta>0, by making O⁡(η−1)O(\eta^{-1}) memory-usage queries each consuming a copy of ρ\rho. The circuit depth for this implementation is also O⁡(η−1)O(\eta^{-1}).

Suppose that the sequence of states {ρk′}k\{\rho^{\prime}_{k}\}_{k} is obtained from such emulation starting from ρ0′=ρ0\rho^{\prime}_{0}=\rho_{0} and thus recursively defined

ρk′=𝒰^[ρk−1′]​(ρk−1′).\displaystyle\rho^{\prime}_{k}=\hat{\mathcal{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k-1}]}\left(\rho^{\prime}_{k-1}\right)\ . (20)

This sequence might deviate from the desired sequence {ρk}k\{\rho_{k}\}_{k} very quickly and, in general, spec⁡{ρk′}≠spec⁡{τ}\spec\{\rho^{\prime}_{k}\}\neq\spec\{\tau\}.

The quantity of interest is the distance

δk​\coloneq​12​‖ρk−ρk′‖1,\displaystyle\delta_{k}\coloneq\frac{1}{2}\|\rho_{k}-\rho^{\prime}_{k}\|_{1}, (21)

and we want to upper bound δN\delta_{N} with an arbitrarily small ϵ>0\epsilon>0. For some state ρ~k\tilde{\rho}_{k}, the triangle inequality gives

δk≤12​‖ρk−ρ~k‖1+12​‖ρ~k−ρk′‖1​\eqcolon​μk+εk,\displaystyle\delta_{k}\leq\frac{1}{2}\|\rho_{k}-\tilde{\rho}_{k}\|_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{\rho}_{k}-\rho^{\prime}_{k}\|_{1}\eqcolon\mu_{k}+\varepsilon_{k}, (22)

where we define μk​\coloneq​12​‖ρk−ρ~k‖1\mu_{k}\coloneq\frac{1}{2}\|\rho_{k}-\tilde{\rho}_{k}\|_{1} and εk=12​‖ρ~k−ρk′‖1\varepsilon_{k}=\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{\rho}_{k}-\rho^{\prime}_{k}\|_{1}.

Now we set {ρ~k}k\{\tilde{\rho}_{k}\}_{k} to be a sequence of states defined by the exact unitary recursion with an erroneous instruction state ρ~k=𝐔^[ρk−1′]​(ρ~k−1)\tilde{\rho}_{k}=\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k-1}]}(\tilde{\rho}_{k-1}) starting from ρ~0=ρ0\tilde{\rho}_{0}=\rho_{0}. Hence, spec⁡{ρ~k}=spec⁡{τ}\spec\{\tilde{\rho}_{k}\}=\spec\{\tau\} for any kk, and ε0=0\varepsilon_{0}=0. We first analyse how εk\varepsilon_{k} scales. Observe that

εk+1=12​‖𝐔^[ρk′]​(ρ~k)−ρk+1′‖1\displaystyle\varepsilon_{k+1}=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\tilde{\rho}_{k})-\rho^{\prime}_{k+1}\right\|_{1} ≤12​‖𝐔^[ρk′]​(ρ~k)−𝐔^[ρk′]​(ρk′)‖1+12​‖𝐔^[ρk′]​(ρk′)−𝒰^[ρk′]​(ρk′)‖1\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\tilde{\rho}_{k})-\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\rho^{\prime}_{k})\right\|_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\rho^{\prime}_{k})-\hat{\mathcal{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\rho^{\prime}_{k})\right\|_{1}
≤εk+η,\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon_{k}+\eta, (23)

from the triangle inequality, the unitary invariance of the trace norm, and Eq. (19). Therefore, εk\varepsilon_{k} scales linearly i.e.

εk≤k​η.\displaystyle\varepsilon_{k}\leq k\eta. (24)

Now we analyse how μk\mu_{k} evolves. Observe that

μk+1=12​‖𝐔^[ρk]​(ρk)−𝐔^[ρk′]​(ρ~k)‖1\displaystyle\mu_{k+1}=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho_{k}]}(\rho_{k})-\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\tilde{\rho}_{k})\right\|_{1} ≤12​‖𝐔^[ρk]​(ρk)−𝐔^[ρ~k]​(ρ~k)‖1+12​‖𝐔^[ρ~k]​(ρ~k)−𝐔^[ρk′]​(ρ~k)‖1\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho_{k}]}(\rho_{k})-\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\tilde{\rho}_{k}]}(\tilde{\rho}_{k})\right\|_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\tilde{\rho}_{k}]}(\tilde{\rho}_{k})-\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\tilde{\rho}_{k})\right\|_{1}
≤r​μk+12​‖𝐔^[ρ~k]​(ρ~k)−𝐔^[ρk′]​(ρ~k)‖1,\displaystyle\leq r\mu_{k}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\tilde{\rho}_{k}]}(\tilde{\rho}_{k})-\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\tilde{\rho}_{k})\right\|_{1}, (25)

with some r<1r<1 from the fast spectral convergence condition in Definition 5.1.

Next, recall that ‖ei​f​(ρ)−ei​f​(σ)‖≤C′​‖ρ−σ‖\left\|e^{if(\rho)}-e^{if(\sigma)}\right\|\leq C^{\prime}\|\rho-\sigma\| for some constant C′C^{\prime}, from the mean value theorem for operators. This implies

‖𝐔^[ρ]−𝐔^[σ]‖Tr≤C​‖ρ−σ‖1\displaystyle\left\|\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho]}-\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\sigma]}\right\|_{\Tr}\leq C\|\rho-\sigma\|_{1} (26)

for some constant CC. Hence, Eq. (25) can be further bounded as

μk+1≤r​μk+C​εk≤r​μk+C​k​η.\displaystyle\mu_{k+1}\leq r\mu_{k}+C\varepsilon_{k}\leq r\mu_{k}+Ck\eta. (27)

This recursive relation gives

μN≤rN​μ0+∑k=0N−1rN−k−1​C​k​η=O⁡(N​η).\displaystyle\mu_{N}\leq r^{N}\mu_{0}+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}r^{N-k-1}Ck\eta=O(N\eta). (28)

Therefore, we obtain the final error

δN≤μN+εN≤O⁡(N​η).\displaystyle\delta_{N}\leq\mu_{N}+\varepsilon_{N}\leq O(N\eta). (29)

The desired upper bound δN≤ϵ\delta_{N}\leq\epsilon for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 can be obtained by setting η=O⁡(ϵ​N−1)\eta=O(\epsilon N^{-1}).

Since the circuit depth for each recursion step scales as η−1\eta^{-1}, regardless of the step number kk, the total circuit depth scales as N​η−1=O⁡(N2​ϵ−1)N\eta^{-1}=O(N^{2}\epsilon^{-1}), as stated in the theorem. ∎

Before we prove the theorem for pure state recursions, we introduce a useful lemma using the mixedness reduction protocol in Section 3.

Lemma 5.1 (QDP mixedness reduction subroutine; original result).

Let ρ\rho be a density matrix with the largest eigenvalue λ1=1−x\lambda_{1}=1-x for some mixedness parameter x∈[0,13]x\in[0,\frac{1}{3}], corresponding to the eigenvector |v1⟩|{v_{1}}\rangle. Given any maximum tolerable failure probability qth≥0q_{\mathrm{th}}\geq 0, one can choose any parameter 𝗀∈ℝ\mathsf{g}\in\mathbb{R} and prepare MM copies of ρ′\rho^{\prime}, such that:

  1. 1.

    ρ′\rho^{\prime} has the largest eigenvalue λ1′≥1−x𝗀\lambda^{\prime}_{1}\geq 1-\frac{x}{\mathsf{g}}, corresponding to the same eigenvector |v1⟩|{v_{1}}\rangle.

  2. 2.

    a number of R=O⁡(log⁡(𝗀))R=O(\log(\mathsf{g})) mixedness reduction rounds in Proposition 3.1 is used,

  3. 3.

    a total of M​(2c)RM(\frac{2}{c})^{R} copies of ρ\rho is consumed, with c∈(0,1)c\in(0,1) satisfying

    c=1−x−M−12​log⁡(Rqth)\displaystyle c=1-x-M^{-\frac{1}{2}}\sqrt{\log\left(\frac{R}{q_{\mathrm{th}}}\right)} (30)
  4. 4.

    the success probability of the entire subroutine is qsucc≥1−qthq_{\mathrm{succ}}\geq 1-q_{\mathrm{th}}.

Note that MM must be sufficiently large to guarantee c>0c>0.

Proof.

To prove this lemma, we analyze RR sequential rounds of the mixedness reduction protocol, with initial and final states ρ\rho and ρ′\rho^{\prime}. Let us denote the intermediate states generated via the mixedness reduction protocols as {χj}j=0R\{\chi_{j}\}_{j=0}^{R}, where χ0=ρ\chi_{0}=\rho and χR=ρ′\chi_{R}=\rho^{\prime}; and let {yj}j=0R\{y_{j}\}_{j=0}^{R} be the mixedness parameter (i.e. 11 minus the largest eigenvalue) for each χj\chi_{j} with y0=xy_{0}=x and yR≤x𝗀y_{R}\leq\frac{x}{\mathsf{g}}. Furthermore, let MjM_{j} be the number of copies of an intermediate state χj\chi_{j} generated; hence, we obtain MR=MM_{R}=M copies of the desired state ρ′\rho^{\prime} at the end, and aim to show that M0=M×(2c)RM_{0}=M\times(\frac{2}{c})^{R} suffices.

From Eq. (22) in Proposition 3.1, the mixedness parameter after jj rounds of the mixedness reduction protocol becomes yj≤1+yj−12−2​yj−1+yj−12​yj−1y_{j}\leq\frac{1+y_{j-1}}{2-2y_{j-1}+y_{j-1}^{2}}y_{j-1}. The final reduction x′x=yRy0≤𝗀−1\frac{x^{\prime}}{x}=\frac{y_{R}}{y_{0}}\leq\mathsf{g}^{-1} is achievable if RR is sufficiently big to satisfy

yRy0=∏j=1Ryjyj−1≤∏j=1R1+yj−12−2​yj−1+yj−12≤(1+x2−2​x+x2)R≤𝗀−1.\displaystyle\frac{y_{R}}{y_{0}}=\prod_{j=1}^{R}\frac{y_{j}}{y_{j-1}}\leq\prod_{j=1}^{R}\frac{1+y_{j-1}}{2-2y_{j-1}+y_{j-1}^{2}}\leq\left(\frac{1+x}{2-2x+x^{2}}\right)^{R}\leq\mathsf{g}^{-1}. (31)

The second last inequality follows from two facts: i) the factor 1+y2−2​y+y2\frac{1+y}{2-2y+y^{2}} monotonically increases as yy increases ii) yj≤y0y_{j}\leq y_{0} for all jj. Since log⁡(1+x2−2​x+x2)>0\log(\frac{1+x}{2-2x+x^{2}})>0 by the assumption x≤13x\leq\frac{1}{3}, the number of rounds R=O⁡(log⁡(𝗀))R=O(\log(\mathsf{g})) is sufficient as claimed.

The parameter cc in the statement of the lemma can be interpreted as the survival rate after each round of the mixedness reduction protocol. More specifically, the jjth round of the protocol is successful if at least c2​Mj−1\frac{c}{2}M_{j-1} output states χj\chi_{j} is prepared from Mj−1M_{j-1} copies of χj−1\chi_{j-1}. If successful, we discard all the surplus output copies and set Mj=c2​Mj−1M_{j}=\frac{c}{2}M_{j-1}. If not, we declare that the whole subroutine has failed. Hence, if the entire subroutine succeeds, the final number of copies M=MRM=M_{R} is related to the initial number of copies as M0=(2/c)R​MM_{0}=(2/c)^{R}M.

Finally, we estimate the success probability qsuccq_{\mathrm{succ}} given R,M,c,xR,M,c,x and require it to be lower bounded with (1−qth)(1-q_{\mathrm{th}}). The failure probability of each round will be bounded using Hoeffding’s inequality. From Proposition 3.1, the success probability of preparing one copy of χj\chi_{j} from a pair χj−1⊗2\chi_{j-1}^{\otimes 2} has a lower bound p⁡(yj−1)≥1−yj−1p(y_{j-1})\geq 1-y_{j-1}. At each round, Mj−12\frac{M_{j-1}}{2} independent trials of this mixedness reduction protocol are conducted. The probability of more than c​Mj−12c\frac{M_{j-1}}{2} attempts succeeds, i.e. the success probability of a round, is

qr(j)=1−F⁡(⌈c​Mj−12−1⌉,Mj−12,p⁡(yj−1))≥1−F⁡(c​Mj−12,Mj−12,1−yj−1),\displaystyle q_{r}^{(j)}=1-F\left(\left\lceil\frac{cM_{j-1}}{2}-1\right\rceil;\frac{M_{j-1}}{2},p(y_{j-1})\right)\geq 1-F\left(\frac{cM_{j-1}}{2};\frac{M_{j-1}}{2},1-y_{j-1}\right), (32)

where F⁡(k,n,q)F(k;n,q) is the cumulative binomial distribution function defined as

F⁡(c​n,n,p)=∑i=0⌊c​n⌋(ni)​pi​(1−p)n−i.\displaystyle F(cn;n,p)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor cn\rfloor}\binom{n}{i}p^{i}(1-p)^{n-i}. (33)

The expected number of success for nn trials of a process with success probability pp is p​npn, and F⁡(c​n,n,p)F(cn;n,p) denotes the probability of having less than c​ncn successes. Hence, the Hoeffding’s inequality gives F⁡(c​n,n,p)≤e−2​n​(p−c)2F(cn;n,p)\leq e^{-2n(p-c)^{2}}, and consequently sets the bound

qr(j)≥1−e−Mj​(1−yj−1−c)2.\displaystyle q_{r}^{(j)}\geq 1-e^{-M_{j}\left(1-y_{j-1}-c\right)^{2}}. (34)

The success probability of an entire subroutine can then be bounded as

qsucc\displaystyle q_{\mathrm{succ}} =∏j=1Rqr(j)≥∏j=1R(1−e−Mj​(1−yj−1−c)2)>1−∑j=1Re−Mj​(1−yj−1−c)2,\displaystyle=\prod_{j=1}^{R}q_{r}^{(j)}\geq\prod_{j=1}^{R}\left(1-e^{-M_{j}\left(1-y_{j-1}-c\right)^{2}}\right)>1-\sum_{j=1}^{R}e^{-M_{j}\left(1-y_{j-1}-c\right)^{2}}, (35)

where the last inequality uses ∏j(1−qj)>1−∑jqj\prod_{j}(1-q_{j})>1-\sum_{j}q_{j} that holds when qj∈(0,1)q_{j}\in(0,1) for all jj. Moreover, by recalling x≥yj−1x\geq y_{j-1} and M≤MjM\leq M_{j} for all jj, the final bound

qsucc>1−R​e−M​(1−x−c)2\displaystyle q_{\mathrm{succ}}>1-Re^{-M\left(1-x-c\right)^{2}} (36)

is obtained. The prescribed failure threshold qthq_{\mathrm{th}} holds when e−M​(1−x−c)2=qthRe^{-M\left(1-x-c\right)^{2}}=\frac{q_{\mathrm{th}}}{R} , or equivalently, when MM is sufficiently large and Eq. (30) is true. ∎

During the earlier recursions, MM is always sufficiently large to guarantee that cc is well separated from 00. For later recursions, in particular for the last recursion where only M=1M=1 is needed, Eq. (30) can become close to zero, or even negative. To guarantee positive and non-vanishing cc, we allow some redundancy of the final state ρN\rho_{N} and prepare M>1M>1 copies of it.

Next we prove the theorem for pure state recursions using Lemma 5.1.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

We again set 𝒰^[ρ]\hat{\mathcal{U}}^{[\rho]} to satisfy Eq. (19), but now we define the sequence {ρk′}k\{\rho^{\prime}_{k}\}_{k} to have an initial state ρ0′=ψ0\rho^{\prime}_{0}=\psi_{0} and follow the recursion relation

ρk′=MR∘𝒰^[ρk−1′]​(ρk−1′),\displaystyle\rho^{\prime}_{k}=\mathrm{MR}\circ\hat{\mathcal{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k-1}]}(\rho^{\prime}_{k-1}), (37)

instead of Eq. (20). MR\mathrm{MR} denotes the RR rounds of the mixedness reduction subroutine as in Lemma 5.1. Suppose that RR is sufficiently large to guarantee that ρk′\rho^{\prime}_{k} has the largest eigenvalue 1−x1-x with a mixedness parameter x<νx<\nu for some small ν\nu and the corresponding eigenvector |ψ~k⟩|{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\rangle. Then we can write

δk​\coloneq​12​‖ψk−ρk′‖1≤12​‖ψk−ψ~k‖1+12​‖ψ~k−ρk′‖1​\eqcolon​μk+εk,\displaystyle\delta_{k}\coloneq\frac{1}{2}\|\psi_{k}-\rho^{\prime}_{k}\|_{1}\leq\frac{1}{2}\|\psi_{k}-\tilde{\psi}_{k}\|_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{\psi}_{k}-\rho^{\prime}_{k}\|_{1}\eqcolon\mu_{k}+\varepsilon_{k}, (38)

as in the proof for Theorem 2.1.

The first term, μk\mu_{k}, can be analysed using the inequality

μk+1=12​‖𝐔^[ψk]​(ψk)−ψ~k+1‖1\displaystyle\mu_{k+1}=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\psi_{k}]}(\psi_{k})-\tilde{\psi}_{k+1}\right\|_{1} ≤12​‖𝐔^[ψk]​(ψk)−𝐔^[ψ~k]​(ψ~k)‖1+12​‖𝐔^[ψ~k]​(ψ~k)−ψ~k+1‖1\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\psi_{k}]}(\psi_{k})-\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\tilde{\psi}_{k}]}(\tilde{\psi}_{k})\right\|_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\tilde{\psi}_{k}]}(\tilde{\psi}_{k})-\tilde{\psi}_{k+1}\right\|_{1}
≤r​μk+12​‖𝐔^[ψ~k]​(ψ~k)−ψ~k+1‖1,\displaystyle\leq r\mu_{k}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\tilde{\psi}_{k}]}(\tilde{\psi}_{k})-\tilde{\psi}_{k+1}\right\|_{1}, (39)

with some r<1r<1 using the fast spectral convergence in Definition 5.1. The second term of Eq. (39) can be further bounded by the triangle inequality

12​‖ψ~k+1−𝐔^[ψ~k]​(ψ~k)‖1≤12​‖ψ~k+1−𝒰^[ρk′]​(ρk′)‖1+12​‖𝒰^[ρk′]​(ρk′)−𝐔^[ψ~k]​(ψ~k)‖1.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\tilde{\psi}_{k+1}-\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\tilde{\psi}_{k}]}(\tilde{\psi}_{k})\right\|_{1}\leq\frac{1}{2}\left\|\tilde{\psi}_{k+1}-\hat{\mathcal{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\rho^{\prime}_{k})\right\|_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathcal{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\rho^{\prime}_{k})-\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\tilde{\psi}_{k}]}(\tilde{\psi}_{k})\right\|_{1}. (40)

Note that mixedness reduction subroutines do not change the eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue of the state; hence ψ~k+1\tilde{\psi}_{k+1} is the eigenvector of 𝒰^[ρk′]​(ρk′)\hat{\mathcal{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\rho^{\prime}_{k}) corresponding to the largest eigenvalue of it. The first term of the bound Eq. (40) is then the mixedness parameter of 𝒰^[ρk′]​(ρk′)\hat{\mathcal{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\rho^{\prime}_{k}). Since ρk′\rho^{\prime}_{k} has the mixedness parameter smaller than ν\nu and 𝒰^[ρk′]\hat{\mathcal{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]} is only η\eta different from the unitary operator 𝐔^[ρk′]\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}, we obtain 12​‖ψ~k+1−𝒰^[ρk′]​(ρk′)‖1≤ν+η\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{\psi}_{k+1}-\hat{\mathcal{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\rho^{\prime}_{k})\|_{1}\leq\nu+\eta. The second term of the bound Eq. (40) can be further expanded as

12​‖𝒰^[ρk′]​(ρk′)−𝐔^[ψ~k]​(ψ~k)‖1\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathcal{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\rho^{\prime}_{k})-\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\tilde{\psi}_{k}]}(\tilde{\psi}_{k})\right\|_{1}
≤12​‖𝒰^[ρk′]​(ρk′)−𝒰^[ρk′]​(ψ~k)‖1+12​‖𝒰^[ρk′]​(ψ~k)−𝐔^[ρk′]​(ψ~k)‖1+12​‖𝐔^[ρk′]​(ψ~k)−𝐔^[ψ~k]​(ψ~k)‖1\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathcal{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\rho^{\prime}_{k})-\hat{\mathcal{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\tilde{\psi}_{k})\right\|_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathcal{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\tilde{\psi}_{k})-\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\tilde{\psi}_{k})\right\|_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}(\tilde{\psi}_{k})-\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\tilde{\psi}_{k}]}(\tilde{\psi}_{k})\right\|_{1}
≤12​‖ρk′−ψ~k‖1+12​‖𝒰^[ρk′]−𝐔^[ρk′]‖Tr+12​‖𝐔^[ρk′]−𝐔^[ψ~k]‖Tr≤C​ν+η,\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\left\|\rho^{\prime}_{k}-\tilde{\psi}_{k}\right\|_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathcal{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}-\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}\right\|_{\Tr}+\frac{1}{2}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\rho^{\prime}_{k}]}-\hat{\mathbf{U}}^{[\tilde{\psi}_{k}]}\right\|_{\Tr}\leq C\nu+\eta, (41)

for some constant CC. The second and third inequalities follow from data processing inequality, definition of the channel distance, and Eqs. (19) and (26). Combining everything, we arrive at the recursive bound

μk+1≤r​μk+(C+1)​ν+2​η,\displaystyle\mu_{k+1}\leq r\mu_{k}+(C+1)\nu+2\eta, (42)

which leads to the explicit upper bound

μN≤rN​μ0+∑k=0N−1rN−k−1​((C+1)​ν+2​η)=O⁡(ν+η).\displaystyle\mu_{N}\leq r^{N}\mu_{0}+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}r^{N-k-1}((C+1)\nu+2\eta)=O(\nu+\eta). (43)

The other error term εk\varepsilon_{k} in Eq. (38) is the distance between ρk′\rho^{\prime}_{k} and its principal component eigenvector ψ~k\tilde{\psi}_{k}, which is bounded by ν\nu by the applications of the mixedness reduction protocol. Hence, we obtain the desired bound

δN≤O⁡(ν)+O⁡(η)≤ϵ,\displaystyle\delta_{N}\leq O(\nu)+O(\eta)\leq\epsilon, (44)

by setting ν=O⁡(ϵ)\nu=O(\epsilon) and η=O⁡(ϵ)\eta=O(\epsilon).

Finally, we derive the number of initial state copies needed for the algorithm. Outlook

Chapter 8 Conclusions and open problems

Section 1 Compositions in resource theories

In this thesis, we have explored how auxiliary systems are utilised for quantum information processing. The journey began within resource theories, where everything is more ordered (pun intended, although it would be more precise to say ‘preordered’). The auxiliary systems of choice are catalysts; they provide surprisingly strong advantages, given the strict recovery condition required for them. We have uncovered secrets behind catalytic advantages by employing an appropriate set of allowed operations, leveraging the clear-cut structure of resource theories.

Firstly, we restricted the operations to be decomposable. Because each operation in the decomposition is implemented with a fresh environment, this decomposability is comparable to imposing memory restrictions or certain degrees of Markovianity; cf. Definition 2.2. Such decomposability, or memory restriction, has provided two methods by which to inspect catalytic advantages. In Section 2, decomposability is directly utilised to unravel the inner working of catalysis. Such access to the process is rare in resource theories, since the main objects of interest are most often the initial and final state pairs, with little focus on the intermediate evolution. From snapshots of the process, obtained after each smaller operation in the decomposition, we observed that catalysts assist the system’s evolution by functioning as a temporary storage for the resource.

In Section 3, further evidence of the catalyst memory-effect has been obtained by using catalysts to bridge memory-unrestricted operations and memory-restricted ones. To be specific, we compared several classes of operations modelling thermodynamic processes, where the sole distinction between them lay in their varying degrees of memory restriction. If a particular factor nullifies the operational gaps between these classes, this nullification is attributed to the memory effect. Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 demonstrate exactly this.

To examine the second reason behind the power of catalysis, we assumed our catalytic operations to be input-state agnostic. This assumption takes into account that real-world operations always involve noise in the state preparation. Surprisingly, it turns out that most catalyses are extremely sensitive to state preparation noise; i.e. a small change in the input system state can break the catalyticity of the operation. Notably, we show in Theorem 3.3 that in any resource theory with a certain composition structure, all catalyses are sensitive to the input state. This implies that the ability to prepare the initial state precisely, according to the catalyst state, is an essential requirement for catalysis.

Finally, we restricted our theories to those robust to input state noise. Theorem 2.1 reveals a connection between two seemingly disparate phenomena: robust catalysis occurs only when resource broadcasting is possible. Resource broadcasting is a better-studied phenomenon, wherein a resource can be transferred from one system to another without altering the original one. Hence, the connection we have established implies another reason for catalytic advantage: namely, the catalyst acting as a seed for broadcasting. Furthermore, in Theorem 3.6, we have found a concrete construction and a necessary and sufficient condition for resource broadcasting applicable to various classes of resource theories, thereby paving the way towards more systematic studies on utilising catalysts for broadcasting.

These first steps into the origins of catalytic advantage have opened up several interesting avenues for future research. For example, we have observed that catalytic assistance can render different sets of thermodynamic free operations equivalent. A similar question can be posed from the opposite direction: if a common restriction is imposed, can distinct sets of free operations become equivalent once more? Should we succeed in finding the common restriction that renders operational and axiomatic classes the same, it would provide valuable insight into the underlying reasons for the separation between them. This separation is apparent, yet not fully understood, in some of the most significant and well-studied theories, such as those of entanglement and magic. In particular, the gap between thermal operations (TO, Definition 1.3) and Gibbs-preserving covariant operations (GPC, Definition 1.2)—two different sets of free operations in resource theory of athermality, where the former is defined operationally and the latter axiomatically—is currently poorly understood; the sole insight to date stems from the existence of a single specific example illustrating this gap [149].

One immediate restriction for consideration is Markovianity. Markovian versions of TO and GPC, namely Markovian TO (MTO, Definition 1.5) and Markovian GPC (MGPC) [168, 169], have been proposed and studied independently, yet it remains unclear whether these two operations are equivalent. Since both must be describable by Lindblad master equations, the question reduces to determining whether Lindbladians that are Gibbs-preserving and covariant can also be described by a Markovian heat bath, a problem we expect to be more tractable.11 1 Some preliminary studies have been taken in Ref. [324].

A related restriction is Gaussianity. Interestingly, Gaussian TO is known to be Markovian [325], as is Gaussian GPC. An advantage of considering Gaussianity is that one can leverage the equivalence between Gaussian completely positive trace-preserving maps on density matrices and Gaussian operations on the covariance matrices of bosonic modes. If either Markovianity or Gaussianity is shown to be the deciding factor in this distinction, a deeper understanding of the missing axiom needed to fully characterise operational thermodynamic operations could be attained.

Another direction for future studies was hinted at in our analysis of robust catalysis and resource broadcasting. In that work, we classified general resource theories in terms of their composition rules, i.e. how the set of composite free states is constructed given the sets for subsystems. It was found that the choice of composition rule significantly alters the behaviour of these theories. Surprisingly, such rules have not been studied extensively, beyond instances where a specific rule is imposed as an assumption [326, 205, 327]. We expect that dedicated research into the impact of compositions would illuminate the field of resource theory at large and, in particular, the effects of auxiliary systems.

A key extension would be to study the composition of free operations instead of the composition of free states. This focus is motivated by the fact that resource theories are defined by free operations, not free states. In our study of free state composition, free operations must first be defined in terms of the free states, e.g. by selecting CRNG operations as free. Such an approach, however, cannot capture theories defined more operationally, such as local operations and classical communication (LOCC) or TO. Formalising the composition of free operations would enable this framework to encompass any properly defined resource theory.

One interesting example is the interplay between locality and symmetry [162, 164]. Locality constraints the number of subsystems upon which an operation can act; for example, each 22-local operation acts, at most, on two subsystems. Symmetry can be represented as a covariance of the operation with respect to all actions of a group describing said symmetry. For general unitary operations, without symmetry governing the dynamics, any kk-local operations for k>1k>1 achieve universality, i.e. any global unitary operation can be expressed as a concatenation of kk-local unitaries. Surprisingly, when local and symmetric operations are composed, universality is lost. To be specific, if the system is nn-partite, there are symmetric unitary operations that cannot be decomposed into a sequence of (n−1)(n-1)-local symmetric unitary operations. Hence, the composition rule, determining the locality of the operations, dictates the final achievable operations.

We are particularly interested in hybridising different resource theories through composition. This problem presents both practical and fundamental motivations. Practically, one can imagine a situation where two distinct physical platforms interact. Each platform is governed by a resource theory suited to addressing its platform-specific difficulties. Hence, to model such hybrid platforms, it is essential to understand how different resource theories are composed together. On the fundamental side, the hybridisation of resource theories indicate that we can study the interconversion of disparate resources. Determining the ultimate rate of converting coherence to entanglement, or athermality to magic, for instance, would provide deeper insight into the nature of each resource.

Section 2 Compositions in quantum computing

The second part of the thesis has made a departure from the clear-cut world of resource theories and undertook studies in quantum computing. In particular, we focused on quantum recursions, which are a generalisation of classical recursions ubiquitous in classical algorithms. Quantum recursions apply unitary operators that depend on the previous quantum states, a process which introduces non-linearity to the evolution. This non-linearity enables myriads of exotic evolutions that were not accessible due to the inherent linearity of conventional unitary evolutions (which are independent of the quantum state). One such example is the imaginary-time evolution mapping |ψ⟩↦e−τ​H‖e−τ​H​|ψ⟩‖2​|ψ⟩|{\psi}\rangle\mapsto\frac{e^{-\tau H}}{\|e^{-\tau H}|{\psi}\rangle\|_{2}}|{\psi}\rangle, which, though clearly non-linear, qualifies as a unitary evolution. In Chapter 6, we presented a way to implement this evolution using quantum recursions. Our implementation, while approximate, inherits the essential properties of the imaginary-time evolution: namely exponential convergence to the ground state (Theorem 2.2) and an average energy decrease proportional to the variance of the energy (Theorem 2.1).

To overcome the inherent linearity of standard unitary evolution, quantum recursions require special methods for implementation. A standard protocol is to unfold the recursion unitary, whereby operations dependent on the previous state are emulated by reapplying and then reversing the unitary operations used to prepare that state. This repeated process of application and reversal introduces redundancies, giving rise to exponential growth in circuit depth with the number of recursion steps. However, in Chapter 6, it was suggested that despite this exponential growth, the imaginary-time evolution algorithm can nonetheless be of practical utility, thanks to its rapid convergence properties.

In Chapter 7, an alternative method for solving quantum recursions was presented. The solution is quantum dynamic programming, which is a generalisation of classical dynamic programming. The crux of this technique is to introduce many quantum systems that function as auxiliary memory states, evolving in tandem with the main system of interest until they are consumed to instruct subsequent recursion steps. As a result, the exponential growth in circuit depth can be mitigated, albeit at the cost of an exponential increase in circuit width, when the recursion satisfies certain convergence conditions. This trade-off between depth and width (or time and space) can be adjusted to match the specifications of available quantum hardware.

Our results on quantum dynamic programming provided initial evidence that an exponential reduction in circuit depth for quantum recursions is possible. However, this is a proof-of-principle result focused on the sufficiency of our technique, without extensive effort dedicated to probing its optimality. Hence, a natural subsequent research question concerns the fundamental limits of the space-time trade-off.

In fact, this question can be posed in more abstract settings beyond quantum recursions. Quantum circuit complexity measures the minimum number of 22-local unitary operations needed for the implementation of a given global unitary operation or a given state transformation. Existing scattered observations indicate that auxiliary systems can be utilised to induce space-time trade-offs [319], or even employed catalytically to expand the set of exactly compilable operations [328]. We aim to systematically study the role of auxiliary systems in circuit complexity and related topics. Initially, a comparison between single-shot transformation complexity and its catalytic or multi-copy counterparts would be interesting. For catalytic transformation, the baseline is that achievable via gate teleportation [320], utilising approximately the same number of 22-local gates. Similarly, for multi-copy transformations, a lower bound can be achieved by parallel, independent applications of the same operations, which achieve an nn-copy transformation with nn-fold complexity. It is probable, however, that more effective alternative pathways exist for achieving the desired transformations by exploiting the interplay between different subsystems in a more intricate manner. Such methods could offer more efficient means of compiling desired operations by embedding the primary system within a larger composite one.

A variant of this problem involves examining the geometric picture of quantum states and their evolutions. Nielsen’s complexity [329, 31, 315, 330] concerns the minimum distance between two states, defined by a Riemannian metric that takes into account the locality of operations. This notion of complexity aligns more closely with the continuous evolution of a state, as opposed to the discrete evolutions typically assumed in gate-based quantum computation. It also naturally relates to speed limits [331], which quantify the minimum time required for a state to evolve into another. This framework also lends itself to investigating catalyst-assisted or multi-copy complexity. In comparison to gate-based complexity, this geometric approach benefits from more developed technical tools. Notably, partial answers for ancilla-assisted transformations [315] and multi-copy transformations [332] already exist, yet further studies are required to obtain conclusive answers.

Section 3 Concluding remarks

Hopefully, this thesis would work as a helpful guide for navigating the infinitely larger spaces accessible with auxiliary systems.

In this thesis, we have investigated the mechanisms behind the catalytic use of auxiliaries, applications to quantum computing that enable space-time trade-offs, and promising avenues for future research involving auxiliary systems.

Stepping back, I wish to conclude by recalling why I have been fascinated by auxiliary systems since the beginning of my PhD. Initially, I was drawn to the puzzling nature of catalysis in resource theories. The catalytic activation of an previously impossible task into a feasible one seemed to be a ’free lunch’. In the course of the research that culminated in this thesis, I came to realise that catalytic advantages, and auxiliary system utilisation in general, are akin to exploring new dimensions—quite literally, by expanding the dimensions of the system itself. As I stated in the introduction of this thesis, the unique joy of being a theorist is tied to the freedom of choosing what to consider. Auxiliary systems subsequently stood out as a versatile tool for expanding the horizons of theorists.

It is my hope that this thesis will serve as a helpful guide for navigating this new horizon, one so vastly expanded thanks to our quantum comrades.

Chapter 9 State transformation conditions and improvements for ETO characterisation

Appendix 9.A Previous results

We summarise known characterisations for state transformations under thermodynamic free operations considered in Chapter 3. First, Gibbs-preserving operations (GP, Definition 1.1) are defined as a channel ℰ\mathcal{E} with the constraint ℰ⁡(γ)=γ\mathcal{E}(\gamma)=\gamma. Therefore, the conditions for state transformations under GP (i.e. the question of whether a GP map ℰ\mathcal{E} exists such that ℰ⁡(ρ)=ρ′\mathcal{E}(\rho)=\rho^{\prime}) can be framed as a special case of the quantum dichotomy problem [333], which asks whether a CPTP map ℰ\mathcal{E} exists that satisfies ℰ⁡(ρi)=ρi′\mathcal{E}(\rho_{i})=\rho^{\prime}_{i} for given pairs (ρ1,ρ1′)(\rho_{1},\rho^{\prime}_{1}) and (ρ2,ρ2′)(\rho_{2},\rho^{\prime}_{2}). When the system S is two-dimensional, this question can be answered by evaluating three inequalities [334]. In general, one can construct a (potentially infinite) family of inequalities that completely characterise the state transformation [335].

For Gibbs-preserving and covariant operations (GPC, Definition 1.2), a similar family of inequalities can be constructed for general asymmetric input states [336]. For symmetric states, Proposition 1.1 implies that the conditions for GPC are equivalent to those for thermal operations (TO, Definition 1.3).

For TO, there is currently no complete characterisation for state transformations among general asymmetric states. Moreover, there is a GPC state transformation that cannot be performed with a TO [149], indicating the inadequacy of the construction in Ref. [336] for TO. On the other hand, when either the initial or the final state is known to be symmetric, TO state transformations are completely characterised by thermomajorisation relations, which we explain below.

The covariance of TO implies that we can safely use population vectors (Definition 1.6) and Gibbs-stochastic matrices (Definition 1.8) in lieu of density matrices and channels. We then define a probability–probability plot, similar to a Lorenz curve, for each population vector.

Definition 9.A.1 (thermomajorisation curve).

For a state 𝐩∈𝒱d\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{V}_{d}, the thermomajorisation curve ℒ𝐩:[0,1]→[0,1]\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{p}}:[0,1]\to[0,1] is a piecewise-linear function that interpolates between the coordinates {(0,0)}\{(0,0)\} and elbow points {(∑k=1lγπ𝐩​(k)β,∑k=1lpπ𝐩​(k))}l=1d\{(\sum_{k=1}^{l}\gamma^{\beta}_{\pi_{\mathbf{p}}(k)},\sum_{k=1}^{l}p_{\pi_{\mathbf{p}}(k)})\}_{l=1}^{d}.

Note that ℒ𝐩\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{p}} is a concave function by definition of the β\beta-ordering (Definition 1.9).

From thermomajorisation curves, a binary relation between two population vectors is defined.

Definition 9.A.2 (thermomajorisation relation).

For two population vectors 𝐩,𝐪∈𝒱d\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{V}_{d}, thermomajorisation relation 𝐩≻β𝐪\mathbf{p}\succ_{\beta}\mathbf{q} if ℒ𝐩​(x)≥ℒ𝐪​(x)\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{p}}(x)\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{q}}(x) for all x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1].

The thermomajorisation relation defines a preorder, analogous to →\to relation for state transformations. The reflexivity (𝐩≻β𝐩\mathbf{p}\succ_{\beta}\mathbf{p}) and the transitivity (𝐩≻β𝐪\mathbf{p}\succ_{\beta}\mathbf{q} and 𝐪≻β𝐫\mathbf{q}\succ_{\beta}\mathbf{r} together implies 𝐩≻β𝐫\mathbf{p}\succ_{\beta}\mathbf{r}) can easily be proven. Indeed, for TO and GPC, thermomajorisation relation defines the preorder for population vectors given by →\to.

Proposition 9.A.1 (Ref. [337], Theorem 2).

For two population vectors 𝐩,𝐪∈𝒱d\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{V}_{d}, there exists a Gibbs-stochastic matrix EE, such that E​𝐩=𝐪E\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{q} if and only if 𝐩≻β𝐪\mathbf{p}\succ_{\beta}\mathbf{q}.

Proofs for this proposition can also be found in Refs. [338, 158, 152]. Combined with Proposition 1.1, we arrive at the desired corollary.

Corollary 9.A.2.

Suppose that the set of free operations is either TO or GPC and that ρS,ρS′∈𝒟SSYM\rho_{S},\rho^{\prime}_{S}\in\mathcal{D}_{S}^{\mathrm{SYM}}. Then, ρS→ρS′\rho_{S}\to\rho^{\prime}_{S} if and only if 𝐩≻β𝐪\mathbf{p}\succ_{\beta}\mathbf{q} for population vectors 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐪\mathbf{q} corresponding to ρS\rho_{S} and ρS′\rho^{\prime}_{S}, respectively.

Now we move on to the construction of the set of reachable states 𝒯X​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{X}}(\mathbf{p}) (Definition 1.7) via some operation X starting from a state 𝐩\mathbf{p}. Earlier works have shown that the set 𝒯TO​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}}(\mathbf{p}) characterised by thermomajorisation can be constructed efficiently. This is summarised in the theorem below.

Theorem 9.A.3 ([154], Lemma 12 and [170], Theorem 2).

For any given 𝐩\mathbf{p}, the set of reachable states 𝒯TO​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}}(\mathbf{p}) is a convex combination of d!d! unique extreme points that correspond to distinct β\beta-orders and are tightly thermomajorised by 𝐩\mathbf{p}.

With Theorem 9.A.3, determining 𝒯TO​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}}(\mathbf{p}) is computationally inexpensive. The importance of tightly thermomajorised states can also be seen from another perspective:

Lemma 9.A.4 (Theorem 12 of [339]).

If two states 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐪\mathbf{q} have the same β\beta-order π𝐩=π𝐪\pi_{\mathbf{p}}=\pi_{\mathbf{q}} and 𝐩≻β𝐪\mathbf{p}\succ_{\beta}\mathbf{q}, then 𝐪\mathbf{q} can be obtained from 𝐩\mathbf{p} by a sequence of two-level partial level thermalisations (PLT).

PLT [339] between two levels can be conceptualised as a process where these two levels are coupled to a Markovian heat bath, bringing their population ratio closer to that of a thermal state; hence, any PLT is both MTO and ETO. Importantly, PLT preserves the β\beta-order of the state; see Figure 2. This leads to the following Corollary.

If a state 𝐪∈𝒯ETO​(𝐩)\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}) is tightly thermomajorised by 𝐩\mathbf{p}, then it is a unique extreme point of 𝒯ETO​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}) among states of the same β\beta-order.

Since elementary thermal operations (ETO) and Markovian thermal operations (MTO) form a strict subset of TO, even for symmetric state transformations, the thermomajorisation relation (Definition 9.A.2) gives a necessary but not sufficient condition for 𝐩→𝐪\mathbf{p}\to\mathbf{q}.
