Another helpful fact is that 𝒯MTO​(𝐩)​\subsetneq​𝒯ETO​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{MTO}}(\mathbf{p})\subsetneq\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}) for any 𝐩∈𝒱d\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{V}_{d} [168].

Now we define a class of T- or β\beta-swaps that typically minimise dissipation/change in athermality. These are thus strong candidates for the swaps needed to perform extremal state transformations under MTO/ETO.

Definition 9.A.3 (neighbouring levels and neighbouring swaps).

Two levels ii and jj are neighbouring for a vector 𝐩\mathbf{p}, if there exists a β\beta-order π𝐩\pi_{\mathbf{p}}, such that π𝐩−1​(i)=π𝐩−1​(j)±1\pi_{\mathbf{p}}^{-1}(i)=\pi_{\mathbf{p}}^{-1}(j)\pm 1, i.e. they are two consecutive levels in the β\beta-order of the input state. Neighbouring T- or β\beta-swaps are the ones that act on two neighbouring levels.

Indeed, extremal MTO state transformations are characterised by sequences of such neighbouring swaps.

Proposition 9.A.6 (Ref. [168], Theorem 4 and Corollary 9).

All elements of extr⁡[𝒯MTO​(𝐩)]\extr[\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{MTO}}(\mathbf{p})] of a state 𝐩\mathbf{p} are given by some sequence of neighbouring T-swaps without repetition. Furthermore if π𝐪=π𝐩\pi_{\mathbf{q}}=\pi_{\mathbf{p}} and 𝐩≻β𝐪\mathbf{p}\succ_{\beta}\mathbf{q}, then 𝐪∈𝒯MTO​(𝐩)\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{MTO}}(\mathbf{p}).

Hence, deciding whether 𝐪∈𝒯MTO​(𝐩)\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{MTO}}(\mathbf{p}) is much more difficult than TO or GPC, but Proposition 9.A.6 guarantees that this decision problem can be solved in finite time.

Appendix 9.B Our improvements

Similarly to MTO, the only known way to determine whether 𝐩→ETO𝐪\mathbf{p}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{ETO}}\mathbf{q}, is to construct the full set 𝒯ETO​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}) by finding all the extreme points of this convex polytope, and check whether 𝐪∈𝒯ETO​(𝐩)\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}). The extreme points extr⁡[𝒯ETO​(𝐩)]\extr[\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p})] are found via checking over a set of swap sequences applied to 𝐩\mathbf{p}. However, there is an additional complexity for ETO, because non-neighbouring swaps are also used for some of the extremal transformations.

Ref. [154] provided a systematic way of finding all extreme points of 𝒯ETO​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}) for an arbitrary dimension dd, which involves an exhaustive search among all possible β\beta-swap sequences with a bounded length ℓmax\ell_{\mathrm{max}}. In other words, this procedure identifies an upper bound on the number of extreme points

#​extreme points≤(d2)ℓmax.\displaystyle\#\penalty\ \text{extreme\penalty\ points}\penalty\ \leq{d\choose 2}^{\ell_{\mathrm{max}}}. (3)

In Ref. [154], ℓmax≤d!\ell_{\mathrm{max}}\leq d! is shown, which means that Eq. (3) grows super-exponentially with the dimension of the system. This presents a serious roadblock to both understanding and determining the possibility of state transitions via ETO, a reason why ETO, despite its strong physical motivation, has not been extensively studied.

We show that the 𝒯ETO​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}) simplifies drastically when 𝐩\mathbf{p} is known to have a particular β\beta-ordering, i.e. when it is monotonic in energy,

π𝐩=(1,⋯,d)​or​π𝐩=(d,⋯,1).\displaystyle\pi_{\mathbf{p}}=(1,\cdots,d)\penalty\ \text{or}\penalty\ \pi_{\mathbf{p}}=(d,\cdots,1). (4)
Theorem 9.B.1.

If π𝐩\pi_{\mathbf{p}} is monotonic in energy, extreme points of 𝒯ETO​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}) are achieved if and only if the corresponding β\beta-swap series that produce them are

  1. 1.

    always neighbouring,

  2. 2.

    containing no repetition of each swap.

Furthermore, when β→1​𝐩,β→2​𝐩∈extr⁡[𝒯ETO​(𝐩)]\vec{\beta}_{1}\mathbf{p},\vec{\beta}_{2}\mathbf{p}\in\extr[\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p})] and πβ→1​𝐩=πβ→2​𝐩\pi_{\vec{\beta}_{1}\mathbf{p}}=\pi_{\vec{\beta}_{2}\mathbf{p}} for such 𝐩\mathbf{p}, the two series are identical (β→1=β→2\vec{\beta}_{1}=\vec{\beta}_{2}).

This is a reiteration of Theorem 2.1 in Chapter 3. Several important simplifications follow from the above theorem, whenever π𝐩\pi_{\mathbf{p}} is monotonic in energy. From the no-repetition condition, ℓmax=d⁡(d−1)/2\ell_{\mathrm{max}}=d(d-1)/2 is obtained. The equivalence of β\beta-swaps outputting the same target state β\beta-order also guarantees the uniqueness of extreme points of 𝒯ETO​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}) at each order, setting the maximum number of extreme points to be d!d!. More importantly, given the target β\beta-order, one can immediately identify a corresponding extreme point without the need of searching over all possible series, since we developed an explicit algorithm to evaluate this extreme point, which we call the standard formation (see Def. 9.B.1 for details).

The rest of this chapter is a route to a proof of Theorem 9.B.1. Nevertheless, each technical lemma or remark provides insights on the construction of 𝒯ETO\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}. We have omitted the results in Ref. [1] that are not directly used for Theorem 9.B.1. These include the full characterisation of the simplest non-trivial case of d=3d=3 or the tightening of the upper bound on ℓmax\ell_{\mathrm{max}} analytically by the factor of d−3d-3 for any dimension dd, see Ref. [1].

Subsection 1 Useful technical tools for constructing 𝒯ETO\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}

Subsection 2 Proof of Theorem 9.B.1

The technical proof of Theorem 9.B.1 can be sketched in the following steps:

  • •

    Firstly, we introduce a specific series of β\beta-swaps that transforms an initial β\beta-ordering to a target ordering (Definition 9.B.1).

  • •

    This structure, which we refer to as the standard formation, is then shown to be equivalent to any β\beta-swap series, where i) all swaps are neighbouring to initial states of the form Eq. (4) and ii) each swap is applied at most once (Lemma 9.B.5).

  • •

    Finally, to prove Theorem 9.B.1, we show that whenever the initial β\beta-ordering is monotonic in energy, then a transformation that is not according to a standard formation always leads to a non-extreme state. This Lemma allows us to conclude that the number of extreme points for such a 𝒯ETO​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}) is at most d!d!, similar to that of 𝒯TO​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{TO}}(\mathbf{p}).

Definition 9.B.1 (Standard formation).

Given a tuple of dd-dimensional β\beta-orderings (π,π′)(\pi,\pi^{\prime}), a standard formation is a β\beta-swap series β→sf\vec{\beta}_{\mathrm{sf}} that transforms an initial state 𝐩\mathbf{p} with an order π\pi into some final state 𝐩′\mathbf{p}^{\prime} having an order π′\pi^{\prime}, with the construction below:

  1. 1.

    Set an initial index of j=1j=1, and identify mm such that πj′=πm\pi^{\prime}_{j}=\pi_{m}. If m=jm=j, define β→(j)\vec{\beta}^{(j)} as an identity. Otherwise, since π1,⋯,πm−1\pi_{1},\cdots,\pi_{m-1} are already occupied by π1′,⋯,πm−1′\pi^{\prime}_{1},\cdots,\pi^{\prime}_{m-1}, we get m>jm>j. Then, define a swap-series β→(j)=β(πj,πm)β(πj+1,πm)⋯β(πm−1,πm)\vec{\beta}^{(j)}=\beta^{(\pi_{j},\pi_{m})}\beta^{(\pi_{j+1},\pi_{m})}\cdots\beta^{(\pi_{m-1},\pi_{m})}. Note that these swaps are always neighbouring when applied to a state initially having the order π\pi, due to Eq. (12). After j=1j=1 round, this swap series will take the initial ordering π\pi to the new ordering (π1′,π1,⋯,πm−1,πm+1,⋯,πd)(\pi_{1}^{\prime},\pi_{1},\cdots,\pi_{m-1},\pi_{m+1},\cdots,\pi_{d}) if β→(1)≠𝟙\vec{\beta}^{(1)}\neq\mathmybb{1}.

  2. 2.

    Iterate the above step for j=2,⋯,d−1j=2,\cdots,d-1, defining {β→(j)}j=1d−1\{\vec{\beta}^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{d-1}.

The standard formation series is then simply the concatenation

β→sf=β→(d−1)⋯β→(2)β→(1).\displaystyle\vec{\beta}_{\mathrm{sf}}=\vec{\beta}^{(d-1)}\cdots\vec{\beta}^{(2)}\vec{\beta}^{(1)}. (35)

By construction, there is no repetition of a swap in this series and they are all neighbouring when applied to an initial state with the order π\pi.

{kaobox}

[frametitle = An example of the standard formation] For the orderings π=1234\pi=1234 and π′=4231\pi^{\prime}=4231, the standard formation is β→sf=β→(3)​β→(2)​β→(1)\vec{\beta}_{\mathrm{sf}}=\vec{\beta}^{(3)}\vec{\beta}^{(2)}\vec{\beta}^{(1)}, where

β→(1)\displaystyle\vec{\beta}^{(1)} =β(1,4)​β(2,4)​β(3,4),β→(2)=β(1,2),β→(3)=β(1,3).\displaystyle=\beta^{(1,4)}\beta^{(2,4)}\beta^{(3,4)},\qquad\vec{\beta}^{(2)}=\beta^{(1,2)},\qquad\vec{\beta}^{(3)}=\beta^{(1,3)}. (36)

The intermediate β\beta-orderings given by this process are

π=1234→β→(1)4123→β→(2)4213→β→(3)π′=4231.\displaystyle\pi=1234\quad\xrightarrow[\vec{\beta}^{(1)}]{}\penalty\ \quad 4123\quad\xrightarrow[\vec{\beta}^{(2)}]{}\penalty\ \quad 4213\quad\xrightarrow[\vec{\beta}^{(3)}]{}\penalty\ \quad\pi^{\prime}=4231. (37)

This formation has a nice property, namely all swaps in each block β→(j)\vec{\beta}^{(j)} acts on level πj′\pi^{\prime}_{j} and the ones in β→(k)\vec{\beta}^{(k)} for any k>jk>j does not act on level πj′\pi^{\prime}_{j}. In the lemma below, we illustrate how certain classes of swap series, which turns out to be the ones producing extreme states, can always rearranged into a standard formulation.

Lemma 9.B.5.

Given an initial state 𝐩\mathbf{p} with ordering π\pi monotonic in energy, denote a β\beta-swap series

β→=∏iβi,\displaystyle\vec{\beta}=\prod_{i}\beta_{i}, (38)

and π′\pi^{\prime} to be the final β\beta-ordering of the state 𝐩′=β→​𝐩\mathbf{p}^{\prime}=\vec{\beta}\mathbf{p}. If β→\vec{\beta} is such that:

  1. 1.

    each βi\beta_{i} is a distinct swap, and

  2. 2.

    when applied to 𝐩\mathbf{p}, is always a neighbouring swap,

then β→\vec{\beta} can always be expressed in the form of a standard formation for (π,π′)(\pi,\pi^{\prime}).

Proof.

We prove this by induction. Suppose the above lemma is true for 𝐩∈𝒱d−1\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{V}_{d-1}. The first goal is to prove this for initial ordering π=(1,2,⋯,d)\pi=(1,2,\cdots,d) and β→\vec{\beta} that satisfies the conditions in the statement of the lemma. By identifying the first and the last swaps acting on the level dd, one can decompose β→\vec{\beta} into

β→=β→(Post)​β→(d−rel)​β→(Pre).\displaystyle\vec{\beta}=\vec{\beta}^{(\text{Post})}\vec{\beta}^{(d-\text{rel})}\vec{\beta}^{(\text{Pre})}. (39)

Here, β→(Pre)\vec{\beta}^{(\text{Pre})} are the swaps coming before the first swap acting on the level dd, and β→(Post)\vec{\beta}^{(\text{Post})} are the ones after the last swap acting on the level dd.

  2. 2.

    Any i∈Ai\in A can move to BB only when β(i,d)\beta^{(i,d)} is implemented.

  3. 3.

  4. 4.

    If k,l∈Ak,l\in A when β(k,l)\beta^{(k,l)} is applied, β(k,l)\beta^{(k,l)} precedes β(k,d)\beta^{(k,d)} and β(l,d)\beta^{(l,d)} when they exist in β→\vec{\beta}.

AA and BB are separated by level dd (point 1 above). Starting from B=∅B=\emptyset, some elements i∈Ai\in A are transferred to BB whenever β(i,d)\beta^{(i,d)} is implemented. Once this happens, ii cannot go back to AA, since it would require the repetition of β(i,d)\beta^{(i,d)} to do so. For d=2d=2, the Lemma is trivially true. Thus by induction, the lemma is proved for π=(1,2,⋯,d)\pi=(1,2,\cdots,d). Following the same logic, this can also be proven for π=(d,d−1,⋯,1)\pi=(d,d-1,\cdots,1). ∎

Now we state the main proof.

Proof of Theorem 9.B.1.

We prove the theorem for the case π𝐩=(1,2,⋯,d)\pi_{\mathbf{p}}=(1,2,\cdots,d) and argue that the proof also holds for π𝐩=(d,d−1,⋯,1)\pi_{\mathbf{p}}=(d,d-1,\cdots,1).

We first prove the only if statement of the theorem, as follows:

  1. 1.

    We show that the repetition of any particular β\beta-swap always leads to a non-extreme state if the series is all-neighbouring. This is done by contradiction: suppose that β→=β(k,l)​β→′\vec{\beta}=\beta^{(k,l)}\vec{\beta}^{\prime}, w.l.o.g. assuming k<lk<l.     β→\displaystyle\vec{\beta} =β→(Irrel)​β(k,l)​∏mi∈M(β(mi,k)​β(mi,l))​β(k,l)​β→(Pre)\displaystyle=\vec{\beta}^{(\text{Irrel})}\beta^{(k,l)}\prod_{m_{i}\in M}\left(\beta^{(m_{i},k)}\beta^{(m_{i},l)}\right)\beta^{(k,l)}\vec{\beta}^{(\text{Pre})}
    =β→(Irrel)​(β(k,l))2​∏mi∈M(β(mi,l)​β(mi,k))​β→(Pre),\displaystyle=\vec{\beta}^{(\text{Irrel})}\left(\beta^{(k,l)}\right)^{2}\prod_{m_{i}\in M}\left(\beta^{(m_{i},l)}\beta^{(m_{i},k)}\right)\vec{\beta}^{(\text{Pre})}, (46)

    which always generates a non-extreme point from Remark 9.B.1.

      after all-neighbouring series β→(NS)\vec{\beta}^{(\text{NS})}. From the first part of the proof, β→(NS)\vec{\beta}^{(\text{NS})} also cannot include any repetition. Using Lemma 9.B.5, we rearrange β→(NS)\vec{\beta}^{(\text{NS})} into the standard formation.

By putting 𝐫=β→(NS)​𝐩\mathbf{r}=\vec{\beta}^{(\text{NS})}\mathbf{p}, the state β→​𝐩\vec{\beta}\mathbf{p} is not extremal in 𝒯ETO​(β→(NS)​𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\vec{\beta}^{(\text{NS})}\mathbf{p}) and thus not extremal in 𝒯ETO​(𝐩)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}}(\mathbf{p}).

          =β(k,m)​β(m,l0)​β→(Pre-​2).\displaystyle=\beta^{(k,m)}\beta^{(m,l_{0})}\vec{\beta}^{(\text{Pre-}2)}. (53)

        2. B.

      As a result, non-neighbouring swaps are completely ruled out from the candidate of extreme point producing β\beta-swaps when starting from monotonic order states.

The sufficient condition of the theorem can be shown by recalling two properties: i) there exists at least one extreme point of 𝒯ETO\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ETO}} for each β\beta-order (Lemma 9.B.3) and ii) β\beta-swap series satisfying the conditions of the lemma are all equivalent if the pair (π,π′\pi,\pi^{\prime}) is identical (Lemma 9.B.5), which makes them the only candidate for an extreme point with order π′\pi^{\prime}.

Lastly, we note that the proof holds for π=(d,d−1,⋯,1)\pi=(d,d-1,\cdots,1) initial states since all we have used are Remark 9.B.3, Lemma 9.B.4, and Lemma 9.B.5, which hold even when the energy ordering is inverted. ∎

Chapter 10 Lie groups and Lie algebras

In this chapter, we introduce some techniques in Lie groups and Lie algebras that is necessary for deriving our results in Chapter 3.

Definition 10..1 (matrix Lie group [340]).

Let GL⁡(n)\mathrm{GL}(n) be the set of all invertible n×nn\times n matrices with complex number entries. A set of n×nn\times n matrices GG is a matrix Lie group if it is a closed subgroup of GL⁡(n)\mathrm{GL}(n).

Here, the binary operation used to define the group is the matrix multiplication. Hence, GG always includes an identity matrix 𝟙\mathmybb{1} and the inverse matrix M−1M^{-1} for any M∈GM\in G. GG is also closed under the matrix multiplication. An example includes U⁡(n)\mathrm{U}(n) the set of all n×nn\times n unitary matrices.

Now we show that a subset of U⁡(n)\mathrm{U}(n) defined by the commutation relation with respect to some n×nn\times n Hermitian matrix H0H_{0}.

G={U|U∈U(n),[U,H0]=0},\displaystyle G=\{U\,|\,U\in\mathrm{U}(n),[U,H_{0}]=0\}, (1)

is also a compact and connected Lie group [153].

If H0H_{0} is set to be the Hamiltonian HS⊗𝟙ℝ+𝟙𝕊⊗ℍℝH_{S}\otimes\mathmybb{1}_{R}+\mathmybb{1}_{S}\otimes H_{R}, this group GG becomes the Lie group corresponding to energy-preserving unitaries given the system and bath Hamiltonian, which is the unitary dilation of thermal operations in Chapter 3. Let us denote the dimensions of the system and bath Hilbert spaces as dSd_{S} and dRd_{R}.

First, we show that it is a Lie group by showing that it is a closed subgroup of U⁡(n)\mathrm{U}(n). We verify that GG is a subgroup of U⁡(n)\mathrm{U}(n) by checking the conditions:

  1. 1.

    U1​U2∈GU_{1}U_{2}\in G whenever U1,U2∈GU_{1},U_{2}\in G because

    [U1​U2,H0]=U1​[U2,H0]+[U1,H0]​U2=0.\displaystyle[U_{1}U_{2},H_{0}]=U_{1}[U_{2},H_{0}]+[U_{1},H_{0}]U_{2}=0. (2)
  2. 2.

    𝟙∈𝔾\mathmybb{1}\in G, since 𝟙\mathmybb{1} commutes with any matrix.

  3. 3.

    U†∈GU^{\dagger}\in G whenever U∈GU\in G because

    [U†,H0]=−([U,H0])†=0.\displaystyle[U^{\dagger},H_{0}]=-\left([U,H_{0}]\right)^{\dagger}=0. (3)

It is also a closed subgroup of U⁡(n)\mathrm{U}(n): if a sequence {Um}m⊂G\{U_{m}\}_{m}\subset G converges to UU, from [Um,H0]=0[U_{m},H_{0}]=0 we also have [U,H0]=0[U,H_{0}]=0.

Since the unitary group U⁡(n)\mathrm{U}(n) is compact, all its closed subgroups are also compact. Finally, we use the fact that any unitary matrix can be written as U=∑iei​θi​|i⟩​⟨i|U=\sum_{i}e^{i\theta_{i}}|{i}\rangle\!\langle{i}| for an orthonormal basis {|i⟩}i\{|{i}\rangle\}_{i} and if [U,H0]=0[U,H_{0}]=0, we can choose this basis to be an eigenbasis of H0H_{0}. By choosing the path U⁡(t)=∑iei​θi​t​|i⟩​⟨i|U(t)=\sum_{i}e^{i\theta_{i}t}|{i}\rangle\!\langle{i}| connecting U=U⁡(1)U=U(1) and 𝟙=𝕌⁡(𝟘)\mathmybb{1}=U(0), we show that GG is path-connected and thus connected [340].

We also define Lie algebras corresponding to matrix Lie groups.

Definition 10..2 (Lie algebra of a group [340]).

For a matrix Lie group GG, the corresponding Lie algebra is defined as

𝔤={K|et​K∈G,∀t∈ℝ}.\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}=\{K\,|\,e^{tK}\in G,\ \forall t\in\mathbb{R}\}. (4)

Hence, the Lie algebra corresponding to our group Eq. (1) can be written as

𝔤={−iH|H∈ℒS​R,H†=H,[H0,H]=0},\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}=\{-iH\,|\,H\in\mathcal{L}_{SR},\ H^{\dagger}=H,\ [H_{0},H]=0\}, (5)

the set of interaction Hamiltonians (times −i-i) that commute with H0H_{0}. Finally, we define the set 𝒦={K1,K2,⋯,KL}\mathcal{K}=\{K_{1},K_{2},\cdots,K_{L}\} that generates the Lie algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g}; that is, 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is the real linear span of a set consisting of all elements of 𝒦\mathcal{K} and their (repeated) commutators. The following lemma then holds for GG and 𝔤\mathfrak{g}.

Lemma 10..1 (Appendix D, Lemma 1 of [341]).

If a set {K1,K2,⋯,KL}\{K_{1},K_{2},\cdots,K_{L}\} generates a Lie algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g}, any element UU of the corresponding connected Lie group GG can be expressed as

U=∏n=1Sexp⁡(Kin​tn),\displaystyle U=\prod_{n=1}^{S}\exp(K_{i_{n}}t_{n}), (6)

where S∈ℕS\in\mathbb{N} is a finite number, in∈{1,⋯,L}i_{n}\in\{1,\cdots,L\}, and tn∈ℝt_{n}\in\mathbb{R}.

Lemma 10..1 is a stronger result than the usual results showing that eA+Be^{A+B} or e[A,B]e^{[A,B]} can be written as a product of infinite sequence of eA​te^{At} and eB​te^{Bt} for some tt. However, Lemma 10..1 lacks the explicit construction, i.e. the existence of Eq. (6) is known, but not its exact form. Therefore, the potentially infinite decomposition of eA+Be^{A+B} and e[A,B]e^{[A,B]} are often used as a universal tool for compiling desired unitaries.

Proposition 10..2 (Lie product formula [340]).

For n×nn\times n-dimensional matrices AA and BB,

(eAm​eBm)m=eA+B+O⁡(1m).\displaystyle\left(e^{\frac{A}{m}}e^{\frac{B}{m}}\right)^{m}=e^{A+B+O(\frac{1}{m})}. (7)

This implies that

limm→∞(eAm​eBm)m=eA+B.\displaystyle\lim_{m\to\infty}\left(e^{\frac{A}{m}}e^{\frac{B}{m}}\right)^{m}=e^{A+B}. (8)

This result can be extended to certain unbounded operators, in which case it is called as the Trotter product formula [342]. Higher-order formulae with better error scaling to the number of et​Ae^{tA} and et​Be^{tB} queries also exist [343].

Similarly, the exponential of a commutator can be decomposed into the exponential of each matrix.

Proposition 10..3 (product formula for commutators [341]).

For two matrices AA and BB,

e−t​A​e−t​B​et​A​et​B=et2​[A,B]+O⁡(t3).\displaystyle e^{-tA}e^{-tB}e^{tA}e^{tB}=e^{t^{2}[A,B]+O(t^{3})}. (9)

This implies that

(e−1m​A​e−1m​B​e1m​A​e1m​B)m=e[A,B]+O⁡(m−32).\displaystyle\left(e^{-\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}A}e^{-\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}B}e^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}A}e^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}B}\right)^{m}=e^{[A,B]+O(m^{-\frac{3}{2}})}. (10)

Again, higher-order formulae can be useful in practice [344].

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research.
